ME/CFS evidence atlas

Published findings in ME/CFS and related post-infectious illness, including long COVID, organised by body system, graded by replication, and linked to the hypotheses they bear on.

Rebuilt 2026-11-08 · 274 findings, 873 study entries, 31 hypotheses · Download as JSON

What is solid, and what has not held up

Findings seen in several independent cohorts are the firmest ground. Refuted ones were tested well and failed. Everything else is in between and is listed by body system below.

Replicated (27, counting each cross-listed finding once)
  • Red cell volume and total blood volume are below predicted in a large minority to about half of ME/CFS patients measured by isotope or CO-rebreathing methods.
  • Left-ventricular volumes and stroke volume are smaller in ME/CFS at rest and fall more than normal on tilt, largely in proportion to low blood volume rather than to weak heart muscle.
  • Large-artery flow-mediated dilation and microvascular post-occlusive reactive hyperaemia are reduced in ME/CFS in two independent Norwegian cohorts and by peripheral arterial tonometry in Berlin.
  • Active long COVID shows persistent complement dysregulation (terminal complex, alternative and classical pathway activation) with thromboinflammation markers, replicated across several cohorts.
  • POTS is present in roughly a fifth of ME/CFS patients on formal testing (prevalence varies 6-43%), but cerebral hypoperfusion and preload failure are found in most patients regardless of whether they meet POTS heart-rate criteria.
  • On a single maximal exercise test, ME/CFS patients have lower peak oxygen uptake (pooled about 5 ml/kg/min below controls) with a low peak heart rate (chronotropic incompetence).
  • People with long COVID have lower peak VO2 than recovered controls on average (about 5 ml/kg/min), with patterns pointing to deconditioning, chronotropic incompetence and impaired peripheral extraction rather than a cardiac or ventilatory limit.
  • Blood flow to the brain falls much more than normal during head-up tilt in ME/CFS (about 26% vs 7% in controls), including in patients whose heart rate and blood pressure stay normal.
  • Many patients over-breathe when upright and lower their end-tidal CO2. This drives part of the fall in brain blood flow, and correcting it with phenylephrine restored blood flow and working memory in one small trial.
  • Resting heart rate is higher and high-frequency heart-rate variability lower in ME/CFS. This fits reduced vagal (parasympathetic) tone.
  • Meta-analysis shows moderate-to-large deficits in information-processing speed, attention, working memory and reaction time in ME/CFS, with intact vocabulary and reasoning. Performance worsens with upright posture and after exertion.
  • Objective autonomic testing in long COVID finds cardiovascular autonomic abnormalities in most referred patients (initial orthostatic hypotension, POTS), whereas resting muscle sympathetic nerve activity is variably normal or increased.
  • Acute-infection symptom severity, and the pro-inflammatory cytokine response and genotypes behind it, predict who develops post-infective fatigue, while microbiological and psychological factors do not.
  • Common-variant genetics shows no enrichment of ME/CFS risk in any blood immune cell type, implying most immune findings are downstream consequences rather than inherited causes.
  • About 11-12% of people with confirmed EBV, Q fever or Ross River virus infection meet CFS criteria at 6 months, at a similar rate for all three pathogens, and the severity of the acute illness predicts it.
  • After infectious mononucleosis in adolescents, 13%, 7% and 4% met paediatric CFS criteria at 6, 12 and 24 months; all 13 cases still ill at 24 months were female.
  • In RECOVER-Adult, new ME/CFS (IOM criteria) developed at 2.66 per 100 person-years after SARS-CoV-2 infection vs 0.93 in uninfected participants (HR 4.93), and 4.5% of infected participants met criteria.
  • Blood metabolome differences between ME/CFS and controls are real at group level but small (mostly 0.2-0.5 SD) and partly cohort-specific; early near-perfect classification did not carry over to new cohorts.
  • Even the deepest blood omics studies sample mainly at rest, in mild-to-moderate patients, in plasma or serum only, and rarely test fresh-cell function or the 48-72 h PEM window.
  • On average, people with ME/CFS have mildly lower free cortisol (salivary awakening and morning cortisol, 24-h urinary cortisol and hair cortisol) than healthy controls.
  • ME/CFS and long COVID are more common in women (ME/CFS prevalence about 1.4% vs 0.9%; DecodeME 82% female), but genetic risk variants are not sex-specific.
  • Stool from ME/CFS patients has fewer butyrate-producing bacteria (notably Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Eubacterium rectale, Roseburia, Coprococcus) and reduced microbial capacity to make butyrate.
  • IBS is about seven times more common in ME/CFS (pooled OR 7.20; prevalence about 37%), and IBS status drives much of the measured microbiome difference.
  • ME/CFS aggregates in families: relatives of cases have about 2-3x the risk, MZ twins are more concordant than DZ twins, and familiality in a 153,803-person Dutch cohort was 42%.
  • The genome-wide DecodeME signal replicates in independent cohorts: genetic correlation 0.65-0.73 with the Million Veteran Program CFS GWAS and 0.80-0.90 with UK Biobank CFS, plus concordant directions for sub-threshold SNPs in FinnGen.
  • Placebo and natural-course improvement in ME/CFS and long-COVID trials is large (35% responders in RituxME, >40% in the LDN trial, both arms improving in IVIG, HBOT and immunoadsorption trials), so uncontrolled response rates of 50-75% are uninterpretable.
  • ME/CFS affects roughly 0.2-1% of adults depending on criteria (US 2021-22: 1.3% self-reported diagnosis; England: 0.16% with a hospital-recorded diagnosis), with women affected 3-4 times as often as men.
Refuted (18)
  • The claim that ME/CFS serum changes healthy myoblast mitochondrial respiration failed a pre-registered replication of 67 patients vs 53 controls, though a small 3D engineered-muscle study reported weaker contraction with patient serum.
  • T-cell receptor repertoires do not distinguish ME/CFS from controls, arguing against a dominant shared antigen-driven clonal expansion.
  • B-cell depletion with rituximab failed in a 151-patient placebo-controlled trial, after positive small phase II results.
  • The most-replicated single cytokine finding, elevated TGF-beta, is largely a blood-handling artefact driven by platelet activation during centrifugation.
  • Blocking IL-1 with anakinra for four weeks did not improve fatigue in CFS, and did not change circulating cytokines beyond IL-1Ra itself.
  • Elevated IgG against beta2-adrenergic and M3/M4 muscarinic receptors, reported in about 30% of patients by ELISA, is not reproduced by unbiased high-throughput antigen profiling.
  • Removing autoantibodies by immunoadsorption helps in open-label cohorts but fails against sham control, and antibody removal does not predict who improves.
  • Three randomised placebo-controlled trials of 15-25 days of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir in established long COVID (STOP-PASC n=155, PAX LC n=100, RECOVER-VITAL n=959; about 1,214 people in total) found no benefit on primary or secondary outcomes.
  • Temelimab, an antibody against HERV-W envelope protein, did not reduce fatigue versus placebo in a 203-person RCT of HERV-W-positive post-COVID patients.
  • The 2009 report of the mouse retrovirus XMRV in 67% of CFS patients was a laboratory contamination artefact: blinded multi-lab and original-investigator studies found no XMRV/pMLV, and the Science paper was retracted.
  • Fludrocortisone, a synthetic salt-retaining steroid, did not improve CFS with neurally mediated hypotension in a 100-person RCT, and failed again in combination with hydrocortisone.
  • Before DecodeME, small GWAS and candidate-gene studies (GRIK2, NPAS2, TPPP, TRA locus and many others) produced no association that replicated in UK Biobank or later cohorts.
  • The anti-HERV-W envelope antibody temelimab did not improve fatigue versus placebo in 203 HERV-W-positive long-COVID patients.
  • The first sizeable placebo-controlled trial of low-dose naltrexone in post-COVID ME/CFS (66 vs 71, 16 weeks, up to 4.5 mg) found no fatigue benefit, with over 40% improving on placebo.
  • Ivabradine lowered standing heart rate but did not improve symptoms in 181 people with long-COVID POTS (RECOVER-AUTONOMIC), despite an earlier positive 22-person crossover in hyperadrenergic POTS.
  • Fludrocortisone did not beat placebo in a 100-person RCT in CFS with neurally mediated hypotension; midodrine reduces orthostatic heart rate acutely in small POTS studies but has no ME/CFS outcome trial.
  • Clonidine did not improve activity or symptoms in adolescent CFS (NorCAPITAL RCT) and trended toward fewer steps, despite lowering noradrenaline and CRP.
  • Fluoxetine did not improve fatigue in CFS in two RCTs.

For an overview, read the summaries by body system, then the hypotheses. To find a specific result, use the search box, the grade filters or the study index.

Replicated Found in several independent cohorts (29) Several studies More than one study, not yet independently settled (63) Early One or two studies, usually small (104) Contested Conflicting results or method doubts (57) Refuted Well-designed work found no effect (21)

Overview by body system

Each bar shows how the findings in one body system are graded. Bar length is the number of findings; green segments are the ones that have replicated.

Blood flow, vessels and blood

Circulation when upright is the most consistent abnormality: low blood volume, small stroke volume and a large fall in brain blood flow.

Strongest

  • Low red cell and total blood volume
  • Brain blood flow falls about 26% on tilt, vs 7%
  • Small heart volumes and stroke volume
  • Reduced vessel dilation (FMD, PORH)
  • Over-breathing when upright
  • Complement activation in long COVID

Disputed

  • Microclots
  • Platelet activation
  • Complement in ME/CFS
Full summary

The most consistent vascular findings in ME/CFS concern circulation when upright: cerebral blood flow falls much more than normal on tilt, stroke volume is low, red-cell and blood volume are below predicted in a large minority to about half, and during exercise the heart is under-filled (preload failure). These are reported by several groups, though the cerebral blood flow and invasive exercise data each come mostly from one centre, and a 2026 study found blood volume did not predict who has orthostatic abnormalities. Reduced endothelial function (FMD, PORH) has been found in three independent cohorts, and newer work shows fewer muscle capillaries than bed rest would explain and narrowed retinal vessels in post-COVID ME/CFS. Complement activation is replicated in long COVID but inconsistent in ME/CFS. Microclots remain contested on method, and pooled blood proteomics do not show raised coagulation, platelet or endothelial-activation proteins.

Muscle, exertion and energy

Exercise capacity is lower and recovery takes days; how much is a muscle defect rather than poor delivery is open.

Strongest

  • Lower peak oxygen uptake
  • PEM starts hours to a day later and lasts days
  • Low cardiac filling and poor oxygen extraction
  • Faster fatigue on repeated grip
  • Not explained by deconditioning

Disputed or refuted

  • Worse on a second exercise test
  • Slow muscle pH recovery
  • Low mitochondrial function in blood cells
  • Patient serum impairs healthy muscle cells
Full summary

People with ME/CFS reliably have lower aerobic capacity and a low peak heart rate on exercise testing, and they report delayed, prolonged PEM that took about two weeks to resolve after a 2-day test. Whether performance measurably drops on a second test 24 hours later is now contested: several linked groups and two meta-analyses say yes, mainly at the ventilatory threshold, while a 2026 replication found no change. Invasive testing points to poor cardiac filling and poor oxygen extraction, and newer biopsy work from one Amsterdam group finds fewer oxidative fibres, fewer capillaries and lower mitochondrial capacity in ME/CFS that bed rest does not reproduce, plus post-exertion muscle damage and amyloid-containing deposits in long COVID. Mitochondrial studies in blood cells disagree in direction, and the idea that patient serum alters muscle-cell mitochondria failed a large pre-registered replication (Ryback 2026). Post-exertion omics (metabolomics, proteomics, EVs) show resting differences and recovery-phase changes, but within-person exercise effects are modest and mostly unreplicated.

Nervous system and brain

Brain blood flow, autonomic tone and cognition are measurably affected; brain imaging and inflammation markers are inconsistent.

Strongest

  • Brain blood flow falls on tilt
  • Higher heart rate, lower heart-rate variability
  • Slower processing speed and attention
  • Raised brain lactate
  • Small-fibre neuropathy in long COVID

Disputed

  • Microglial activation on PET
  • Small-fibre neuropathy in ME/CFS
  • Altered 'effort preference'
  • Nerve injury markers in blood or CSF
Full summary

The most consistent nervous-system findings in ME/CFS are physiological rather than anatomical. Brain blood flow drops more than normal when patients are upright, often with over-breathing (low CO2), and resting heart-rate variability is lower; both are seen across several independent labs. Small-fibre nerve loss on skin biopsy is common in referral clinics (roughly 30-55%), but the main controlled NIH study found no difference, and nobody has yet shown that nerve loss explains symptoms. Brain imaging gives many positive but small and mostly unreplicated results: raised ventricular lactate (mostly one group), raised brain temperature (one study), TSPO-PET neuroinflammation (one positive and one negative ME/CFS study), and newer diffusion MRI signals. Structural MRI, routine sleep studies and markers of nerve injury are mostly normal or inconsistent. The NIH 'effort preference' interpretation has been seriously challenged, because patients in that study often could not complete the hard task. Claims about craniocervical instability rest on uncontrolled clinic series and case reports.

Immune system

Many immune differences are reported and few replicate; genetics finds no risk enrichment in immune cells.

Strongest

  • Severe acute illness predicts who goes on to ME/CFS
  • No genetic enrichment in immune cells
  • Exhaustion features in CD8 T cells
  • Long COVID IgG transfers symptoms to mice
  • IgG subclass deficiency in a minority

Disputed or refuted

  • Low NK-cell killing
  • Adrenergic and muscarinic autoantibodies
  • Raised TGF-beta (a handling artefact)
  • Rituximab

Early leads

  • Plasma-cell depletion (daratumumab)
  • Reduced TRPM3 current in NK cells
Full summary

Immunology is the oldest and most heavily worked area of ME/CFS research, and the one with the widest gap between positive reports and independent replication. Reduced natural-killer-cell killing is the most repeated finding (meta-analytic Hedges g about 0.96 across 28 papers), yet the largest standardised multi-site attempt (MCAM, 174 vs 86) and two careful phenotyping studies found nothing, so the honest grade is 'contested and not usable as a test'. Several newer cell-level findings are more consistent in direction than in detail: CD8 T-cell exhaustion programmes, shifts in B-cell maturation (more naive, fewer switched-memory), monocyte dysregulation, and an exaggerated innate response to microbial stimulation that worsens after exercise. Cytokines look disturbed in aggregate (TNF, IL-2, IL-4, TGF-beta, CRP in meta-analysis) but no single cytokine survives as a marker, TGF-beta turned out to be largely a blood-handling artefact, and the clearest pattern is that abnormalities depend on illness duration (Hornig 2015) and severity (Montoya 2017) rather than on diagnosis alone. The autoimmunity strand has had the clearest negative resolution: GPCR autoantibodies against beta2/M3/M4 receptors are not reproduced by unbiased antigen profiling, removing them by immunoadsorption fails against sham, rituximab failed in a 151-patient RCT, and BC007's larger trial failed; what survives is narrower and interesting - patient IgG does things to endothelial mitochondria and, in long COVID, transfers pain and fatigue-like phenotypes to mice, and plasma-cell depletion with daratumumab produced striking but uncontrolled responses in 6 of 10 patients. Common-variant genetics (DecodeME) shows no enrichment in any blood immune cell type, which pushes most of these immune findings toward being consequences or state markers rather than inherited causes.

Infection and viruses

Infection is an established trigger; the evidence that a virus is still active is much weaker.

Strongest

  • About 1 in 10 meet criteria after EBV, Q fever or Ross River virus
  • New ME/CFS after COVID at 2.66 per 100 person-years
  • SARS-CoV-2 antigen persists in a minority
  • Standard herpesvirus serology does not differ

Disputed or refuted

  • Paxlovid in established long COVID
  • Temelimab against HERV-W
  • XMRV (contamination)
  • Enterovirus in stomach biopsies
Full summary

The most solid finding in this area is about onset: about 1 in 10 people meet ME/CFS criteria six months after several unrelated infections (EBV, Q fever, Ross River virus, Giardia, SARS-CoV-2), and how severe the first illness was predicts this better than psychological factors do. Post-COVID cohorts confirm that infection raises the rate of new ME/CFS several-fold. Whether any virus is still active in people who already have ME/CFS is far less clear. Blood antibody and PCR studies of herpesviruses give mixed results. Tissue findings for enterovirus, HHV-6 and SARS-CoV-2 are small or unreplicated, though some of them are striking. SARS-CoV-2 antigen and RNA do persist in a minority of people for months, but three randomised trials of nirmatrelvir in established long COVID (about 1,200 people) were negative, and antiviral trials in ME/CFS are tiny and unreplicated. The XMRV episode, a retrovirus finding that turned out to be lab contamination, is a reminder that one striking virus finding needs blinded multi-lab replication.

Metabolism and blood omics

Blood chemistry differs at group level, but the effects are small and most single markers and classifiers do not replicate.

Strongest

  • Real but small metabolome differences
  • Lower aromatic lactates
  • Lower indole-3-propionate
  • Lower plasmalogens
  • Muscle-protein set modestly lower in blood

Disputed

  • A uniform 'hypometabolic' state
  • Classifiers outside their training cohort
  • DNA methylation differences
  • Kynurenine pathway disruption
Full summary

Blood metabolomics and proteomics consistently find that ME/CFS patients differ from controls on average, but the differences are small (mostly 0.2-0.5 SD), partly cohort-specific, and confounded by medication, caffeine, diet and sample handling. The better-supported signals are modest: lower plasmalogens and some phosphatidylcholines, slightly lower carnitines, lower gut-derived IPA, lower aromatic lactates (a new cross-cohort re-analysis finding), higher methionine sulfoxide, and lower muscle-derived proteins in blood that are not explained by activity. Bigger claims, such as a uniform hypometabolic 'cell danger' state, an IDO metabolic trap, divergent metabolic or proteomic responses to exercise, reproducible methylation signatures, and diagnostic classifiers with near-perfect accuracy, have not held up in independent data or remain untested outside the original lab. No omics test is ready for diagnosis. The largest gaps are severe patients, sampling during the 48-72 h PEM window, disease controls, and pairing omics with fresh-cell function.

Hormones

Cortisol is slightly low and the hormones that should restore blood volume fail to rise; hormone replacement has helped little.

Strongest

  • Mildly lower cortisol
  • Blunted cortisol response to challenge
  • Renin and aldosterone not raised despite low volume
  • More common in women

Disputed or refuted

  • Hydrocortisone
  • Fludrocortisone
  • Low cortisol in long COVID

Early leads

  • Low vasopressin after fluid deprivation
  • Adrenal and pituitary disease in a minority
Full summary

The most consistent hormone finding in ME/CFS is a mildly under-active stress-hormone (HPA) axis: on average cortisol is slightly low in saliva, urine and hair, and feedback suppression is exaggerated. A 2026 meta-analysis of 46 case-control studies confirms this pattern. The shifts are small, most patients fall inside normal reference ranges, and they may be a consequence of illness, sleep disruption or inactivity rather than a cause. Low-dose hydrocortisone gave at best a small, short-lived benefit with side effects, and fludrocortisone failed in two large trials. Newer leads concern the hormones that hold water and salt in the body: low vasopressin and a 'renin-aldosterone paradox' that would fit the low blood volume seen in many patients. These come from small or uncontrolled studies, and the vasopressin finding is not matched by copeptin, which is the more reliable test. The female preponderance (about 1.5 to 3 times more women) is solid, but genetics shows no sex-specific risk variants, and the role of sex hormones, menopause and gynaecological conditions is still only descriptive.

Gut and microbiome

Butyrate-producing bacteria are reduced and IBS is common, but genetics does not point to the gut as a cause.

Strongest

  • Fewer butyrate-producing bacteria
  • IBS about seven times more common
  • Overgrowth of R. gnavus and related species
  • Lower indole-3-propionate

Disputed

  • Bacterial translocation markers
  • Bacteria tracking severity

Early leads

  • Dysbiosis fades after about 10 years
  • Gut metabolites not causal by genetics
Full summary

Gut bacteria differ between people with ME/CFS and healthy controls more consistently than almost any blood measure. Fewer butyrate-producing species (Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, Coprococcus, Anaerostipes, Eubacterium rectale) and more Ruminococcus gnavus-type species appear in at least four independent cohorts across three labs, including a pre-specified test in the NIH cohort. The same pattern appears in long COVID. Blood levels of a gut-made metabolite, indole-3-propionate (IPA), are lower in four of four plasma cohorts, and re-analysis traces this to the R. gnavus-type overgrowth. What is not established is whether any of this causes symptoms. Dysbiosis is milder in long-standing illness, does not track severity reliably, and genetically predicted gut metabolite levels do not change ME/CFS risk. Markers of a 'leaky gut' (LPS, sCD14) come from a handful of studies, and the only randomised faecal transplant trial (n=11) was negative. Larger trials are under way.

Genetics

Risk is heritable and polygenic, and the signal sits in neurons rather than immune cells.

Strongest

  • Runs in families
  • DecodeME signal replicates in other cohorts
  • 8 genome-wide loci in DecodeME
  • Enriched in brain and neurons
  • Overlap with chronic pain, IBS and migraine

Disputed or refuted

  • HLA associations
  • TRPM3 variants
  • Early candidate genes
Full summary

ME/CFS runs in families, and twin, genealogy and three-generation cohort studies put familial or heritable risk at roughly 20 to 50%. In 2025 DecodeME (15,579 cases) found the first eight robust genome-wide loci, with SNP heritability of about 8 to 10%. Each variant shifts risk only slightly (odds ratios 1.07 to 1.10), so no gene test can diagnose or predict ME/CFS. The overall genetic signal replicates in independent biobanks (MVP, FinnGen, UK Biobank), but the individual loci mostly do not yet, partly because those biobanks use loose case definitions. Across several analyses the signal points to neurons in the brain (and possibly the pituitary), not blood immune cells. It overlaps strongly with chronic pain, fibromyalgia, IBS and migraine, and partly with depression, though the specific ME/CFS loci do not share causal variants with depression. Earlier small candidate-gene and HLA findings mostly failed to replicate. Several 2025–2026 follow-ups (Mendelian randomisation, rare variants, a UK Biobank/All of Us GWAS) are preprints that still need confirmation.

Treatment trials and natural history

No treatment has a large, positive, placebo-controlled trial, and placebo response is large.

Strongest

  • Large placebo and natural-course improvement
  • Full recovery is uncommon
  • Graded exercise reported as harmful

Failed controlled trials

  • Rituximab
  • Immunoadsorption
  • Paxlovid
  • Low-dose naltrexone
  • Ivabradine

Early leads

  • Daratumumab
  • Pyridostigmine
  • Rapamycin
Full summary

No treatment has replicated, placebo-controlled evidence of benefit in ME/CFS or post-COVID ME/CFS. Since 2019 the large, well-controlled trials have been negative: rituximab, Paxlovid (three trials), immunoadsorption against sham (two trials), ivabradine for long-COVID POTS, temelimab, and low-dose naltrexone for fatigue. The positive signals (daratumumab, cyclophosphamide, low-dose rapamycin, low-dose aripiprazole, single-dose pyridostigmine, 40-session HBOT) come from small, open-label or single-centre studies, and they need to be read against placebo response rates of 35-40% or more. Graded exercise is no longer recommended in England (NICE 2021), and patient surveys and a German rehab study report frequent worsening, while pacing and volume/compression measures are the most highly rated but untested by trials. Natural history data show low full recovery in adults (median ~5%), prevalence of ~0.2-1%, a female excess of 3-4:1, no clear rise in all-cause mortality, and a marked rise in suicide.

Hypotheses

The main explanations proposed for ME/CFS. Several can be true at once, and many describe different links in the same chain. The bar beside each shows the grades of the atlas findings linked to it, which includes findings that count against it. Tap one to open it.

Active (16) · Speculative (7) · Weakened (6) · Largely refuted (2)

ActiveSupported by current data and still being tested

Autonomic dysfunction and small-fibre neuropathyDamage to small autonomic and sensory nerves impairs vascular tone, heart rate control and pain processing.37+2 −3

Where it stands. Autonomic abnormalities are common and replicated, but small-fibre neuropathy rates vary widely between centres, and treatments aimed at heart rate or autoimmune nerve damage have not helped.

A sizeable minority of ME/CFS and POTS patients have reduced intraepidermal nerve fibre density on skin biopsy. Loss of sympathetic fibres to veins would cause venous pooling and preload failure; sensory fibre loss would add pain. The neuropathy may be immune-mediated after infection. It is a likely contributor in a subgroup rather than a universal mechanism.

Working modelStep 2 · Brain and autonomic controlStep 8 · Sympathetic arousal, poor sleep
Proposed byOaklander (MGH), Systrom, Novak, Blitshteyn

Evidence for 2

  • Small-fibre neuropathy frequent in biopsied iCPET patients (Joseph 2021)
  • POTS and low HRV common in ME/CFS

Evidence against 3

  • IVIG negative vs albumin in autoimmune POTS (Vernino 2024)
  • Prevalence estimates vary widely between centres
  • Ivabradine trial negative for symptoms

If true, we should see

  • Low IENFD on skin biopsy
  • Abnormal QSART/sudomotor tests
  • Response to IVIG in immune-mediated subgroup

Tests that would settle it

  • Population-representative skin biopsy study with blinded counting
  • IVIG trial restricted to biopsy-proven SFN with function endpoints

Mitochondrial / energy metabolism impairmentCells cannot produce energy normally, especially during exertion, causing early lactate and PEM.54+4 −3

Where it stands. Many signals point at energy metabolism, but most are early or contested, and the claim that patient serum impairs muscle mitochondria failed a pre-registered replication.

Several lines suggest impaired pyruvate dehydrogenase, Complex V inefficiency or reduced oxidative capacity. This would force early reliance on glycolysis and slow recovery. It may be intrinsic or secondary to poor perfusion or circulating factors.

  • Abnormal mitochondrial respiration in patient cells
  • Benefit from metabolic supplements

  • Muscle 31P-MRS and biopsy respiration before/after PEM vs deconditioned controls

Low blood volume and preload failureToo little blood returns to the heart, especially upright and during exercise, reducing cardiac output and brain flow.29+5 −4

Where it stands. The physiology is among the best replicated in the field. What is missing is a sham-controlled trial showing that restoring volume or preload improves symptoms.

Isotope and CO-rebreathing studies show reduced plasma and red-cell volume, and invasive CPET shows low right-heart filling pressure during exercise in many patients. Upright, this lowers stroke volume and brain blood flow (seen on tilt even without POTS). It could stem from small-fibre neuropathy, low ADH/renin response, or reduced red-cell production. It explains orthostatic intolerance well; whether it explains PEM is less clear.

Working modelStep 3 · Low blood volumeStep 5 · Tissue under-perfusion
Proposed bySystrom/Joseph (Harvard), van Campen/Visser (Netherlands), Levine/Fu (POTS), Rowe (Johns Hopkins)

Evidence for 5

  • Preload failure common in iCPET series (Joseph 2021, n=160)
  • Cerebral blood flow falls on tilt in ~90% of patients (van Campen 2020)
  • Single-dose pyridostigmine maintained cardiac output on repeat iCPET (Joseph 2022)
  • Patients rate fluids and compression among the most helpful (Eckey 2025)
  • Low reticulocytes with adequate iron in postviral fatigue (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis, FinnGen; unreplicated)

Evidence against 4

  • Fludrocortisone negative in RCT (Rowe 2001)
  • Ivabradine reduced HR without symptom benefit (RECOVER-AUTONOMIC 2026)
  • No sham-controlled trial of IV saline
  • Blood-volume hormones normal in proteomics (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis)

If true, we should see

  • Low measured blood volume
  • Low RAP on iCPET
  • CBF drop on tilt
  • Symptom relief with fluids, compression and pyridostigmine

Tests that would settle it

  • Sham-controlled IV saline crossover with function endpoints
  • Results of LIFT (pyridostigmine x LDN)
  • Blood volume measurement before/after illness onset in prospective post-COVID cohorts

Innate immune hyperactivationOngoing activation of monocytes, interferon and cytokine pathways sustains symptoms.41+2 −3

Where it stands. Cytokine findings in ME/CFS are small and poorly replicated, and steroid trials in long COVID did not help. Activation may be strongest early in the illness.

Cytokine profiles differ early in ME/CFS, with an activated pattern in the first three years that later fades. Persistent interferon or inflammasome activity could cause sickness symptoms and metabolic shifts. Effects in blood are inconsistent across studies.

For: T-cell and macrophage infiltration in long COVID muscle after exertion (Appelman 2024); exaggerated innate responses and complement after exercise (Che 2025); complement up in male EVs (Glass 2025). For: Exaggerated whole-blood responses to microbial antigens, worse 24 h after exercise and correlated with symptom intensity (Che/Lipkin 2025, 56 vs 52); Q fever fatigue syndrome PBMCs over-produce IL-6, TNF and IL-1beta on antigen stimulation; monocyte dysregulation in scRNA (Vu 2024); meta-analytic small elevations of TNF, IL-2, IL-4, CRP; 17 cytokines rising with severity (Montoya 2017); UK Biobank inflammation and liver/insulin markers shifted in both sexes. Against: IL-1 blockade with anakinra gave no clinical benefit and changed no cytokine but IL-1Ra; the best-replicated single cytokine (TGF-beta) is a platelet/centrifugation artefact; re-analysis of five blood RNA cohorts found no gene set passing FDR and interferon only nominally up (meta p=0.12); monocyte scRNA findings do not survive independent re-analysis of the same data; no immune cell type is genetically enriched.

Against: Few studies measure the acute immune response prospectively, and baseline cytokines have predicted outcome inconsistently.
  • Gut and microbiome. For: Raised LPS/LBP/sCD14 in some studies. In BioMapAI, the microbiome links to MAIT/γδT inflammatory cells. Against: Re-analysis found 0/622 immune-module associations at q<0.1. The Quadram feasibility study found reduced anti-microbial IgG.

Gut dysbiosisAltered gut microbiota and barrier function drive immune activation and metabolic changes.23+4 −3

Where it stands. Loss of butyrate producers is replicated, but Mendelian randomisation finds no causal effect of the gut metabolites tested, and dysbiosis fades with illness duration.

Butyrate producers such as Faecalibacterium prausnitzii are reduced in ME/CFS, and short-duration patients show stronger dysbiosis. Microbial products may affect immunity and metabolism. A synbiotic improved several long-COVID symptoms in one trial. Dysbiosis could also be a consequence of illness, diet and inactivity.

Proposed byLipkin and Hornig (Columbia), Unutmaz (JAX), Hong Kong SIM01 group

Evidence for 4

  • Reduced butyrate producers (Guo 2023, n=106 vs 91)
  • Dysbiosis stronger early (Xiong 2023)
  • R. gnavus/F. plautii overgrowth replicates and explains low IPA (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis)
  • SIM01 synbiotic positive in long COVID (Lau 2024, n=463)

Evidence against 3

  • MR finds no causal effect of IPA and related metabolites (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis)
  • Aromatic lactate deficit not explained by gut bacteria (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis)
  • Faecal transplant data anecdotal

If true, we should see

  • Reduced butyrate producers
  • Microbial metabolites tracking symptoms
  • Benefit from microbiome interventions

Tests that would settle it

  • Replication of SIM01-type trial in ME/CFS
  • Prospective microbiome sampling before onset

Capillary and microvascular damageCapillaries in muscle and elsewhere are structurally damaged or rarefied, limiting oxygen delivery.23+4 −2

Where it stands. Biopsy evidence for fewer or thickened capillaries is consistent but comes from small studies, mostly from one network, and no treatment aimed at it has a clean controlled result.

Muscle biopsies show thickened capillary basement membranes and fewer capillaries, and long-COVID studies show capillary loss under the tongue and in the retina. If blood reaches the tissue but bypasses capillary beds or cannot exchange oxygen, extraction falls, as seen in the 'high-flow' iCPET phenotype. This would explain exertional intolerance unrelated to fitness. Cause could be immune, complement or viral damage to pericytes.

Working modelStep 4 · Vessels and capillaries
Proposed byWüst group (VU Amsterdam), Appelman/van Vugt (Amsterdam UMC), Systrom (high-flow preload failure)

Evidence for 4

  • Capillary basement membrane thickening and lower capillarisation in ME/CFS and post-COVID biopsies (Wüst group 2025 preprint)
  • Muscle damage, amyloid deposits and mitochondrial drop after exercise in long COVID (Appelman 2024)
  • Reduced oxygen extraction in preload failure (Joseph 2021)
  • 40-session HBOT improved symptoms in one RCT (Zilberman-Itskovich 2022)

Evidence against 2

  • Biopsy studies are small and largely from one network
  • 10-session HBOT trial negative (HOT-LoCO 2025)

If true, we should see

  • Low oxygen extraction on iCPET
  • Basement membrane thickening and capillary rarefaction on biopsy
  • Improvement with treatments that repair microvasculature

Tests that would settle it

  • Blinded biopsy morphometry in large ME/CFS vs deconditioned controls
  • Correlation of capillary measures with 2-day CPET in the same patients

Neuroinflammation (microglial activation)Activated microglia and astrocytes in the brain produce fatigue, cognitive problems and pain.26+3 −3

Where it stands. PET evidence splits: positive in one small ME/CFS study and one long COVID study, negative in two others, one of which found the signal in muscle instead.

PET and MR spectroscopy studies suggest brain inflammation in ME/CFS and long COVID. Inflammation in brainstem or limbic regions could generate sickness behaviour and PEM. Results conflict and tracer studies are small.

Where it stands. The DecodeME signal replicates and points at neurons. Individual loci and how they act are still unconfirmed.

DecodeME (15,579 cases) found genome-wide significant loci, with tissue enrichment in brain and pituitary rather than immune tissues. The overall genetic signal replicates in the Million Veteran Program and FinnGen. Candidate genes include pain-sensitisation and immune-response genes. Genetics marks susceptibility, not necessarily the ongoing mechanism.

Herpesvirus reactivation (EBV, HHV-6)Latent herpesviruses reactivate after a trigger and drive immune and neurological dysfunction.23+4 −3

Where it stands. Herpesviruses are clear triggers, but evidence of ongoing reactivation rests on antibody patterns that track replication poorly, and no antiviral trial has met its primary endpoint.

EBV and HHV-6 are carried latently by most adults. In ME/CFS, abortive reactivation or high antibody responses are reported, and EBV is a common trigger of onset. Reactivated virus or its proteins (e.g. dUTPase) could activate innate immunity. Antivirals have shown modest benefit in small selected groups.

  • Genetically higher EBV DNA load suggestive risk factor (OR 1.59, MVP; Solving ME/CFS re-analysis)
  • Elevated EBV gp42 reactivity in antigen profiling (Germain 2025)

Evidence against 3

  • STOP-PASC found no EBV reactivation differences (Maestri 2025 preprint)
  • Antibody titres poor marker of active replication
  • No replicated antiviral RCT

If true, we should see

  • Antivirals help selected patients
  • Genetic predisposition to EBV control affects risk

Tests that would settle it

  • Antiviral RCT selected by viral PCR/early antigen, not IgG
  • Prospective serial viral load from acute infection through ME/CFS onset

Endothelial dysfunctionThe lining of blood vessels fails to dilate and regulate flow, so tissues are under-supplied during effort.22+3 −3

Where it stands. Reduced vessel dilation is replicated in Norwegian cohorts, but it is an average difference with wide overlap, and the antibody treatments aimed at its proposed cause have failed.

Endothelial cells normally release nitric oxide and other signals so arteries widen when tissue needs more blood. In ME/CFS this response is reported to be blunted, possibly through autoantibodies, inflammation or oxidative stress. Poor flow regulation would leave muscle and brain short of oxygen during exertion and could set off PEM. It is a mechanism layer rather than a root cause, and it could result from several upstream triggers.

Working modelStep 4 · Vessels and capillariesStep 5 · Tissue under-perfusion
Proposed byScheibenbogen and Wirth (Charité), Fluge and Mella (Bergen), Sandvik/Sørland (Bergen)

Evidence for 3

  • Flow-mediated dilation 5.1% vs 8.2% (Sandvik 2023, n=39); reduced endothelial function in CycloME substudy (Sørland 2021)
  • Patient IgG fragments endothelial mitochondria vs MS and healthy IgG (Prusty 2026, single lab)
  • Lower vessel-wall/connective-tissue proteins (ITGAV, NOTCH3, TGF-beta set) in 4 cohorts and long COVID (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis)

Evidence against 3

  • Effects are average differences with large overlap; deconditioning not always excluded
  • BC007 and immunoadsorption (aimed at vasoactive GPCR antibodies) failed controlled trials
  • Vericiguat (VERI-LONG) results not reported

If true, we should see

  • Lower flow-mediated dilation and reactive hyperaemia in patients
  • Endothelial markers or patient IgG effects on endothelial cells in vitro
  • Vasoactive treatments improving exercise tolerance

Tests that would settle it

  • Within-person FMD before and during PEM versus sedentary controls
  • Placebo-controlled trial of a vasoactive drug with 2-day CPET endpoint

Immune (T-cell) exhaustionChronic antigen stimulation leaves CD8 T cells and NK cells exhausted and less able to clear infection.25+3 −2

Where it stands. Exhaustion features in CD8 T cells are reported by more than one group, but immune-cell data give few signals that reproduce across cohorts.

Exhausted T cells express inhibitory receptors and lose function after prolonged stimulation. In ME/CFS, single-cell and epigenetic data suggest CD8 T cells are primed toward exhaustion, and NK cytotoxicity is reduced. This fits with a persistent antigen or reactivating virus. It may be consequence rather than cause.

Evidence against 2

If true, we should see

  • Reduced NK cytotoxicity
  • Changes after exercise provocation

Tests that would settle it

  • Replication of exhaustion signatures in independent cohorts
  • Longitudinal tracking from infection to ME/CFS onset

Complement activation and thromboinflammationChronic complement activation damages vessel lining and platelets, so clotting and inflammation feed each other.19+2 −3

Where it stands. Replicated in long COVID, thin and inconsistent in ME/CFS. No complement inhibitor has been tested.

The terminal complement complex is persistently activated in active long COVID, with signs of haemolysis, platelet activation and monocyte-platelet aggregates. This could injure endothelium and capillaries. It is the best-replicated blood abnormality in long COVID but is less studied in classic ME/CFS.

Sodium-calcium overload in muscle (Wirth & Scheibenbogen)Under-perfused muscle accumulates sodium and then calcium via the sodium-calcium exchanger, damaging mitochondria and causing PEM.7+3 −3

Where it stands. A coherent mechanism with little direct data: one 12-person sodium MRI study, and its proposed upstream antibody trigger has weakened.

The model proposes that beta2-adrenergic dysfunction (perhaps via autoantibodies) and vasoconstriction reduce muscle blood flow. Hypoxic muscle relies on glycolysis; protons are exported by NHE1, loading the cell with sodium, which reverses the sodium-calcium exchanger and raises intracellular calcium, injuring mitochondria. This cycle explains delayed, prolonged PEM and suggests drugs that block NHE1 or reduce sodium loading. Elements are testable with 23Na-MRI.

Using 2-day CPET with blood sampling, the Cornell group reports that patients fail to mount and resolve normal exercise responses in plasma proteins, metabolites and immune cells, with CD8 T-cell exhaustion features. Where it stands. Accurate as a catalogue of abnormalities, but broad enough to be hard to falsify.

Two influential reviews catalogue overlapping findings: neuroinflammation, immune activation and exhaustion, autoantibodies, impaired energy metabolism, endothelial and autonomic dysfunction, and gut dysbiosis. They argue the two illnesses are variants of the same post-infectious process and that research on each informs the other. It is a synthesis, not a single falsifiable mechanism.

Where it stands. Fits the symptoms and the post-infectious onset, but there is no direct evidence of persistent vagal signalling, and anti-inflammatory trials have been negative.

During infection, cytokines signal to the brain and cause fatigue, malaise and withdrawal. If a local infection or inflammation near the vagus nerve persists, or the brain's set point changes, sickness behaviour could persist. This frames many symptoms but is hard to test directly.

For: Central fatigability (brain fails to ramp up motor drive), lower CSF catechol metabolites, altered task activation after exertion: consistent with a brain-level 'sickness' state. For: Dubbo cohort: 11% met CFS criteria six months after three different pathogens with a stereotyped phenotype predicted by acute illness severity, not by pathogen or psychological factors; PBMC IL-1beta and IL-6 release tracks acute fever, malaise, pain, fatigue, mood and concentration; IFN-gamma and IL-10 polymorphisms synergistically set severity and duration; interferon-alpha reliably produces neurovegetative fatigue within two weeks (Capuron 2002) and persistent fatigue in a third of patients, predicted by higher baseline IL-10 and a bigger early surge (Russell 2019). Against: The model explains onset far better than persistence: cytokines are not persistently abnormal in long-duration illness (Hornig 2015), cytokine inhibition does not help, and the acute cytokine signal fades while the illness does not.
  • Infection and viruses. For: Stereotyped phenotype across pathogens, with no ongoing pathogen required (Dubbo, QFS doxycycline failure). Against: Does not explain why only ~10% persist, or tissue-specific viral findings.
  • Hormones. For: Hypocortisolism with enhanced feedback fits a chronic post-infectious or inflammatory state. Against: This cannot be separated from deconditioning or sleep effects in cross-sectional data.
  • Treatment trials and natural history. For: Large placebo responses show symptoms are modifiable by expectation and context (not specific to this hypothesis). Against: PACE effects confined to self-report and not durable; GET rated harmful by patients; rehab worsened 42/97 in CFS_CARE.

Cell danger response (Naviaux)Cells stuck in a protective low-energy 'danger' state after a threat fail to complete the healing cycle.9+2 −2

Where it stands. A broad framework whose main metabolomic prediction, uniform hypometabolism, does not reproduce in later cohorts.

The cell danger response (CDR) is a conserved metabolic reaction to threat in which mitochondria shift from energy production to defence, with extracellular ATP (purinergic) signalling. Naviaux proposes that ME/CFS is a persistent CDR, a hypometabolic state like dauer. His 2016 metabolomics found most altered metabolites decreased, consistent with hypometabolism. Antipurinergic drugs such as suramin are the proposed test.

Proposed byRobert Naviaux (UCSD)

Evidence for 2

  • Naviaux 2016 PNAS: 80% of altered metabolites decreased (n=45 vs 39)
  • Rapamycin responders show purine metabolism changes (Gile 2026)

Evidence against 2

  • Metabolomic findings vary across cohorts; Hoel/Germain datasets do not show uniform hypometabolism
  • No ME/CFS trial of suramin

If true, we should see

  • Hypometabolic metabolomic profile
  • Raised extracellular ATP/purinergic signalling
  • Response to antipurinergic therapy

Tests that would settle it

  • Low-dose suramin RCT in ME/CFS
  • Replication of hypometabolic signature with standardised fasting samples

Where it stands. Rests on one uncontrolled series. It is cheap to test properly with stimulated copeptin.

A 2025 study reported undetectable vasopressin in most patients despite high plasma osmolality. If true, this would explain polyuria, thirst and low blood volume, and suggest desmopressin for a subgroup. DecodeME tissue enrichment pointing to pituitary gives indirect support.

Where it stands. Case series only, from selected referral samples, and surgery carries real risk without a controlled trial.

Some patients, often with hypermobility, are reported to have craniocervical instability or intracranial hypertension compressing the brainstem. IDO metabolic trap (Phair, Davis)A bistable tryptophan-kynurenine circuit, set by IDO1/IDO2 variants and substrate inhibition, flips into a persistent low-tryptophan state.7+2 −3

Where it stands. Genetics and Mendelian randomisation give it no support, and blood kynurenine data are inconsistent.

IDO1 converts tryptophan to kynurenine and is inhibited by high tryptophan. Combined with a deleterious IDO2 variant, a mathematical model predicts two stable states, one of which traps cells with low tryptophan and serotonin and high kynurenine after an inflammatory trigger. Exiting the trap would need a perturbation. It is a mathematical model with limited direct data.

Proposed byRobert Phair, Ron Davis (OMF / Stanford), Alex Kashi

  • Plasma kynurenine findings inconsistent

If true, we should see

  • Enrichment of IDO2 deleterious variants
  • Altered intracellular tryptophan/kynurenine
  • Bistable behaviour in patient cells

Tests that would settle it

  • Intracellular tryptophan/kynurenine measurement in patient cells with IDO genotypes
  • Test of predicted bistability in culture

Where it stands. Observational support only, with inconsistent diagnostic criteria and no controlled trials.

Mast cell activation syndrome overlaps clinically with POTS, hypermobility and ME/CFS. Histamine and other mediators could cause vasodilation and orthostatic symptoms. Treatment with H1/H2 antihistamines is common. Diagnostic criteria are contested and data are observational.

Autoimmunity (functional autoantibodies)Post-infectious autoantibodies, for example against adrenergic or muscarinic receptors, cause vascular and autonomic dysfunction.32+3 −4

Where it stands. The leading antibody targets did not hold up and three antibody-targeting treatments failed controlled trials. Plasma-cell depletion and IgG-transfer results in mice keep a narrower version alive.

A subset of patients may develop antibodies that disturb receptor signalling or nerve function after infection, similar to other post-infectious autoimmune conditions. Female predominance, infection onset and immune genetics fit. Antibody removal or B-/plasma-cell depletion should then help. Recent controlled trials have narrowed the GPCR version, while plasma-cell depletion and IgG transfer keep a broader version alive.

Proposed byScheibenbogen (Charité), Fluge and Mella (Bergen), Wallukat (GPCR antibodies), Iwasaki (IgG transfer)

Evidence for 3

  • Daratumumab 6/10 sustained responders with IgG fall (Fluge 2025, open-label)
  • Long-COVID IgG transfers pain hypersensitivity to mice (Chen 2026; Mignolet 2026)
  • Cyclophosphamide 55% open-label response with HLA association (Rekeland 2020)

Evidence against 4

  • Rituximab phase III negative (Fluge 2019)
  • Immunoadsorption no better than sham (IAMPOCO, IA-PACS-CFS 2026)
  • No GPCR autoantibody elevation on REAP/Luminex, q>0.68 (Germain 2025)
  • BC007 company trial negative (2024)

If true, we should see

  • Elevated specific autoantibodies
  • Benefit from antibody removal or plasma-cell depletion
  • Symptom transfer with patient IgG

Tests that would settle it

  • Randomised placebo-controlled daratumumab trial
  • IgG transfer from ME/CFS (non-COVID) patients with blinded readouts
  • Pre-specified antibody-selected sham-controlled trial

Viral persistenceVirus or viral antigen persists in tissue reservoirs and drives ongoing immune activation.29+2 −3

Where it stands. Viral antigen persists in some people after COVID, but three antiviral trials in established long COVID were null, which argues against ongoing replication as the main driver.

After SARS-CoV-2 and possibly other infections, viral RNA or protein may persist in gut, lymphoid or nervous tissue. Persistent antigen would keep the immune system activated and could explain chronic symptoms. Evidence is strongest in long COVID, where viral proteins are detected months later. Whether it applies to classic ME/CFS is unknown.

Working modelStep 1 · Infection and immune priming
Proposed byProal and VanElzakker (PolyBio), Peluso and Deeks (UCSF), Iwasaki (Yale)

Evidence for 2

  • SARS-CoV-2 antigen detected in tissue and plasma months after infection (reviewed Proal 2023)
  • ME/CFS incidence ~5x higher after SARS-CoV-2 (Vernon 2025)

Evidence against 3

  • Three nirmatrelvir-ritonavir RCTs null (RECOVER-VITAL 2026, STOP-PASC 2024, PAX LC 2025)
  • Temelimab (HERV-W) null
  • Antigen detected also in recovered people in some studies

If true, we should see

  • Viral RNA/protein in tissue biopsies
  • Antivirals or monoclonals improving symptoms
  • Antigen levels tracking symptoms

Tests that would settle it

  • Trials of longer or combination antivirals and monoclonals with tissue antigen as a selection marker
  • Tissue antigen load vs symptom severity in matched recovered controls

For: Chronic antigenic stimulation interpretation of the naive/switched-memory B-cell shift (Walitt 2024); exhaustion programmes in CD8+ T cells; early-immunosenescence phenotype in mild/moderate patients 'indicative of persistent viral infection' (Lee 2025); exaggerated response to microbial antigens. Against: Three RCTs of nirmatrelvir in established LC (about 1,200 people) were null, and spike levels did not fall with treatment. Enterovirus findings are unreplicated with blinded methods. XMRV was contamination. The Giardia and Q fever triggers and failed doxycycline in QFS fit a 'hit-and-run' rather than persistent infection.
  • Genetics. For: Infection-response genes at 3 loci, a larger OLFM4 effect in infection onset, and suggestive EBV-load MR (MVP p=0.012). Against: Infection and non-infection onset are genetically similar, EBV MR control viruses align too, and immune cell types are not enriched.
  • Treatment trials and natural history. For: Post-COVID ME/CFS incidence HR 4.93 (Vernon 2025); rintatolimod modest effect. Against: Three nirmatrelvir RCTs null; temelimab null.

Where it stands. Mildly low cortisol is replicated, but it is small and nonspecific, and replacement gives little benefit, so it looks more like a consequence than a cause.

Mild hypocortisolism, a flattened diurnal rhythm and enhanced negative feedback are reported in ME/CFS. This is probably a consequence of illness, inactivity or sleep disturbance rather than a cause, but it could amplify symptoms. Low-dose hydrocortisone had small effects and suppressed the adrenal axis.

Where it stands. The assay is not standardised, independent replication is lacking, and one large cohort found no difference from controls.

Fluorescence microscopy of platelet-poor plasma shows amyloid microclots, reported in long COVID and ME/CFS. They could obstruct capillaries and reduce oxygen delivery. Anticoagulant 'triple therapy' was promoted on this basis. The method is difficult to standardise and independent labs disagree.

Altered 'effort preference' (NIH)Patients choose fewer hard-effort options in a decision task, which the NIH team interpreted as a defining feature rather than fatigue or weakness.umbrella model+2 −2

Where it stands. Based on 17 patients and an unvalidated task, and avoiding PEM explains the result equally well.

In deep phenotyping of 17 post-infectious ME/CFS patients, participants chose the hard task less often in the Effort-Expenditure for Rewards Task, and the authors proposed altered effort preference linked to low CSF catecholamines and motor-network changes. They framed fatigue as arising from brain integrative circuits. Critics argue the task was not validated in ME/CFS and that choosing less effort is a rational response to PEM, not a preference.

Where it stands. Two-day exercise decline, preload failure and post-exertional muscle damage are not seen in sedentary controls, so lost fitness cannot be the whole explanation.

If symptoms reflect detraining, patients should look like sedentary controls on exercise testing, recover normally between tests, and improve with graded training. Deconditioning certainly coexists in severe illness. The question is whether it explains the disease.

Where it stands. Gains are confined to self-report and fade, and the model does not explain the objective abnormalities or the harm reported after graded exercise.

The model holds that after a trigger, beliefs that activity is harmful lead to avoidance, deconditioning and symptom focus, maintaining disability. It predicted that CBT and graded exercise would produce recovery. PACE and Dutch trials reported modest self-reported benefits. The model is now widely disputed: objective outcomes were null and PEM is not explained by beliefs.

Findings by body system

Blood flow, vessels and blood

The most consistent vascular findings in ME/CFS concern circulation when upright: cerebral blood flow falls much more than normal on tilt, stroke volume is low, red-cell and blood volume are below predicted in a large minority to about half, and during exercise the heart is under-filled (preload failure). These are reported by several groups, though the cerebral blood flow and invasive exercise data each come mostly from one centre, and a 2026 study found blood volume did not predict who has orthostatic abnormalities. Reduced endothelial function (FMD, PORH) has been found in three independent cohorts, and newer work shows fewer muscle capillaries than bed rest would explain and narrowed retinal vessels in post-COVID ME/CFS. Complement activation is replicated in long COVID but inconsistent in ME/CFS. Microclots remain contested on method, and pooled blood proteomics do not show raised coagulation, platelet or endothelial-activation proteins.

Blood volume

Red cell volume and total blood volume are below predicted in a large minority to about half of ME/CFS patients measured by isotope or CO-rebreathing methods. Replicated

Many patients have less blood than expected for their size, mainly because they have fewer red cells. Less blood means less returns to the heart when upright.

Hurwitz 2009 (Clin Sci): total blood volume -15%, plasma volume -13%, red cell volume -19% in CFS, and the blood-volume deficit explained 91-94% of group differences in cardiac volume indices. Newton 2016 linked lower plasma volume to smaller cardiac MRI volumes and to fatigue severity but not to illness duration (argues against pure deconditioning). Five independent groups report a red-cell-volume deficit (Streeten 2000, Hurwitz, Newton, van Campen 2018, Yamazaki 2026). Measurement methods differ (I-131 albumin, Cr-51, CO-rebreathing) and predicted values depend on body-size formulas, so prevalence figures are not comparable across studies.

Working model: step 3, Low blood volume (evidence for) · Open question: Why is blood volume low, and is the marrow involved?

Bears on: Low blood volume and preload failure Pituitary / vasopressin deficiency · Test: Haemoglobin mass by CO-rebreathing (some sports-science and research labs); isotope blood volume (Daxor BVA-100, a few US centres). Reticulocytes, ferritin, transferrin saturation are routine.

The hormones that should rise to restore blood volume (renin, aldosterone, EPO) are not raised in ME/CFS or POTS despite low volume, and blood proteomics shows no consistent change in them. Several studies

If blood volume is low the body should release hormones to retain salt and water. In many patients these hormones stay normal or low, which suggests the volume set-point itself is off.

In POTS, low aldosterone and an inappropriately low renin for the plasma-volume deficit (the renin-aldosterone paradox) were described by Raj et al. 2005; adrenal responsiveness to ACTH is intact (Laurin 2023), so the defect sits upstream. Older ME/CFS work reported low renin in tilt-positive patients and normal EPO. A Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of SomaScan and UK Biobank Olink data (about 150 patients plus UKB) found renin, ACE, BNP, EPO and hepcidin flat across cohorts.

Cardiac size and stroke volume

Left-ventricular volumes and stroke volume are smaller in ME/CFS at rest and fall more than normal on tilt, largely in proportion to low blood volume rather than to weak heart muscle. Replicated

The heart is not damaged, but it is under-filled, so each beat pumps less blood, especially when upright.

Hurwitz 2009: severe CFS had about 10% lower stroke index and end-diastolic volume; adjusting for blood volume removed most of the difference. Hollingsworth 2012 (cardiac MRI) reported markedly lower end-diastolic volume and stroke volume. Miwa reports a 'small heart' (cardiothoracic ratio <0.42) subgroup with orthostatic intolerance. van Campen 2024 (233 POTS, many more normal HR-BP response) showed larger stroke-volume-index falls on tilt in all ME/CFS groups than in controls, with two patterns: venous pooling (HR rise 30-39) and a hyperadrenergic pattern (HR rise >=40) with relatively preserved SVI.

Open questions

  • Do stroke-volume deficits normalise after volume loading, and does that predict symptomatic benefit?
  • How much of the van Campen echo data has been reproduced in another centre with blinded readers?

Working model: step 3, Low blood volume (evidence for)

Bears on: Low blood volume and preload failure Autonomic dysfunction and small-fibre neuropathy · Test: Echocardiogram (routine, but usually reported normal at rest); tilt with stroke-volume monitoring (Finapres/bioimpedance at autonomic units).

Exercise haemodynamics

During upright invasive exercise testing most ME/CFS patients have abnormally low right-atrial filling pressure (preload failure), and a high-flow subgroup shows poor systemic oxygen extraction. Several studies

When patients exercise, too little blood returns to the heart. In some, blood also bypasses the muscles, so oxygen goes unused.

Joseph/Systrom 2021 (Chest): of 1,516 iCPETs, 160 met ME/CFS criteria with RAP <6.5 mmHg; peak RAP 1.9 vs 8.3 mmHg, peak VO2 80% vs 101% predicted. Low-flow tertile had lower peak cardiac output; high-flow tertile had lower systemic O2 extraction (0.74 vs 0.86-0.88). Selection by low RAP is built into the cohort, so the prevalence of preload failure in ME/CFS generally is not established. Novak 2026 reports preload failure in 92% of the 66 ME/CFS patients who had iCPET (same Harvard group). Long COVID iCPET shows the same pattern (Singh 2022; Joseph 2023 review). Independent replication outside the Systrom network is lacking.

  • Can non-invasive tests (pulse pressure narrowing on stand, Day 2023; CO-rebreathing cardiac output) stand in for iCPET?
  • Does preload failure precede or follow illness onset?

Working model: step 3, Low blood volume (evidence for)

Bears on: Low blood volume and preload failure Autonomic dysfunction and small-fibre neuropathy Capillary and microvascular damage · Test: Invasive CPET at a few US centres (Brigham, Yale, Mount Sinai); not routine. Two-day CPET is non-invasive but does not measure preload.

A subset of patients with unexplained exertional intolerance cannot extract oxygen normally from blood during exercise, associated with hypocapnia and possible arteriovenous shunting. Several studies

Blood arrives at the muscles but leaves with too much oxygen still in it, so the muscles get less than they need.

Melamed 2019 (Systrom group) described a poor-extraction phenotype with relative hypocapnia (PaCO2 29.9 vs 37.5 mmHg) and high mixed-venous O2 saturation at peak (44% vs 31%). Proposed causes: microvascular shunting from small-fibre neuropathy, mitochondrial limitation, or a left-shifted oxyhaemoglobin curve from hyperventilation. Muscle-oxygenation work by the Wüst group (NIRS post-occlusion) points in the same direction. All iCPET data come from one network.

Cerebral blood flow

Cerebral blood flow falls about 26% during head-up tilt in ME/CFS versus 7% in controls, including in patients with normal heart rate and blood pressure responses. Replicated

Standing up reduces blood flow to the brain far more than normal, even when pulse and blood pressure look fine, and the drop tracks orthostatic symptoms.

van Campen 2020 (429 patients, 44 HC, extracranial carotid+vertebral Doppler): 82% of normal-response, 98% of delayed-OH and 100% of POTS patients exceeded the control lower limit (13%). Flow recovery after tilt is incomplete and slowest in severe patients (van Campen 2021). The CO-CBF relation is roughly 1:1 in most patients, unlike the 3:1 seen in health (van Campen 2024, 2025). Transcranial Doppler work from other groups (Medow/Stewart; Novak 2026: reduced orthostatic CBF velocity in 88% ME/CFS) agrees. Caveats: most volume-flow data come from one Dutch clinic, operators are not blinded to diagnosis, controls are few relative to patients, and the 2025 POTS paper found CBF reduction did not differ between its two haemodynamic subgroups.

Raising blood pressure with phenylephrine during tilt blocked hyperventilation, restored cerebral blood velocity and improved working memory in ME/CFS, whereas CO2 or acetazolamide alone did not. Early

In a lab test, a drug that tightens blood vessels improved both brain blood flow and thinking speed when patients were upright.

Medow 2014 and Medow & Stewart 2024 (same New York group) used acute infusions with n-back testing; numbers are small (single-digit to low teens per condition). These are mechanistic studies, not treatment trials. Compression of legs and abdomen reduced cardiac output fall (-15% vs -27%) and CBF fall (-14% vs -25%) on tilt in van Campen 2021 (n=16).

Breathing and CO2

Many ME/CFS patients over-breathe when upright (orthostatic hypocapnia), and during exercise hyperventilation and dysfunctional breathing are common. Replicated

When standing, some patients breathe off too much CO2. Low CO2 narrows brain arteries, which can add to dizziness and brain fog.

End-tidal CO2 falls on tilt in several groups (Naschitz 2000, Razumovsky 2003, Natelson 2007, Medow 2014, Novak's 'hypocapnic cerebral hypoperfusion'). Yamazaki 2026: postural orthostatic syndrome of hypocapnia (POSH) in 41% of 49 on a lean test. Mancini 2025: hyperventilation and/or dysfunctional breathing during CPET common, with VE/VCO2 34.7 vs 28.1 in hyperventilators. But van Campen 2023 found CO2 reactivity normal and the PETCO2 fall explained only a modest share of the CBF fall, so hypocapnia is probably a contributor, not the main driver. Whether over-breathing is primary (chemoreflex/autonomic) or compensatory (e.g. to aid venous return via thoracic pump) is unresolved.

Endothelium

Large-artery flow-mediated dilation and microvascular post-occlusive reactive hyperaemia are reduced in ME/CFS in two independent Norwegian cohorts and by peripheral arterial tonometry in Berlin. Replicated

The lining of blood vessels does not widen properly when it should. This has been found in several groups with different methods.

Sandvik 2023 (RituxME substudy, 39 patients): FMD 5.1% vs 8.2% (p<0.0001, adjusted for diameter and sex), PORH 1354 vs 2208 PU; rituximab had no effect; PORH but not FMD improved over 18 months and PORH correlated with daily steps. Sørland 2021 (cyclophosphamide cohort, 35 patients): FMD 5.9% vs 7.7%, PORH 1331 vs 1886 PU. Scherbakov 2020 (EndoPAT): endothelial dysfunction (RHI <=1.81) in 51% of 35 vs 20% of 20 controls, linked to severity. Haffke 2022: reduced RHI in 5/14 post-COVID ME/CFS. Caveats: inactivity lowers FMD, controls were mostly not activity-matched, and FMD and PORH did not correlate with each other.

Bears on: Endothelial dysfunction Circulating (serum) factor Autoimmunity (functional autoantibodies) · Test: FMD ultrasound and EndoPAT in vascular research labs; not standard clinical tests.

Plasma or purified IgG from ME/CFS patients alters cultured endothelial cells: lower nitric oxide production, more mitochondrial fragmentation, and anti-endothelial antibody binding. Early

Something in patients' blood seems to make lab-grown vessel-lining cells work less well. This has been seen by three labs using different tests, none yet repeated by another lab using the same test.

Bertinat 2022: HUVECs exposed to ME/CFS plasma (11 vs 12) produced less NO with higher inhibitory eNOS Thr495 phosphorylation. Flaskamp 2022 (Charité): more anti-endothelial antibody binding in post-COVID ME/CFS, and sera lacked the pro-angiogenic effect seen in non-ME post-COVID sera. Prusty 2026 (BBIH): purified IgG from 39 ME/CFS and 15 post-COVID ME/CFS fragmented endothelial mitochondria versus MS and healthy IgG; single lab, nominal p-values over many readouts (summarised in Solving ME/CFS serum-factors review). No lab has reproduced another's assay.

Microvasculature

Retinal imaging shows narrower arterioles, lower arteriolar-to-venular ratio, reduced flicker-induced venular dilation and lower capillary vessel density in post-COVID patients, most pronounced in those meeting ME/CFS criteria. Several studies

The tiny vessels at the back of the eye, which can be photographed without needles, look narrower and respond less in post-COVID ME/CFS.

Wallraven 2026 (BMC Med, 'All Eyes on PCS'): 102 PCS (62 with ME/CFS) vs 102 recovered and 96 never-infected; CRAE 178 vs 186 um, AVR 0.83 vs 0.87, venular flicker dilation 3.7% vs 4.8%; ME/CFS subgroup most affected (AUC 0.79); robust to CV-risk adjustment except AVR attenuated. Schlick 2022 (Erlangen, OCT-A): lower vessel density in superficial and intermediate capillary plexus in PCS, lower still with chronic fatigue. Data are almost entirely post-COVID; pre-2020 ME/CFS cohorts have not been imaged with these methods.

Sublingual video-microscopy shows reduced perfused capillary density and glycocalyx changes in long COVID, persisting many months after infection. Early

Under the tongue, fewer small vessels carry blood in long COVID patients.

Osiaevi/Rovas/Kümpers (Münster) used sideStream dark-field microscopy with automated analysis (GlycoCheck) and reported persistent capillary rarefaction in long COVID (Nephrol Dial Transplant 2024; Angiogenesis 2023). No ME/CFS-specific cohort has been published with this method; whether rarefaction correlates with ME/CFS-defined PEM is unknown.

Muscle biopsies show fewer capillaries per fibre in ME/CFS and less capillary supply per fibre size in both ME/CFS and long COVID, unlike the pattern after 60 days of bed rest; thickened capillary basement membrane has been reported but is not yet peer-reviewed. Several studies

Muscles of patients have fewer and possibly thicker-walled small blood vessels, and this is different from what happens to healthy people kept in bed.

Charlton 2026 (Nat Commun, Wüst group): ME/CFS (n=23-24) had lower capillary-to-fibre ratio than controls (p<0.001, n=30) and long COVID; both patient groups had lower capillary density and lower capillary supply for a given fibre area; healthy bed rest (n=17-24) instead raised capillary density because fibres shrank. This argues against inactivity as the full explanation. Slaghekke 2025 (conference poster, electron microscopy, about 11 patients per group) reported basement membrane thickening (p<0.0001) and smaller capillary lumens in ME/CFS and post-COVID; the composite CF x collagen IV measure that correlated with CPET has been questioned. Appelman 2024 found amyloid-containing deposits in long COVID muscle that increased after induced PEM.

Pericytes and vascular smooth-muscle cells have not been examined directly in ME/CFS tissue, but blood proteins from mural cells and vessel matrix (NOTCH3, ITGAV, TGF-beta set, LUM) are lower across several ME/CFS cohorts and in long COVID. Early

Pericytes are the cells wrapped around capillaries that control their width. Nobody has looked at them in ME/CFS tissue yet; indirect blood clues suggest they may be fewer or less active.

Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of SomaScan (Hoel, Germain, Walitt) and UK Biobank Olink data: ITGAV d -0.34 (UKB q=0.002), NOTCH3 -0.32, THBS1 -0.50, LUM -0.92; vascular smooth-muscle tissue score d -0.48 (p=0.001) but flat in UKB competitive tests. The long COVID UK Explore set also showed lower endothelial/TGF-beta proteins (ANGPT2 -0.84, EDN1 -0.65). Lower circulating NOTCH3 could reflect less shedding rather than fewer cells. The basement-membrane thickening reported in muscle (where pericytes help build the membrane) is a possible link.

Blood biomarkers

Proteomic panels do not show a consistent rise in classic endothelial-activation or vasoactive proteins in ME/CFS; most named candidates are null and the endothelial-activation set trends down. Contested

Blood tests for vessel damage markers mostly come back normal in ME/CFS when large datasets are pooled, which differs from what small studies suggested.

Solving ME/CFS re-analysis: VWF, SELP, SELE, VCAM1, ANGPT1/2, VEGFA, EDN1, ADM, ACE, REN, NPPB null; ICAM1 +0.20 (driven by UKB), ACE2 +0.21, NPPC +0.23; endothelial-activation set d -0.30 (q=0.09, down). By contrast, smaller ELISA studies report raised endothelin-1 (Haffke 2022) and Wallraven 2026 found raised IL-6, ICAM-1, VCAM-1 in PCS and ME/CFS. Post-COVID ME/CFS may differ from pre-pandemic cohorts.

VEGF-A has been reported lower, not higher, in ME/CFS plasma, and proteomic re-analysis finds no consistent change; long COVID cohorts more often report raised VEGF. Contested

VEGF is a signal that makes new small vessels. Results in ME/CFS are inconsistent, and they differ from long COVID.

Landi 2016 reported clustered reductions of IL-7, IL-16 and VEGF-A in ME/CFS that were not seen in liver-disease fatigue controls. Large cytokine panels (e.g. Montoya 2017) did not find VEGF among robust differences; the Solving ME/CFS proteome re-analysis found VEGFA null. In long COVID several cohorts report raised VEGF (e.g. Patel 2022). Flaskamp 2022 found post-COVID non-ME sera pro-angiogenic but post-COVID ME/CFS sera not, consistent with a missing compensatory angiogenic response in ME/CFS.

Red blood cells

Red blood cells from ME/CFS patients were stiffer in one microfluidic study, and real-time deformability cytometry found altered red-cell deformation persisting after COVID-19. Early

Red cells need to bend to squeeze through capillaries. In a small study, patients' red cells were stiffer.

Saha 2019 (Stanford/OMF, custom microfluidic channels, small paired sample, about 12-14 patients) reported slower entry and reduced elongation of ME/CFS red cells. Kubánková 2021 (Biophys J, real-time deformability cytometry) found altered erythrocyte deformation and size heterogeneity persisting months after COVID-19. No independent ME/CFS replication; older reports of abnormal red-cell shape (stomatocytes) are from the 1990s and used subjective scoring.

Coagulation

Fibrinaloid microclots (thioflavin-T-positive amyloid fibrin deposits) are reported to be increased in platelet-poor plasma in ME/CFS and long COVID, but the method is not standardised and haemostasis experts dispute the inference that they cause symptoms. Contested

One research network sees tiny clot-like particles in patients' plasma. Other experts say the method is unreliable and the particles may not exist in circulating blood. Anticoagulant treatment based on them is not supported.

Nunes 2022 (25 ME/CFS vs 15 HC): microclot image area commonly >10-fold higher, platelet spreading score 2.72 vs 1.00, hypercoagulable TEG; load lower than in long COVID. Kruger 2022 found entrapped inflammatory proteins in long COVID microclots. Dalton 2024 (Sheffield, independent group, semi-automated counting) found higher counts in long COVID as a cohort, with wide overlap and high counts also after recent COVID. Critiques: visual scoring, uncertain blinding, ex vivo artefact possible, no in vivo demonstration; Hunt 2024 (RPTH) concluded the hypothesis is not evidence-based and unlicensed antithrombotics or apheresis are not justified outside trials; Kell 2024 rebutted. Solving ME/CFS proteome re-analysis found a platelet/microclot protein set slightly lower, not higher.

Platelet activation findings in ME/CFS are inconsistent: one network reports hyperactivated platelets, while an earlier controlled study found no platelet activation or hypercoagulability. Contested

Whether platelets are overactive in ME/CFS depends on who measured and how.

Nunes 2022 reported PAC-1 and CD62P staining and spreading consistent with activation. Kennedy 2006 (Dundee) measured platelet aggregation, P-selectin and coagulation markers and found no evidence of activation or hypercoagulability, explicitly arguing against antiplatelet therapy. In long COVID, Cervia-Hasler 2024 found monocyte-platelet aggregates and platelet-activation markers raised. No ME/CFS-specific flow cytometry replication.

Complement and thromboinflammation

Active long COVID shows persistent complement dysregulation (terminal complex, alternative and classical pathway activation) with thromboinflammation markers, replicated across several cohorts. Replicated

Complement is part of the innate immune system. In long COVID it stays switched on months after infection, together with signs of platelet and vessel injury.

Cervia-Hasler 2024 (Science): >6,500 proteins in 268 longitudinal samples; terminal complement dysregulation, classical activation linked to herpesvirus antibody titres, raised haemolysis, tissue-injury and platelet markers. Baillie 2024 (Med, 166 LC vs 79): iC3b, TCC, Ba and C5a predicted LC (AUC 0.785). Further partial replication in Klein 2023 and Barratt-Due 2024; one adjusted null (Farztdinov preprint). Long COVID only; ME/CFS evidence is separate.

Complement may be abnormal in some ME/CFS patients, but studies disagree on which part and in which direction.

POTS overlap

POTS is present in roughly a fifth of ME/CFS patients on formal testing (prevalence varies 6-43%), but cerebral hypoperfusion and preload failure are found in most patients regardless of whether they meet POTS heart-rate criteria. Replicated

POTS is a fast heart rate on standing. Only some ME/CFS patients have it, but most have reduced brain blood flow when upright anyway.

Novak 2026: POTS 19% ME/CFS and 22% long COVID, but reduced orthostatic CBFv 88-92%. van Campen 2020: CBF abnormal in 82% of patients with normal HR/BP response. van Campen 2024/2025 split ME/CFS-POTS into a venous-pooling profile and a hyperadrenergic profile (HR rise >=40) with different CO-CBF relations, which may have different treatment implications. Yamazaki 2026: hypocapnia more common than POTS on a lean test. Low plasma volume and the renin-aldosterone paradox are well described in POTS itself.
