Key reviews

  • Joseph 2021, Chest: Defines preload failure and impaired extraction phenotypes in the largest iCPET series.
  • van Campen 2020, Clin Neurophysiol Pract: Largest cerebral blood flow on tilt study (429 patients).
  • Nunes, Kell, Slaghekke, Wüst 2026, Cell Death Dis: Recent synthesis proposing endothelial senescence as a unifying model (hypothesis paper, not evidence).
  • Hunt 2024, Res Pract Thromb Haemost: Haemostasis-expert critique of the microclot hypothesis.
  • Novak 2026, PLOS One: Shared autonomic/cerebrovascular phenotype of long COVID and ME/CFS in 313 patients.
  • Westermeier, Pretorius, Untersmayr 2026, Cardiovasc Diabetol: Cardiometabolic and vascular perspective on PEM.

Muscle, exertion and energy

People with ME/CFS reliably have lower aerobic capacity and a low peak heart rate on exercise testing, and they report delayed, prolonged PEM that took about two weeks to resolve after a 2-day test. Whether performance measurably drops on a second test 24 hours later is now contested: several linked groups and two meta-analyses say yes, mainly at the ventilatory threshold, while a 2026 replication found no change. Invasive testing points to poor cardiac filling and poor oxygen extraction, and newer biopsy work from one Amsterdam group finds fewer oxidative fibres, fewer capillaries and lower mitochondrial capacity in ME/CFS that bed rest does not reproduce, plus post-exertion muscle damage and amyloid-containing deposits in long COVID. Mitochondrial studies in blood cells disagree in direction, and the idea that patient serum alters muscle-cell mitochondria failed a large pre-registered replication (Ryback 2026). Post-exertion omics (metabolomics, proteomics, EVs) show resting differences and recovery-phase changes, but within-person exercise effects are modest and mostly unreplicated.

PEM definition and timing

PEM is usually delayed by hours to a day, lasts days to weeks, and after a 2-day CPET took ME/CFS patients a mean of about 13 days to recover versus about 2 days in sedentary controls. Several studies

After overdoing it, people with ME/CFS often feel worse later rather than at once, and the crash can last much longer than ordinary tiredness after exercise.

Chu 2018 (n=150 survey): 84% reported PEM lasting 24 h or more; onset varied, and only 11% had a consistent delay of at least 24 h. Moore 2023 (80 vs 64, Ithaca 2-day CPET): judged recovery 12.7 ± 1.2 d vs 2.1 ± 0.2 d, range 1-64 d; one patient had not recovered at one year. NIH qualitative work (Stussman 2024, 10 vs 9) found every patient's PEM had a different onset, trajectory and worst symptom, and VAS scales missed changes that interviews caught. Self-report designs and one centre for the recovery data are the main limits.

Exercise capacity (single CPET)

On a single maximal exercise test, ME/CFS patients have lower peak oxygen uptake (pooled about 5 ml/kg/min below controls) with a low peak heart rate (chronotropic incompetence). Replicated

Patients can take in and use less oxygen at maximal effort than healthy people, and their heart rate does not rise as high.

Large clinical series (VanNess 2003, n=189) and case-control studies (Keller 2024, Walitt 2024 NIH, Charlton 2026) agree. Effort criteria (RER, perceived exertion) are usually met, which argues against low effort. The main confounder is deconditioning; Keller 2024 used VO2-matched pairs and Charlton 2026 compared with 60-day bed rest, and both found patterns that inactivity did not reproduce. A single CPET's peak VO2 overlaps heavily with sedentary controls, so it is not diagnostic on its own.

Working model: step 5, Tissue under-perfusion (evidence for)

Bears on: Low blood volume and preload failure Mitochondrial / energy metabolism impairment Autonomic dysfunction and small-fibre neuropathy Deconditioning · Test: Cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) at cardiology/sports-medicine labs; carries PEM risk

People with long COVID have lower peak VO2 than recovered controls on average (about 5 ml/kg/min), with patterns pointing to deconditioning, chronotropic incompetence and impaired peripheral extraction rather than a cardiac or ventilatory limit. Replicated

On an exercise bike, people with long COVID reach a lower maximum oxygen use than people who recovered. The heart's pumping is usually normal; the problem looks more like heart-rate control, fitness loss and muscles taking up less oxygen.

Bridges ME/CFS single-CPET findings to LC; selection (hospitalised vs mild, active vs sedentary) explains much of the heterogeneity.

2-day CPET

ME/CFS patients perform worse on a second maximal exercise test 24 h after the first, most clearly in workload and VO2 at the ventilatory threshold, but two independent groups (Lien 2019; Mancini and Natelson 2026) did not reproduce the VO2 effect. Contested

Several labs found that patients cannot repeat their performance a day after a hard test, while healthy people can. A 2026 study using the same design found no drop, so the test's reliability as a PEM marker is in doubt.

Positive studies: Snell 2013 (51 vs 10 women; 95% classification), van Campen 2020/2021 (82 women by severity; idiopathic chronic fatigue improved on day 2 while ME/CFS declined), Keller 2024 (84 vs 71; declines of ~5-7% in peak VO2 and VO2 at threshold), Hodges 2018 (MS controls improved), Davenport 2026 preprint (84 ME/CFS, 79 long COVID, 71 controls). Meta-analyses: Lim 2020 (workload at VT difference -10.8 day 1 vs -33.0 day 2) and Franklin & Graham 2022 (work at anaerobic threshold -21 W, 78% predictive probability of exceeding a 10 W MCID). Most positive data come from the Workwell/Pacific/Ithaca network and the van Campen clinic, so they are not fully independent. Mancini/Natelson 2026 (58 vs 25) and Lien 2019 (VO2peak day-2 fall not different between groups) did not reproduce the VO2 effect. Effect sizes are small relative to test-retest noise, and threshold detection is operator-dependent.

Lactate and glycolysis

Some patients produce more lactate for a given workload, and this worsens on a repeat test, but plasma studies after one maximal test show a smaller total lactate rise that mainly reflects lower achieved workloads. Several studies

Muscles in some patients seem to lean on the quick, lactate-producing fuel route earlier than expected, especially the day after hard effort.

Lien 2019 (18 vs 15 women): arterial lactate per power output was higher in patients on both tests and rose on day 2 while it fell in controls (interaction p<0.001). Lane 1998: about a third of patients had an abnormal lactate rise on a sub-anaerobic-threshold test, and this subgroup had fewer type 1 fibres (n=105 biopsies). Wong 1992 (31P-MRS) inferred accelerated glycolysis. The Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of Germain 2022 found the post-exercise lactate rise was smaller in patients (log2 +1.02 vs +1.40), which disappears as a signal once effort is considered. Lactate per watt, not peak lactate, is the informative measure.

Long COVID patients show early lactate accumulation and reduced fat oxidation during exercise, with plasma metabolite and lipid shifts consistent with impaired mitochondrial fatty-acid use. Several studies

Muscles of long COVID patients switch early to burning sugar and make lactate sooner, and they burn less fat, suggesting the energy factories are not working normally.

Oxygen delivery and extraction

Invasive exercise testing shows two peripheral limits in ME/CFS: low cardiac filling (preload failure) and, in a high-flow subgroup, poor systemic oxygen extraction by tissue. Several studies

During exercise, either not enough blood returns to the heart, or the blood that reaches muscle passes through without giving up enough oxygen.

Joseph 2021 (Systrom lab, 160 ME/CFS vs 36 controls from 1,516 iCPETs): right atrial pressure 1.9 vs 8.3 mmHg, peak VO2 80% vs 101% predicted; the high-flow tertile had impaired extraction (0.74 vs 0.86-0.88), consistent with peripheral shunting; 31% had small-fibre neuropathy on skin biopsy. Melamed 2019: impaired extraction was the sole limit in 12.5% of unexplained exertional intolerance. Vermeulen 2014 (non-invasive, 178 CFS women) estimated lower peak extraction and a steep cardiac output/VO2 slope. McCully 1999 (NIRS) found slower muscle oxygen delivery. Invasive data come largely from one centre; capillary rarefaction in Charlton 2026 offers a structural explanation for low extraction.

Invasive CPET in long COVID with exercise intolerance repeatedly shows low systemic oxygen extraction with normal or high cardiac output, and in a subset reduced biventricular filling (preload failure), mirroring ME/CFS iCPET findings. Several studies

When doctors measure oxygen in arteries and veins during exercise, many long COVID patients' muscles take less oxygen out of the blood even though the heart pumps plenty. Some also have too little blood returning to the heart.

Should cross-link to vascular-oxygen-extraction and muscle-exertion-oxygen-extraction.

31P-MRS muscle energetics

31P-MRS studies from Newcastle found exaggerated muscle acidosis and up to ~4-fold slower pH recovery after repeated exercise in a subset of patients, but other MRS studies found no consistent group abnormality. Contested

Magnetic scans of calf muscle during exercise suggest that some patients' muscles become more acidic and clear acid slowly, but not all studies see this.

Jones 2010 (16 vs 8): proton efflux immediately post-exercise 1.1 vs 3.6 mmol/L/min, time to maximal efflux 25.6 vs 3.8 s, and the normal link between efflux and pH nadir was lost, possibly via autonomic dysfunction. Jones 2012 (18 vs 12): 10 of 18 had low PCr depletion; the other 8 showed more acidosis over three bouts, no adaptation and about 4-fold longer pH recovery. Lane 1998 found lower end-exercise pH and slower ATP synthesis only in the lactate-responder subgroup. Barnes 1993 (46 patients) found no consistent abnormality overall, with 12 outliers; Wong 1992 found similar end-points; a 2025 7 T study found no resting muscle differences. Small samples, subgroup analyses and heterogeneous criteria dominate.

Muscle sodium MRI

23Na-MRI in 6 women with ME/CFS and 6 controls found higher resting muscle sodium in all lower-leg compartments and a larger sodium rise after exercise, inversely related to grip strength. Early

A special MRI scan found more salt inside leg muscles of patients, which in theory could disturb muscle energy and calcium handling. The study was very small.

Petter 2022: anterior compartment 12.20 ± 1.66 vs 9.38 ± 0.71 mM (p=0.0034); medial gastrocnemius rose 30% vs 17% at 12 min after plantar flexion. Sodium correlated with lower handgrip strength (R2=0.38). This fits the Wirth/Scheibenbogen model in which hypoperfusion overloads the Na+/H+ exchanger, then Na+/Ca2+ exchange, loading muscle with calcium and damaging mitochondria. No independent replication; n=12 total.

Muscle biopsies (pre-2020)

Older ME/CFS muscle biopsy studies mostly found normal or nonspecific histology, without the fibre atrophy and type 2 shift expected from inactivity, with abnormalities confined to subgroups. Contested

Muscle samples taken in the 1990s mostly looked normal or only mildly abnormal under the microscope.

Lane 1998 (105 quadriceps biopsies): type 1 predominance (23%) was more common than type 2 predominance (3%); atrophy in 10%; no ultrastructural abnormality in 41 EM samples; the abnormal-lactate subgroup had fewer type 1 fibres. Grau 1992 (n=20): only minor nonspecific changes in 9. Wassif 1994 (n=10): normal ischaemic lactate responses. Behan 1991 reported mitochondrial structural changes and Bowles 1993 enteroviral RNA in muscle (41/158 postviral fatigue vs 2/152 controls), neither reproduced with modern methods. Criteria, techniques and selection varied widely.

Muscle biopsies after exertion

In long COVID with PEM, muscle biopsies taken one day after a maximal exercise test showed lower mitochondrial enzyme activity, more fibre necrosis, more T-cell infiltration and more amyloid-containing deposits than before exercise and than in controls. Early

When patients with long COVID were biopsied before and after a hard exercise test, their muscle looked more damaged and inflamed afterwards, and had more abnormal protein clumps.

Appelman 2024 (25 vs 21, Amsterdam): lower VO2max and gas exchange threshold; more glycolytic fibres; SDH activity fell after exercise in patients; large necrotic areas in 36% of patients after exercise (group p=0.09, so not firmly significant); CD3+ T cells present in patients but absent in controls; CD68 macrophages higher. Biopsies were scored as present/absent because sizes varied, and a first biopsy can itself cause regeneration at the second site. It is long COVID, not ME/CFS, and the amyloid-deposit finding has not been reproduced by another lab. The study prompted published criticism and replies in Nat Commun 2025.

Evidence

Appelman 2024, Nat Commun data25 long COVID vs 21 controlslongitudinal case-control; vastus lateralis biopsies before and 1 day after a maximal CPETLower exercise capacity; after exercise, lower SDH activity, more atrophic fibres and focal necrosis, more T-cell infiltration, more amyloid-containing deposits in patients
Charlton 2025, Trends Endocrinol Metabreviewopinion article from the same groupArgue for intrinsic mitochondrial dysfunction, endothelial abnormalities and glycolytic fibre shift as drivers; PEM trigger unknown

  • Are the amyloid-containing deposits fibrin(ogen)-derived and do they occlude capillaries?
  • Is necrosis specific to PEM or a nonspecific response to unaccustomed maximal effort?

Bears on: Fibrin amyloid microclots Mitochondrial / energy metabolism impairment Innate immune hyperactivation Capillary and microvascular damage Viral persistence · Test: Research only

Fibre type and capillaries

ME/CFS muscle has a lower proportion of type I (oxidative) fibres, type I-specific atrophy, lower mitochondrial capacity and fewer capillaries per fibre, a pattern that 60 days of strict bed rest in healthy people did not reproduce. Early

Patients' muscles have fewer endurance-type fibres and fewer tiny blood vessels. Healthy volunteers kept in bed for two months did not develop the same pattern, so lack of activity alone does not seem to explain it.

Charlton 2026 (Amsterdam group; 19-23 ME/CFS, 24-25 long COVID, 29-30 controls, 24 bed rest): type I proportion lower (p<0.001), type IIa/IIx higher; ME/CFS-only lower SDH; both patient groups lower OXPHOS; capillary-to-fibre ratio lower in ME/CFS than in long COVID and controls (p<0.001), whereas bed rest caused atrophy with unchanged capillary-to-fibre ratio and fibre type. OXPHOS correlated with VO2max in controls and after bed rest but not in patients. Same lab as Appelman; bed-rest cohort was a different (younger, male) population studied separately. Lane 1998 reported type 1 predominance more often than type 2 in older ME/CFS biopsies, which does not fit; differences in criteria and methods may explain this.

Muscle mitochondria

WASF3 protein is raised in ME/CFS muscle, and in cells and mice it disrupts respiratory supercomplex assembly and lowers exercise capacity via ER stress. Early

One protein, WASF3, was found at high levels in patients' muscle; in experiments it jammed the parts of mitochondria that make energy.

Wang/Hwang 2023 (NIH): started from one patient with high WASF3; transgenic mice overexpressing WASF3 ran less, with lower complex IV; endotoxin-induced ER stress raised WASF3; the ER-stress inhibitor 4-PBA lowered WASF3 and improved the patient's cell respiration. A cohort of ME/CFS muscle biopsies showed raised WASF3 and ER stress markers (small cohort; group n not given in abstract). Glass 2025 also found ER-stress proteins in post-exercise EVs tracking PEM severity. No independent replication of the WASF3 biopsy finding.

Cultured patient muscle cells

Muscle cells grown from ME/CFS patients failed to activate AMPK and raise glucose uptake after electrical pulse stimulation, and secreted less IL-6, suggesting a defect that persists outside the body. Early

Patients' muscle cells grown in a dish did not respond to simulated exercise the normal way, which hints at a built-in problem rather than one caused only by something in the blood.

Brown 2015 (Newcastle): control cultures increased AMPK phosphorylation and glucose uptake after 16 h EPS; CFS cultures did not, though insulin-stimulated uptake was preserved; IL-6 secretion lower. Sample sizes small. Tomas 2019 (same group) found no differences in individual complex activity in patient myotubes (n=6), so the defect, if real, is in signalling rather than respiratory chain capacity.

Mitochondria in blood cells

Mitochondrial function in patients' blood cells has been reported as lower (PBMC maximal respiration, T-cell glycolysis), higher (lymphoblast maximal respiration with Complex V inefficiency) or normal, depending on lab and cell type. Contested

Studies of energy production in white blood cells disagree with each other, so it is unclear whether blood cells show an energy defect.

Tomas 2017: lower PBMC maximal respiration (p<=0.003), but control groups were small (fresh n=3, frozen n=12, vs 25 and 38 patients). Mandarano 2020 (53 vs 45, Hanson lab): reduced glycolysis in CD4 and CD8 T cells at rest and reduced CD8 membrane potential, with normal mitochondrial respiration in most measures. Missailidis 2020/2021 (51 CCC patients; immortalised lymphoblasts): higher maximal respiration and spare capacity but lower ATP synthesis fraction (Complex V inefficiency), with TCA, PPP and beta-oxidation enzymes up; claimed high discrimination, unreplicated. Vermeulen 2010 and Tomas 2019 found normal PBMC OXPHOS or complex activity. Directions conflict between studies, freezing affects results, and blood cells may not reflect muscle.

Pyruvate dehydrogenase

Fluge 2016 proposed impaired pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) function from low TCA-fuelling amino acids and raised PDK mRNA in blood cells; this has not been independently confirmed. Early

One group suggested that the step that lets sugar enter mitochondria to be burned cleanly is partly blocked, pushing cells toward lactate. Others have not yet confirmed it.

Fluge 2016 (200 vs 102): lower serum amino acids feeding the TCA cycle (mainly women), raised 3-methylhistidine in men, PDK1/2/4, SIRT4 and PPARdelta mRNA up in PBMC. Mughal 2025 found PDK3/PDK4 up in 3D muscle exposed to patient serum (n=4 ME/CFS). The serum-transfer part of Fluge 2016 failed replication (Ryback 2026). Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of resting plasma metabolomics found low acylcarnitines and fatty acids (lower fat-fuel supply) rather than a pile-up pattern, and a 5-cohort aromatic-lactate deficit, which point to related but different steps. No study has measured PDH activity directly in ME/CFS muscle.

Serum factors and muscle cells

The claim that ME/CFS serum changes healthy myoblast mitochondrial respiration failed a pre-registered replication of 67 patients vs 53 controls, though a small 3D engineered-muscle study reported weaker contraction with patient serum. Refuted

An influential idea was that something in patients' blood harms muscle cells' energy production. A large, careful repeat of the original experiment found no difference.

Ryback 2026: blinded, randomised, 1,926 wells, primary maximal OCR +2.50 pmol/min (95% CI -1.62 to 6.62); recomputed participant-level d=0.14 (CI -0.22 to 0.50), excluding the original d=1.32. Limits: mostly mild-moderate (only 6 severe), resting samples, batch partly collinear with group, one myoblast donor, single readout. Mughal 2025 (4/5/4 donors, IBEC) found reduced contractile force at 48 h and mitochondrial fragmentation later, with pseudoreplication risk. Prusty 2026 found patient IgG fragments endothelial (not muscle) mitochondria, with MS controls. The refutation applies to the 2D myoblast respiration readout, not to all serum-factor ideas.

Exercise-induced gene expression

After moderate exercise, leukocyte mRNA for metabolite-detecting (ASIC3, P2X4/5, TRPV1), adrenergic and immune genes rose for up to 48 h in most CFS patients but not in controls or MS patients. Early

In one lab's studies, a 25-minute bout of moderate exercise switched on 'muscle-fatigue sensing' genes in patients' white blood cells for two days, and this tracked how tired and sore they felt.

Light 2012 (48 CFS, 18 FM, 49 controls; 25 min at 70% age-predicted HR, blood at 0.5, 8, 24, 48 h, blinded qPCR of 13 genes): 71% of CFS had increases correlating with fatigue and pain; the other 29% showed decreased alpha-2A receptor mRNA and more orthostatic intolerance. White 2012 (22 CFS, 20 MS, 23 controls) added a disease control. All from the Utah Light lab with a small targeted gene panel; no independent replication. Vu 2024 single-cell RNA-seq after exercise found minimal immune changes other than platelets.

Post-exertion metabolomics

Plasma metabolomics across a 2-day CPET shows clear resting differences in ME/CFS, but once each person is compared with themselves the exercise response differs little from controls. Contested

Blood chemistry differs between patients and healthy people even at rest. Whether hard exercise changes it in a disease-specific way is less clear.

Germain 2022 reported growing patient-control divergence (women: 6 to 54 metabolites at q<0.05 across four timepoints) and glutamate/TCA-linked recovery pathways. The Solving ME/CFS re-analysis reproduced those counts but found day-1 and day-2 differences correlate at 0.85 and the within-person response is at chance; alpha-ketoglutarate did not reproduce. Surviving modest signals: blunted post-exercise glucose rise (p=0.018, survives lactate adjustment), oxidised cys-gly rise in patients (q=0.033), lower day-2 N-acetylarginine and C6-DC acylcarnitine. Che 2025 (56 vs 52, Lipkin) reported TCA, beta-oxidation and urea-cycle abnormalities worse 24 h after exercise, but with only pre/24 h timepoints. Five of the most impaired male patients lacked post-exercise samples in Germain 2022.

Post-exertion proteomics

Plasma proteomics of 79 ME/CFS and 53 sedentary controls across a 2-day CPET found the largest patient-specific changes in the 24 h recovery phase, with suppressed T/B-cell and IL-17 signalling and raised glycolysis proteins. Contested

The biggest differences in blood proteins appeared during the recovery day, when PEM begins, rather than straight after exercise.

Germain 2025 (SomaScan 7K, 6,361 proteins; 96 F, 36 M): persistent dysregulation of immune, metabolic and neuromuscular pathways; protein-VO2max/AT relationships present in controls were disrupted in patients; sex-specific responses. Che 2025 proteomics added complement activation and extracellular-matrix ligands after exercise. The Solving ME/CFS proteome re-analysis found resting muscle-derived proteins lower in 3 SomaScan cohorts (including Germain) and UK Biobank (d -0.50). Pathway enrichment across thousands of aptamers is vulnerable to multiplicity; no independent post-exertion proteomics cohort yet.

Extracellular vesicles after exercise

Extracellular-vesicle protein cargo responds to maximal exercise differently in ME/CFS (blunted in women; TCA proteins down and complement up in men), and recovery-phase changes correlate with PEM severity. Early

Tiny packages that cells release into the blood carry different proteins after exercise in patients than in healthy people.

Giloteaux 2024 (18 vs 17 women; pre, 15 min, 24 h; TMT proteomics): patients' EV changes differed and correlated with symptom severity, involving coagulation, muscle contraction, cytoskeleton, immune and brain proteins. Glass 2025 (10 vs 12 men): TCA-cycle proteins down and complement up at 15 min; ER-stress and protein-folding changes in recovery correlated with PEM; EV-VO2 correlations seen in controls were absent in patients. Both from the Hanson lab, small, many comparisons; no transfer experiment shows patient EVs act on cells.

Muscle strength and fatigability

Repeated maximal handgrip testing shows lower strength, faster decline across repetitions and poorer recovery after 60 minutes in ME/CFS, correlating with severity and PEM. Several studies

Squeezing a grip meter ten times in a row, twice an hour apart, shows patients' strength fading faster and recovering less than healthy people's. It is cheap and quick.

Jäkel 2021 (105 ME/CFS, 18 cancer-related fatigue, 66 controls; Charité): lower Fmax and Fmean (p<0.0001), higher fatigue ratio, lower recovery ratio (Fmean2/Fmean1); lower grip linked to severity, PEM, muscle pain and post-exertion CK/LDH. Paffrath 2024 (144 women with post-COVID, 78 meeting CCC): grip impaired across post-COVID, but linked to key symptoms only in ME/CFS. Walitt 2024 (NIH) found normal MVC but shorter time to failure at 50% MVC (p=0.0002) and faster decline on repetitive grip, which the authors attributed to 'effort preference', an interpretation that has been disputed. Paul 1999 (10 vs 10) showed slower quadriceps strength recovery up to 24 h. Most data come from one centre; effort and motivation cannot be fully excluded from voluntary tests.

Muscle proteins in blood

Muscle-derived proteins are lower, as a group, in ME/CFS blood at rest in three SomaScan cohorts, not explained by step counts or walking pace; creatine kinase (CKM) and MYL3 are the most consistent single proteins, while myoglobin, CA3 and troponins disagree between cohorts. Several studies

Proteins that leak from muscle into blood are slightly lower in patients, which suggests less muscle mass or slower muscle turnover rather than ongoing damage.

Solving ME/CFS re-analysis: muscle-damage set d -0.50 (95% CI -0.76 to -0.24, q=0.002, I2 0.07) across Hoel (-0.85), Germain (-0.43) and Walitt (-0.34); UK Biobank competitive shift negative; not mediated by walking pace; unrelated to steps, Bell score or illness duration within patients. Lean mass was not available, so reduced muscle mass from inactivity cannot be excluded. Resting CK and myoglobin are expected to be low-normal. Per-protein re-pool (Solving ME/CFS kb matrix v2, Nov 2026): no single muscle protein replicates at FDR. CKM g -0.44 (3 of 3 cohorts, p=0.02, q=0.63; not measured in UK Biobank) and MYL3 g -0.32 (3 of 3) are the most consistent; myoglobin (-0.66 / -0.04 / +0.49 / -0.24 across Germain, UKB, Hoel, Walitt), CA3 (low only in Hoel) and troponins (pooled within ±0.1) disagree. The set-level shift is therefore real but modest and weighted by Hoel 2026.

Deconditioning versus disease

Several designs (aerobic-capacity-matched controls, idiopathic-fatigue and MS comparison groups, and a 60-day bed-rest model) indicate that deconditioning alone does not explain the exercise and muscle abnormalities in ME/CFS. Several studies

It is often said patients are just unfit from resting. Studies that compared them with equally unfit people or with healthy volunteers kept in bed found differences that inactivity did not produce.

Keller 2024: day-2 declines persisted in 55 pairs matched for peak VO2. van Campen 2021 and Hodges 2018: idiopathic chronic fatigue and MS patients improved on day 2. Lane 1998: biopsy changes were not those of inactivity. Charlton 2026: bed rest caused atrophy with preserved fibre type and capillary-to-fibre ratio; patients showed the opposite pattern; OXPHOS-VO2max coupling present after bed rest but absent in patients. Vermeulen 2014: a high cardiac output/VO2 slope argues against central deconditioning. These are mostly cross-sectional and from enthusiast centres; Mancini 2026 found no day-2 decline at all.

Blood markers of muscle and mitochondrial stress

Serum GDF15, a mitochondrial stress hormone, is higher in severe ME/CFS but only marginally in mild and moderate cases, and does not reach the levels seen in mitochondrial myopathy. Several studies

A blood marker of cell energy stress is raised in the sickest patients, but much less than in genetic mitochondrial disease.

Melvin 2019 (UK Biobank cohort, 150 ME/CFS vs 150 controls vs 50 MS): 602 vs 491 pg/ml in severe cases (P=0.01), stable over 7 months, correlated with fatigue. Bermejo-Guerrero 2023 used GDF15 to separate primary mitochondrial myopathy (high) from CFS (near normal). GDF15 also rises with age, kidney function and many illnesses, so it is a non-specific stress marker.

Muscle excitability

About half of patients (39 of 72) had altered muscle membrane excitability (M-wave) at rest and in exercise, with more oxidative stress and less potassium outflow; the rest looked normal. Early

Electrical tests of muscle split patients into two groups, one with abnormal muscle membrane behaviour and signs of oxidative stress.

Jammes 2020 (Marseille). Same group has reported oxidative stress and M-wave changes since 2005. Supports subgrouping; needs independent replication.

Key reviews

  • Scheibenbogen & Wirth 2025, J Cachexia Sarcopenia Muscle: Collects the evidence for skeletal muscle disturbance and the sodium/calcium overload model (advocacy-leaning, from the model's authors).
  • Charlton 2025, Trends Endocrinol Metab: Opinion piece from the Amsterdam biopsy group on muscle adaptations and PEM in long COVID.
  • Lim 2020, J Clin Med: Meta-analysis of 2-day CPET; workload at ventilatory threshold is the most discriminating measure.
  • Franklin & Graham 2022, Fatigue: Biomed Health Behav: Meta-analysis estimating clinically meaningful day-2 drop in work at anaerobic threshold (-21 W).
  • Stevens 2018, Front Pediatr: Methods paper for administering 2-day CPET in ME/CFS.
  • Fanò-Illic 2026, Diagnostics: Recent review of skeletal muscle involvement in ME/CFS (title/abstract seen only).
  • Solving ME/CFS re-analyses (PEM, serum-check, proteome): Within-person re-analysis of Germain 2022 metabolomics; participant-level check of Ryback 2026; muscle-protein meta-analysis.

Nervous system and brain

The most consistent nervous-system findings in ME/CFS are physiological rather than anatomical. Brain blood flow drops more than normal when patients are upright, often with over-breathing (low CO2), and resting heart-rate variability is lower; both are seen across several independent labs. Small-fibre nerve loss on skin biopsy is common in referral clinics (roughly 30-55%), but the main controlled NIH study found no difference, and nobody has yet shown that nerve loss explains symptoms. Brain imaging gives many positive but small and mostly unreplicated results: raised ventricular lactate (mostly one group), raised brain temperature (one study), TSPO-PET neuroinflammation (one positive and one negative ME/CFS study), and newer diffusion MRI signals. Structural MRI, routine sleep studies and markers of nerve injury are mostly normal or inconsistent. The NIH 'effort preference' interpretation has been seriously challenged, because patients in that study often could not complete the hard task. Claims about craniocervical instability rest on uncontrolled clinic series and case reports.

Cerebral perfusion / orthostatic

Blood flow to the brain falls much more than normal during head-up tilt in ME/CFS (about 26% vs 7% in controls), including in patients whose heart rate and blood pressure stay normal. Replicated

When patients are tilted upright, less blood reaches the brain than in healthy people, even if their pulse and blood pressure look normal. That can explain light-headedness and brain fog when standing.

van Campen 2020 measured extracranial carotid plus vertebral flow by Doppler during a 30-min tilt in 429 patients vs 44 controls. End-tilt drop was 7% in controls and 26% in patients overall: 24% with a normal HR/BP response, 28% with delayed orthostatic hypotension and 29% with POTS. About 90% exceeded the control range. Transcranial Doppler studies (Medow 2014; Novak 2026, 88% of 170 ME/CFS) agree. A 2025 systematic review (118 studies) found reduced CBF in 12 of 26 ME/CFS-only studies and a larger fall when ME/CFS and orthostatic intolerance coexist. Caveats: most data come from referral clinics; controls are few; and CBF velocity (transcranial Doppler) is not the same as volume flow.

Bears on: Low blood volume and preload failure Autonomic dysfunction and small-fibre neuropathy Endothelial dysfunction · Test: Tilt with extracranial Doppler (few centres, e.g. Netherlands) or transcranial Doppler in some autonomic labs; mostly research or specialist only

Many patients over-breathe when upright and lower their end-tidal CO2. This drives part of the fall in brain blood flow, and correcting it with phenylephrine restored blood flow and working memory in one small trial. Replicated

Standing makes some patients breathe off too much carbon dioxide. Low CO2 narrows brain blood vessels, so less blood reaches the brain. A drug that tightens blood vessels prevented this and improved a memory test in a small study.

Medow 2014: on tilt, ETCO2 was 33.9 vs 42.8 Torr in 15 CFS vs 11 controls. Phenylephrine prevented the hypocapnia, cut the CBFv fall from 22.5% to 8.1%, and returned n-back reaction time to supine levels. Yamazaki 2026: 40.8% of 49 adults met the criteria for postural orthostatic syndrome of hypocapnia (POSH) on a lean test with capnography, more often than POTS. Novak 2026 defines a hypocapnic cerebral hypoperfusion phenotype. In long COVID (O'Brien 2026, n=50), 64% had supine or orthostatic hypocapnia. Solving ME/CFS re-analysis: hypocapnia on tilt is reported by 5 groups and the CBF fall by 4. Treatment evidence is still single-group and acute.

Autonomic

POTS occurs in a minority of ME/CFS patients, and published rates vary widely (about 6-43%) with the setting, the age group and the test protocol. Contested

Some, but not most, people with ME/CFS meet the heart-rate criteria for POTS. How many depends a lot on who was tested and how.

van Campen 2020: 120 of 429 tilt-tested patients (28%) had POTS. Novak 2026: POTS in 19% of ME/CFS and 22% of long COVID, but widespread mild autonomic failure in 89-95%. Adolescents (Leone 2026): PoTS in 7/18 ME/CFS vs 0/18 controls on a 10-min stand, although 83% reported OI symptoms. In the NIH cohort (Walitt 2024, n=17), tilt showed no excess tachycardia. Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of the literature: POTS prevalence is inconsistent (6-43%) and lists it among the contradictory findings. Orthostatic intolerance symptoms are far more common than POTS defined by heart rate.

Resting heart rate is higher and high-frequency heart-rate variability lower in ME/CFS. This fits reduced vagal (parasympathetic) tone. Replicated

The 'rest and digest' nerve signal to the heart looks weaker. The heart beats a little faster at rest, and its beat-to-beat variation is reduced.

Nelson 2019 meta-analysis (64 case-control studies): resting HR +4.1 bpm, HR on tilt SMD 0.92, resting LF/HF SMD 0.39 higher, HF-HRV SMD -0.34, and peak HR 13.8 bpm lower. Walitt 2024: 24-h Holter SDNNi, rMSSD and pNN50 were lower, HF and LF power reduced, and Valsalva baroreflex-cardiovagal function was lower. Effects are moderate. They are not specific to ME/CFS, and deconditioning, medications and sleep loss confound them. HRV is not a diagnostic test.

On the 10-minute NASA lean test, a subgroup of recent-onset patients shows a rising heart rate with an abnormally narrow pulse pressure. Autonomic specialists say the test has not been validated against tilt or active stand. Several studies

The lean test (standing against a wall for 10 minutes while pulse and blood pressure are recorded) is a cheap way to see orthostatic problems. It is useful for spotting a pattern, but it is not an approved test for diagnosing POTS.

Lee 2020 (Bateman Horne Center): 150 ME/CFS (75 ill <4 y, 75 ill >10 y) vs 75 controls. At least 5 min was needed to see changes. The <4-y group had higher HR, a narrower pulse pressure and more OI symptoms, interpreted as inadequate ventricular filling. Yamazaki 2026 found lean-test abnormalities (most often hypocapnia) in 55% of 49 patients, unrelated to measured blood volume. Teuschl 2025 (European autonomic experts) argue that NLT criteria were borrowed from 1970s NASA physiology, that the leaning posture mixes active stand and passive tilt, and that the NLT 'may currently not be used as a diagnostic tool'.

Blood adrenaline is modestly raised in ME/CFS (pooled SMD 0.49 across 37 studies), with atypical catecholamine responses to exercise. Several studies

Pooling many small studies, patients have somewhat higher levels of the stress hormone adrenaline in blood, which fits a body running on sympathetic drive.

Hendrix 2025 meta-analysed 37 studies (543 ME/CFS, 747 controls): adrenaline SMD 0.49 (95% CI 0.31 to 0.67). Noradrenaline differences were less consistent. Exercise studies showed atypical rises. The pattern was clearer in ME/CFS than in fibromyalgia. Caveats: small heterogeneous studies, sampling posture and time of day vary, and catecholamines are sensitive to stress of venepuncture. CSF catechol metabolites are lower (Walitt 2024), so central and peripheral signals may differ.

Evidence

StudynDesignResult
Hendrix 2025, Eur J Clin Invest37 studies; 543 vs 747meta-analysisAdrenaline SMD 0.49 (0.31 to 0.67); atypical exercise responses

  • Is the rise driven by low blood volume (a compensatory response) or by a primary central change?
  • Does it track severity or PEM?

Heart-rate variability is lowest relative to controls during sleep, particularly deep sleep, consistent with sympathetic arousal persisting at night, and lower nocturnal HRV predicts poorer subjective sleep. Several studies

The nervous system seems to stay on alert during sleep, which may be part of why sleep does not refresh.

Burton 2010 (20 vs 20): nocturnal HRV lower and predicted unrefreshing sleep. Fatt 2020 (24 vs 24): normalised HF-HRV reduced in deep sleep but not awake. Meeus 2013 review: HRV differences in CFS mainly during sleep. Polysomnography adds more micro-arousals (Neu 2009) and alpha intrusion into NREM sleep (older studies). Gotts 2013 (343 patients): 30% had a primary sleep disorder and 89% an objective sleep problem; Mariman 2012 found an insomnia-like subgroup (69 of 415). Togo 2010: a maximal exercise test did not worsen the following night's sleep, so PEM is not simply a result of bad sleep.

Small-fibre neuropathy

Skin biopsies show reduced small-nerve-fibre density in about 31-53% of ME/CFS patients from specialist referral cohorts, but the controlled NIH study found no difference from healthy volunteers. Contested

In some clinics, a third to a half of patients have lost some of the thinnest nerves in the skin. Those nerves control sweating and blood vessels. But a carefully matched NIH study did not find this, so how common and how important it is remains uncertain.

Joseph 2021 (Systrom/Oaklander, Harvard): 31% of 160 ME/CFS biopsies were consistent with SFN (epidermal innervation <=5th percentile of predicted). Denervation severity did not correlate with exertional measures. Novak 2026 (same network): SFN in 53% of ME/CFS and 67% of long COVID; hEDS had more severe neurodegeneration. Azcue 2025 (30 ME/CFS, 30 long COVID, 30 HC) found corneal fibre tortuosity and heat-detection changes rather than a clear length-dependent pattern. Walitt 2024: no difference in small-fibre density. Major caveats: the positive cohorts were referred for exertional intolerance or dysautonomia; biopsy normative cut-offs and patchy, non-length-dependent SFN make rates sensitive to method; and ME/CFS-specific matched-control biopsy studies are few. Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of Finnish registry data: an SFN diagnosis is about 8-10 times more common than expected in post-viral fatigue (crude, shared with fibromyalgia).

Long COVID patients referred for neuropathy evaluation often have small-fibre neuropathy on skin biopsy, including loss of autonomic fibres to sweat glands and hair muscles. Several studies

Similar nerve damage turns up in long COVID, especially in patients with pain or nerve-type symptoms.

Oaklander 2022 (NIH/MGH): 10 of 16 skin biopsies (63%) in referred long COVID were abnormal; 52% average improvement over 1.4 years, often after immunotherapy (uncontrolled). Falco 2026: piloerector and sweat-gland nerve density reduced in 31 painful long COVID vs 42 controls, even with normal IENFD, but not correlated with COMPASS-31 symptom scores. These are selected samples with neuropathic complaints, so the results do not give a general prevalence.

Brain structure

Conventional structural MRI (grey matter volume, routine clinical reads) shows no consistent abnormality in ME/CFS. Reported regional volume differences rarely replicate across groups. Contested

Standard brain scans usually look normal. Studies that report bigger or smaller brain regions mostly disagree with each other.

Shan 2020 systematic review (63 imaging studies to 2018): the only findings reported by multiple teams were extra brain-area recruitment during cognitive tasks (11 studies), brainstem abnormalities (9), sluggish BOLD responses, reduced serotonin transporter and regional hypometabolism. Volumetric findings were inconsistent. Lee 2023 meta-analysis (65 studies, 1529 patients) reported insular and thalamic hypoactivity but noted poor inter-rater reliability. Walitt 2024: brain MRI unremarkable. Kimura 2026 (38 ME/CFS, 27 LC, 47 HC): amygdala subfield differences did not survive correction. For contrast, the UK Biobank pre/post scans (Douaud 2022) show that SARS-CoV-2 infection itself produces small grey-matter changes, although that sample was not long COVID or ME/CFS.

Advanced diffusion MRI models report widespread white-matter differences in ME/CFS that conventional DTI misses, and the pattern may differ between post-infectious and gradual-onset cases. Early

Newer scan analyses suggest subtle changes in the brain's wiring, possibly swelling or inflammation. Standard analyses of the same scans find little.

Yu 2026 (Shan group, 67 vs 67 matched): a neuroinflammation-imaging (NII) model gave lower hindered and restricted water fractions and higher fibre fraction across association, commissural and projection tracts. The authors read this as oedema, cellular infiltration and axonal reorganisation, while conventional DTI showed minimal differences. Yu 2025 (same group): post-infectious cases had higher axial diffusivity, while gradual-onset cases had lower AD in the corpus callosum. Singh 2026 (Griffith, 37 ME/CFS, 19 LC, 27 HC) found DTI/DKI alterations in the cingulum, SMA and corpus callosum. The model-based metrics are not validated against histology in ME/CFS, the analyses carry many degrees of freedom, and independent replication is missing.

Brainstem differences (volume larger or smaller, altered signal or connectivity) are among the more often repeated imaging findings in ME/CFS, though the methods differ between studies. Several studies

The brainstem controls breathing, heart rate and arousal. Several groups using different scans have reported differences there.

Shan 2020 counted brainstem abnormalities in 9 studies from different teams and modalities. Bader 2026 (preprint, 26 vs 27): brainstem volume 1.46 vs 1.55% of eTIV (FDR p=0.039), with deep grey matter and whole-brain volume unchanged. Inderyas 2026 (7T fMRI, 32 ME/CFS): altered cuneiform-nucleus to medulla connectivity during Stroop. The Griffith (Barnden/Thapaliya) group produced several of the brainstem reports, so the evidence is not fully independent. This imaging work does not support the mechanical 'craniocervical compression' model, which is a separate claim (see neuro-cci).

Functional MRI

After a single 30-minute exercise bout, women with ME/CFS performed worse on a demanding cognitive task and recruited more parietal and cingulate cortex. Controls improved. Early

Exercise made patients' thinking worse the next day, and their brains had to work harder at the same task. This is one of the few direct brain measurements of post-exertional malaise.

Cook 2017: 15 vs 15 women, scanned 1 week before and 24 h after 30 min of cycling at 70% peak HR. Group x time interactions showed worse PASAT performance in patients and increased activation in bilateral inferior/superior parietal and cingulate cortex, correlated with symptom change. Finger tapping did not differ. Patients cycled at lower watts, so absolute workload differed. Related work: Schönberg 2024 (34 vs 34) found that BOLD signals in ME/CFS did not adapt across repeated task blocks as they did in controls, and Shan 2020 counted extra task recruitment as a finding repeated by several teams. A direct replication of the exercise-provocation design has not been published.

Bears on: Neuroinflammation (microglial activation) Mitochondrial / energy metabolism impairment Persistent sickness behaviour / vagal signalling · Test: research only

During a sustained grip task, ME/CFS patients fatigue earlier while their brain motor-network activity fails to ramp up as it does in controls (NIH; reduced temporoparietal-junction activation). Early

When squeezing repeatedly, patients tire sooner. Their brains do not step up the drive to the muscle the way healthy brains do.

Walitt 2024 reported decreased right temporoparietal junction activation during repeated 50% MVC grip in fMRI and a faster decline in force. The authors linked it to 'effort preference', which is disputed. Bedard 2026 (NIH, 15 vs 19, EEG+EMG+fMRI) found that maximum force was equal, but patients reached fatigue much earlier and showed minimal change in brain and muscle activity across blocks. Healthy controls increased activity until fatigue. Interpretation: a central contribution to fatigability. Both studies come from the same NIH programme and have small samples.

MR spectroscopy

Brain lactate measured by MR spectroscopy is raised in ME/CFS: ventricular CSF lactate in three cohorts from one group, and thalamic or regional lactate in two other groups. It is also raised in depression, so it is not specific. Several studies

Brain scans that measure chemicals show more lactate, a by-product of energy production without enough oxygen, in patients' brains. The same change appears in depression.

Mathew 2009: ventricular lactate +348% vs healthy and +297% vs anxiety disorder (16 vs 15 vs 14). Shungu 2012 (third cohort, 15 vs 13): raised lactate and lower cortical glutathione, not different from major depression. Natelson 2017 replicated higher lactate, lower GSH and lower CBF in pooled CFS. Mueller 2020 (Younger group, whole-brain EPSI, 15 vs 15): raised LAC/CR in some regions, overlapping with raised temperature. Bader 2026 (Vienna, 26 vs 27, preprint): thalamic Lac/tCr 0.171 vs 0.135 at normoxia, with no further rise under hypoxia, unlike controls. Bradley 2016 found raised ventricular lactate in adolescent depression. Small samples, MRS quantification at 3T near detection limits, and the lack of specificity limit interpretation.

MRS thermometry found raised temperature in several brain regions (insula, putamen, frontal cortex, thalamus, cerebellum) in women with ME/CFS, not explained by body temperature. Early

One study found parts of the brain running slightly warmer in patients, which could signal low-grade inflammation. It has not been repeated.

Mueller 2020: 15 vs 15 women, whole-brain echo-planar spectroscopic imaging. Temperature was raised in the right insula, putamen, frontal cortex, thalamus and cerebellum (p<0.05, many regions tested), along with raised choline/creatine in the left anterior cingulate. The method responded to an experimental inflammatory challenge (typhoid vaccine) in 44 of 47 regions, but whole-brain temperature did not change (Plank 2022), so its sensitivity is modest. No independent ME/CFS replication was found.

PET neuroinflammation

TSPO-PET evidence of microglial activation in ME/CFS is contested: one Japanese study found 45-199% higher binding in limbic and brainstem regions, and a Dutch study using the same tracer found none. Contested

A special scan for brain immune cells showed inflammation in one small study and none in another of the same size. The question is open.

Nakatomi 2014: [11C]-(R)-PK11195, 9 vs 10. BPND was higher in the cingulate, hippocampus, amygdala, thalamus, midbrain and pons, and correlated with cognitive impairment and pain. Raijmakers 2021: same tracer, 9 CFS, 10 Q-fever fatigue and 9 matched women, stricter exclusion. No difference, and a negative correlation with severity in CFS. Both used the cerebellum as reference region, which can bias results if the reference is also affected. PK11195 has a low signal-to-noise ratio, and second-generation tracers need TSPO genotyping. Stanford DPA-713 data exist only as a conference abstract (not verified). A Belgian [18F]DPA714 study is in protocol (Dooms 2026).

In long COVID, one [11C]PBR28 PET study found widespread raised TSPO signal that correlated with vascular markers, and a [11C]PK11195 study found no group difference. Contested

Long COVID brain-inflammation scans also disagree. One found widespread signal and another found none.

VanElzakker 2024: 12 PASC vs 43 normative controls. Raised PBR28 in the mid and anterior cingulate, corpus callosum, thalamus, basal ganglia and periventricular regions, correlated with plasma vascular-dysfunction analytes. Cerebral perfusion

Resting (supine) cerebral blood flow by ASL or SPECT is reported as lower in some ME/CFS studies, but the results are inconsistent and often confounded by unmeasured orthostatic intolerance. Contested

Lying-down brain blood flow is sometimes lower, but not consistently. The clearest effect appears when patients are upright.

Shungu 2012 (ASL) found lower rCBF in the left anterior cingulate and right lingual gyrus vs controls, but not vs depression. Natelson 2017 pooled CFS had lower CBF. Christopoulos 2025 review: only 12 of 26 ME/CFS-only studies found reduced CBF, and most did not record OI status. Bader 2026: whole-brain CBF responses to hypoxia were similar in mean but far more variable in patients (variance ratio up to 6.9).

Cerebrospinal fluid

In the NIH cohort, CSF levels of the catechol metabolites DOPA, DOPAC and DHPG were lower in post-infectious ME/CFS. Noradrenaline and dopamine did not differ. Early

Spinal fluid showed lower breakdown products of dopamine and noradrenaline, which hints at reduced activity of these brain chemical systems. It comes from one small study.

Walitt 2024: CSF DOPA, DOPAC and DHPG were reduced; noradrenaline, cys-DOPA and dopamine were unchanged. Excluding participants on central-acting drugs did not change the result. Catechols correlated with perceived symptoms and, in patients, with only one cognitive test (WCST). CSF metabolomics also showed lower glutamate, tryptophan, spermidine and citrate. n was about 17 vs 21, with many outcomes and no correction across domains. Solving ME/CFS re-analysis: plasma VMA showed nothing, which fits a central rather than peripheral signal but is weak support.

CSF cytokine and proteome studies report differences (e.g. raised eotaxin/CCL11, distinct immunotypes), but no CSF protein signature has replicated, and ME/CFS and fibromyalgia CSF proteomes were indistinguishable. Contested

Spinal-fluid tests have hinted at immune changes, but different studies point in different directions, and none gives a reliable marker.

Baraniuk 2005: pooled and individual CSF proteomics (about 10-20 per group) gave a 5-protein set with 80% concordance; pilot only. Hornig 2016 (online 2015): 32 cases vs 40 MS vs 19 controls, 51-plex. CCL11 was raised and the IL-1 network disturbed, with interpretation hindered by the small control group. Schutzer 2023: 2083 proteins quantified; no protein differed between ME/CFS with and without fibromyalgia. Bastos 2025 (40 cases, CSF in cases only) found two MMP-defined clusters. Bragée 2026 (31 cases, no CSF controls) found complement/coagulation pathways associated with severity and POTS. Solving ME/CFS re-analysis: the Walitt CSF SomaScan set gives 0 FDR hits, and CSF neuronal markers do not replicate.

Targeted CSF metabolomics found raised serine and phospholipids and reduced 5-methyltetrahydrofolate in ME/CFS, with different metabolite responses to exercise than in controls. Early

Spinal fluid chemistry suggests changes in a vitamin/amino-acid pathway (folate and serine), possibly affecting brain fats. These are single-group results.

Baraniuk 2025 (Sci Rep; separate non-exercise and post-exercise LP cohorts): ME/CFS showed raised serine, sarcosine, creatine, purines and sphingomyelins and lower 5MTHF, dimethylglycine and choline. After exercise, metabolites were consumed in ME/CFS but generated in controls. The design is cross-sectional with separate cohorts per condition, not paired. Earlier Baraniuk 2021 work found little non-exercise ME/CFS vs GWI difference. NIH found lower CSF glutamate, tryptophan and spermidine (Walitt 2024), so the two sets point in different directions.

Craniocervical / intracranial pressure

Uncontrolled clinic series report high rates of craniocervical 'obstruction', low-lying tonsils and signs of raised intracranial pressure in severe ME/CFS, and surgical case reports describe improvement. There are no controlled imaging studies or trials. Early

Some clinics report that many severe patients have crowding where the skull meets the neck, or high spinal-fluid pressure, and a few patients improved after neck surgery. Without comparison groups or controlled trials, it is unknown whether these findings are more common than in healthy people or whether surgery helps.

Bragée 2020 (Swedish referral clinic, 229 CCC patients, retrospective): hypermobility 50%, enlarged optic-nerve-sheath ratio 55%, possible IH signs 83%, tonsils below McRae line 56%, and cervical 'craniocervical obstructions' 80% of 125 scanned. No controls; MRI reads were not blinded and the radiological thresholds are not validated. Jolley 2026 (34 cases, no controls): LP opening pressure >=20 cmH2O in 38%; that group reported more relief after LP (80% vs 19%, unblinded). Rowe/Edwards case reports (3+1 patients) describe improvement after cervical decompression. Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of Finnish registry data: CSF-leak codes are not specific (36% of LPs in ME/CFS vs 32% in fibromyalgia, 45% in hypermobility). Neurosurgical series (Ruhoy 2025, n=717) are in connective-tissue-disorder cohorts, not ME/CFS. The evidence quality is low, and surgery carries serious risk.

Effort and motivation

The NIH claim that altered 'effort preference' defines post-infectious ME/CFS rests on the EEfRT (OR 1.65 for choosing hard tasks). Patients completed only 65% of the hard tasks they chose vs 96% for controls, which confounds preference with ability. Contested

The NIH team said patients chose the harder button-pressing task less often and called this 'effort preference'. Critics showed that many patients could not physically finish the hard task, so the choice more likely reflects ability than wanting to avoid effort.

Walitt 2024: 15 PI-ME/CFS vs 16 HV on EEfRT. Controls were 1.65x more likely to choose hard (95% CI 1.03-2.65, p=0.04), and no group difference in task-related fatigue response was reported. Kirvin-Quamme 2025 re-analysed mapMECFS data. Hard-task completion was 65% (SD 37) in patients vs 96% (SD 8) in controls; 7/15 patients completed fewer hard tasks than any control. Choice correlated with completion (rs 0.38). This fails the EEfRT's own ability check (Treadway 2009). Davenport 2025 (Nat Commun Matters Arising) also criticised the single-day CPET, matching for deconditioning and generalisation from n=17. The NIH reply defended single CPET on safety grounds. The effort result also sits on p=0.04 with no multiplicity correction.

Cognition

Meta-analysis shows moderate-to-large deficits in information-processing speed, attention, working memory and reaction time in ME/CFS, with intact vocabulary and reasoning. Performance worsens with upright posture and after exertion. Replicated

'Brain fog' shows up on tests as slower processing and difficulty holding information, especially over sustained effort, rather than loss of intelligence or knowledge.

Cockshell & Mathias 2010: 50 studies, deficits mainly in attention, memory and reaction time, with fine motor speed, vocabulary and reasoning spared. On tilt, n-back reaction time rose from 96 to 148 ms in CFS but not controls (Medow 2014). Post-exercise, PASAT performance fell (Cook 2017). The NIH study found no differences on any of 15 neuropsychological tests despite large subjective complaints (n=17), which shows that small samples and unprovoked testing can miss deficits. Reaction-time variability and sustained-attention tasks are more sensitive than standard batteries.

Sleep

Objective sleep in adult ME/CFS shows modestly longer sleep latency, more wake after sleep onset and lower sleep efficiency. Standard polysomnography usually finds no clinical disorder that explains non-restorative sleep. Several studies

Sleep studies show patients take longer to fall asleep and wake more, but the differences are small. They do not explain why sleep feels so unrefreshing.

Mohamed 2023 meta-analysis: 20 adult studies (426 vs 375) showed more time in bed, longer SOL and WASO, lower efficiency, less N2, more N3 and longer REM latency. In 4 adolescent studies (242 vs 235), total sleep was longer. Heterogeneity was high, and the stage-level findings are inconsistent with older reviews (Jackson & Bruck 2012: few PSG differences; microstructure, such as instability and alpha intrusion, more promising). Walitt 2024: PSG without clinically relevant findings. Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of Finnish registries: hypersomnia codes are enriched about 20-50x and sleep apnoea precedes diagnosis (HR 15), probably reflecting diagnostic work-up as well as biology. Primary sleep disorders still need excluding clinically.

Sensory sensitivity

Self-reported light and sound sensitivity is common in ME/CFS. One ERP study found normal early sensory gating (P50) but a reduced P300, pointing to higher-order processing rather than early filtering. Early

Many patients find light and noise hard to tolerate. The single brain-wave study suggests that the basic filtering of sounds is normal and that later attention steps are affected.

Kumar 2026: 31 vs 30, auditory paired-click and oddball paradigms. Patients reported more sensory problems; the P50 suppression index did not differ, while P300 amplitude was reduced. Severe and very severe patients report extreme sensitivity (Vink 2026 review), but they are largely absent from laboratory studies. There are no controlled studies of photophobia thresholds, hyperacusis audiometry or migraine-type central sensitisation specific to ME/CFS. The genetic overlap with chronic pain and migraine (Solving ME/CFS genetics re-analysis) is consistent with shared central sensitisation.

ME/CFS patients show generalised hyperalgesia, impaired conditioned pain modulation, and pain thresholds that fall (rather than rise) after exercise, correlating with post-exertional symptoms; comorbid fibromyalgia confounds several studies. Several studies

Most patients report that cognitive effort and emotional stress, not only physical exertion, bring on post-exertional malaise, and noise and light hypersensitivity is more common in ME/CFS than in MS and goes with worse symptoms. Several studies

Crashes are not only caused by physical activity. Thinking, conversation, stress, noise and light can set them off, according to patient surveys.

Chu 2018 (Stanford, 150 Fukuda-diagnosed): 90% had PEM after both physical or cognitive exertion and emotional distress; 10% reported no effect of emotion; exertion produced more symptoms than emotional distress. Maeda 2023 (DePaul Symptom Questionnaire, 2,240 people with ME/CFS or MS): noise and light hypersensitivity more frequent in ME/CFS, and people with both had worse symptom and SF-36 scores. Sandoval 2025 (2,313 ME/CFS, 299 long COVID) found noise/light hypersensitivity loads on a distinct neurocognitive factor. All self-report; no study has provoked a crash with a controlled sensory or cognitive challenge and measured breathing, brain blood flow and 72-hour symptoms.

Immune system

Immunology is the oldest and most heavily worked area of ME/CFS research, and the one with the widest gap between positive reports and independent replication. Reduced natural-killer-cell killing is the most repeated finding (meta-analytic Hedges g about 0.96 across 28 papers), yet the largest standardised multi-site attempt (MCAM, 174 vs 86) and two careful phenotyping studies found nothing, so the honest grade is 'contested and not usable as a test'. Several newer cell-level findings are more consistent in direction than in detail: CD8 T-cell exhaustion programmes, shifts in B-cell maturation (more naive, fewer switched-memory), monocyte dysregulation, and an exaggerated innate response to microbial stimulation that worsens after exercise. Cytokines look disturbed in aggregate (TNF, IL-2, IL-4, TGF-beta, CRP in meta-analysis) but no single cytokine survives as a marker, TGF-beta turned out to be largely a blood-handling artefact, and the clearest pattern is that abnormalities depend on illness duration (Hornig 2015) and severity (Montoya 2017) rather than on diagnosis alone. The autoimmunity strand has had the clearest negative resolution: GPCR autoantibodies against beta2/M3/M4 receptors are not reproduced by unbiased antigen profiling, removing them by immunoadsorption fails against sham, rituximab failed in a 151-patient RCT, and BC007's larger trial failed; what survives is narrower and interesting - patient IgG does things to endothelial mitochondria and, in long COVID, transfers pain and fatigue-like phenotypes to mice, and plasma-cell depletion with daratumumab produced striking but uncontrolled responses in 6 of 10 patients. Common-variant genetics (DecodeME) shows no enrichment in any blood immune cell type, which pushes most of these immune findings toward being consequences or state markers rather than inherited causes.

NK cells

Natural-killer-cell cytotoxicity is reduced in ME/CFS in meta-analysis of the older literature (Hedges g ~0.96), but the largest standardised multi-site study and two deep-phenotyping studies found no difference. Contested

The most-repeated immune finding in ME/CFS is that one type of white blood cell kills target cells less well. When labs tried to turn it into a standardised test, the difference disappeared.

Baraniuk, Eaton-Fitch and Marshall-Gradisnik 2024 pooled 28 papers and 55 effector:target data points: cytotoxicity about half of control levels, overall Hedges g 0.96 (0.75-1.18), heterogeneity high and explained by E:T ratio and method. Against this: the CDC Multi-Site Clinical Assessment (MCAM) sub-study used an assay validated for overnight-shipped blood in 174 ME/CFS vs 86 healthy controls and found 34.1% vs 33.6% cytotoxicity (p=0.79), with no association with symptom domains; Theorell 2017 found no reproducible difference in two cohorts (48 patients) across granule content, exocytosis, killing or adrenaline sensitivity; Cliff 2019 found no difference in NK numbers, subsets or in vitro responsiveness in 251 patients (54 severe) vs 107 controls. The assay requires fresh blood and is highly method-sensitive, so publication-era and logistics effects are plausible explanations for the discrepancy. Treat reduced NK function as a real signal in some cohorts with some assays, not as a disease marker.

Bears on: Immune (T-cell) exhaustion Herpesvirus reactivation (EBV, HHV-6) Viral persistence · Test: Private NK-function assays exist but need a same-day fresh sample; not validated for diagnosis (MCAM explicitly says so)

Reduced TRPM3 ion-channel current and calcium influx in patients' NK cells has been reported repeatedly, including a two-site study (36 vs 42), but only ever by one research group. Early

One Australian group finds that a calcium channel on immune cells works poorly in patients, which they argue explains weak NK killing. No other lab has tested it.

Sasso 2026 (Front Med) ran whole-cell patch-clamp on isolated NK cells at two laboratory sites with independent investigators: 36 CCC-defined ME/CFS vs 42 healthy controls, significant reduction in all TRPM3 parameters with no site effect. Earlier work in the same programme: Eaton-Fitch 2022 (impaired TRPM3-dependent calcium influx, restored in vitro by naltrexone), Eaton-Fitch 2021 (TRPM3/PIP2 co-localisation), Magawa 2026 (deficient TRPM3-linked mitochondrial calcium influx), plus a post-COVID extension (Magawa 2026, Eur J Immunol) and LDN restoration in long COVID NK cells (Sasso 2025). The 'two sites' are both within the same group's network, so this is internal consistency rather than independent replication; patch-clamp of isolated NK cells is a demanding, low-throughput method available in very few labs. Against it indirectly: DecodeME common-variant genetics shows no enrichment in any blood immune cell type, and the low-dose naltrexone RCT in post-COVID ME/CFS (n=137) was negative, which weakens the therapeutic corollary.

Bears on: Sodium-calcium overload in muscle (Wirth & Scheibenbogen) Immune (T-cell) exhaustion Autonomic dysfunction and small-fibre neuropathy · Test: research only

T cells

CD8+ effector-memory T cells in ME/CFS show transcriptional and chromatin features of exhaustion, with supporting flow cytometry and an independent cell-free RNA signature. Several studies

Killer T cells in patients look 'worn out', like cells that have been fighting an infection for a long time.

Iu 2024 (PNAS) integrated scRNA-seq, bulk RNA-seq and ATAC-seq across sorted T-cell subsets (336,269 T-lineage cells from 28 patients and 30 sedentary controls at baseline and after symptom provocation), finding upregulated exhaustion transcription factors, altered chromatin accessibility and metabolic reprogramming most marked in CD8+ effector-memory and innate-like T cells, validated by flow cytometry in an extended cohort (15 patients, 11 controls, female, age/BMI matched). Gardella 2025 independently found T-cell-exhaustion and cytokine-signalling signatures in plasma cell-free RNA (93 vs 75). Supporting but not identical: Mandarano 2020 found reduced CD8+ mitochondrial membrane potential and reduced glycolysis at rest in 53 vs 45. The main caveat is that the Cornell scRNA cohorts are not independent of each other and a re-analysis of the same public scRNA data found no exhausted-CD8 composition difference once cell typing was redone, so the effect may live in gene programmes rather than cell counts.

Bears on: Immune (T-cell) exhaustion Viral persistence Herpesvirus reactivation (EBV, HHV-6) · Test: research only (specialist flow cytometry)

T-cell abnormalities differ by severity: mild/moderate patients show cytotoxic/immunosenescence features, severe patients show activated lymphocytes and higher stimulated pro-inflammatory cytokines. Early

Mildly and severely affected patients show different immune pictures, which may mean different disease mechanisms rather than one disease of different intensity.

Lee, Cliff and colleagues (UK ME/CFS Biobank; medRxiv 2025, J Transl Med Dec 2025) compared 43 mild/moderate with 53 severe patients by flow cytometry. Mild/moderate: increased cytotoxic effector molecules and more CD28-CD57- early-immunosenescent cells, a pattern associated with persistent viral infection. Severe: more CD69+ and CD38+ activated circulating lymphocytes and more IFN-gamma, TNF and IL-17 after in vitro stimulation, consistent with non-specific ongoing inflammation. Changes spanned CD8+ T cells, MAIT cells and NK cells. This is a within-patient-group comparison without a healthy-control contrast for the severity axis, and severe patients differ in sampling conditions (home visits, deconditioning, medication), so confounding by illness state is not excluded.

Increased mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cell proportions and a shift in CD8+ memory subsets were found in the largest single ME/CFS flow-cytometry cohort, but the finding has not been reproduced in independent data. Contested

One large study found more of a gut-associated T-cell type in patients, especially severe ones. Re-analyses of other datasets do not show it.

Cliff 2019 (251 patients incl. 54 severe, 107 controls, 46 MS) reported increased effector-memory CD8+ and decreased terminally differentiated effector CD8+ T cells, plus a significantly increased proportion of MAIT cells, most marked in severe patients, with no differences in herpesvirus seroprevalence. Iu 2024 also flagged 'certain innate T cells' as among the most dysregulated. Against: a re-analysis across five cohorts and three data types (scRNA of 503,739 PBMCs, four methylation cohorts, B- and T-cell repertoires) found MAIT, gamma-delta T, Th17 and exhausted-CD8 gating all null, and blood RNA cohorts do not show reduced Th17 (meta p=0.39).

Bears on: Gut dysbiosis Immune (T-cell) exhaustion · Test: research only

T-cell receptor repertoires do not distinguish ME/CFS from controls, arguing against a dominant shared antigen-driven clonal expansion. Refuted

If one infection or self-target were driving the disease, you would expect to see armies of identical T cells. Sequencing says they are not there.

Dibble 2024 (BMC Research Notes) sequenced alpha/delta, beta and gamma TCR loci in 40 samples each from severe ME, mild/moderate ME, MS disease controls and healthy controls, and applied P-SVM classification: the method worked on simulated data but could not partition the real samples significantly. A re-analysis of UK ME/CFS Biobank T-cell repertoires (304 samples) likewise found nothing passing FDR in more than one dataset, with only exploratory herpesvirus-related trends (higher share of EBV-specific TCR-beta in severe patients' CD8, 0.88% vs 0.45%, p=0.06). A near-genome-wide candidate, the TRA locus (Ueland 2022), has not replicated either.

Evidence

Dibble 2024, BMC Research Notes data4 groups x 40bulk TCR repertoire sequencing + machine learningNo statistically significant partitioning; 'findings do not support altered T-cell receptor diversity'

Open questions

  • Would antigen-specific sorting (rather than bulk repertoire) reveal expansions invisible in bulk?
  • Could tissue (muscle, gut, brainstem) repertoires differ while blood looks normal?

Bears on: Autoimmunity (functional autoantibodies) Viral persistence · Test: research only

B cells

The NIH deep-phenotyping study found more naive and fewer switched-memory B cells in post-infectious ME/CFS, consistent with chronic antigenic stimulation; supporting signals exist but are weak. Early

Patients seem to have more 'untrained' B cells and fewer that have already matured, as if the immune system keeps being prodded by something.

Walitt 2024 (Nat Commun) did intensive inpatient phenotyping of a small, rigorously selected post-infectious ME/CFS cohort (17 PI-ME/CFS vs 21 healthy volunteers for immune measures) and reported increased naive and decreased switched-memory B cells, interpreted as chronic antigenic stimulation and linked to STAT4-TLR9 B-cell pathway signals; PBMC gene-expression and metabolic differences were sex-dependent. A Solving ME/CFS re-analysis found plasma-cell/immunoglobulin transcripts lower in 2 of 4 blood RNA cohorts (meta d -0.42, p=0.06), which points the same way without reaching significance. Earlier B-cell phenotype work (Mensah 2016, 2018) found no reproducible subset differences but raised CD24 expression on naive and memory B cells. The cohort is tiny and much of Walitt 2024's framing (effort preference) is contested, so this should be read as a lead, not an established feature.

Reported skewing of the B-cell receptor repertoire (IGHV3-30/3-33 overuse) partially replicates in mild/moderate patients but shows no clonality, somatic-hypermutation or autoimmunity signature. Contested

An early report said patients over-use certain antibody genes. A careful follow-up found a trace of that but none of the signs you would expect if antibodies were driving the disease.

Sato 2021 (Brain Behav Immun) reported biased IGHV/IGHD/IGHJ usage in ME/CFS peripheral B cells with ROC separation from controls. Ryback and Cowan 2025 (Front Immunol) sequenced BCR heavy-chain repertoires in 25 mild/moderate ME/CFS, 36 severe, 21 healthy controls and 28 MS: no increased clonality and no differential somatic hypermutation versus healthy controls or MS; IGHV3-30 usage was replicated in mild/moderate patients only, but with no evidence of ongoing antigen-driven responses within IGHV3-30 repertoires and no infection or autoimmunity signature; a skewed IgM:IgG ratio in mild/moderate patients was the one new preliminary observation. A Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of UK ME/CFS Biobank repertoires (123 people) found IgM IGHV3-30/3-33 usage essentially identical (9.34% vs 9.37%, p=0.96).

Bears on: Autoimmunity (functional autoantibodies) Viral persistence · Test: research only

B-cell depletion with rituximab failed in a 151-patient placebo-controlled trial, after positive small phase II results. Refuted

A drug that wipes out antibody-making B cells looked promising in small studies, then failed completely in a proper large trial.

Fluge 2011 (PLOS ONE, n=30 randomised) reported major or moderate response in 10/15 on rituximab vs 2/15 on saline (p=0.003), with delayed onset 2-7 months. RituxME (Fluge 2019, Ann Intern Med) randomised 151 CCC patients to induction plus 4 maintenance infusions over 12 months or placebo: response rates 26.0% rituximab vs 35.1% placebo (difference -9.2 points, 95% CI -5.5 to 23.3 for placebo advantage, p=0.22), no difference in fatigue score over 24 months or any secondary endpoint, with more serious adverse events on drug (26.0% vs 18.9%). The high placebo response rate (35%) is the key number for reading every uncontrolled immunotherapy report in this field. A 6-year follow-up showed SF-36 physical function 45.5 vs 43.1, i.e. both groups improved similarly.

Evidence

  • Does rituximab's failure exclude autoantibodies, or only short-lived B-cell-dependent ones (long-lived plasma cells are CD20-negative)?

Bears on: Autoimmunity (functional autoantibodies) · Test: Not indicated

Plasma cells

Plasma-cell depletion with daratumumab produced marked, in some cases sustained, improvement in 6 of 10 patients in an open-label pilot, with low baseline NK count predicting non-response. Early

A myeloma drug that kills the cells making long-lived antibodies helped six of ten patients, some of them a lot and for years. It was a small study with no placebo group.

Fluge 2025 (Front Med, corrected 2025; EudraCT 2022-000281-18): 10 female moderate-to-severe patients, 12-week run-in, then subcutaneous daratumumab 1800 mg at weeks 0/2/4/6 (last four patients received three additional injections from week 14). No serious adverse events. All 10: mean SF-36 physical function 25.9 to 55.0 at 8-9 months (p=0.002), DSQ-SF 72.3 to 43.1 (p=0.002). Six responders: SF-36 PF 32.2 to 78.3, DSQ-SF 71.1 to 24.3, and five of the six sustained improvement with mean SF-36 PF 88 toward end of follow-up and step counts above 10,000/day for periods. Serum IgG fell 54% in improvers vs 40% in non-improvers. Low baseline blood NK-cell count was significantly associated with lack of response (responders 238 vs 97 cells/microlitre, rho 0.77). The design cannot separate drug effect from the 35%+ open-label/placebo response documented in RituxME, and n=10 with a post-hoc predictor is hypothesis-generating; an RCT is planned.

Bears on: Autoimmunity (functional autoantibodies) Circulating (serum) factor · Test: Lymphocyte subsets (NK count) and serum IgG are routine; the treatment is research/trial only

Cytokines

Plasma cytokine abnormalities depend strongly on illness duration: a pro- and anti-inflammatory activation pattern early (under 3 years) that is absent in long-established illness. Several studies

Blood inflammation markers look disturbed in people ill for a short time and normal in people ill for years, which may be why studies disagree.

Hornig 2015 (Sci Adv) used two multicentre cohorts with controls frequency-matched on season, site, age and sex: 52 cases ill under 3 years, 246 ill longer, 348 controls. Early cases showed prominent activation of both pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines and dissociation of inter-cytokine regulatory networks; this was not present in the longer-duration group. Cytokine alterations correlated more strongly with duration than with severity measures. This duration-dependence is the single most useful explanation for the field's inconsistency, and it has been widely cited but not formally replicated with a comparably large early-illness sample; it also cannot distinguish a biological evolution from survivorship/sampling differences between recent-onset and long-ill cohorts.

Bears on: Innate immune hyperactivation Persistent sickness behaviour / vagal signalling Immune (T-cell) exhaustion · Test: research only (multiplex cytokine panels are not clinically interpretable)

In the largest single cytokine study, 17 cytokines rose in step with disease severity although only TGF-beta (up) and resistin (down) differed between all patients and controls. Several studies

Comparing all patients with all controls shows almost nothing, but the sicker the patient, the higher a group of inflammatory signals.

Montoya 2017 (PNAS) measured 51 cytokines by Luminex in 192 ME/CFS patients and 392 healthy controls, regressing each on severity with covariates for age, sex, race and non-specific binding. On average only TGF-beta was elevated (p=0.0052) and resistin lower (p=0.0052). Seventeen cytokines showed significant upward linear trends with severity (CCL11, CXCL1, CXCL10, IFN-gamma, IL-4, IL-5, IL-7, IL-12p70, IL-13, IL-17F, leptin, G-CSF, GM-CSF, LIF, NGF, SCF, TGF-alpha), 13 of them pro-inflammatory; CXCL9 correlated inversely with fatigue duration. Caveats: severity is self-reported and correlates with inactivity, BMI and sleep; multiplex platforms have substantial non-specific binding (which this paper explicitly modelled, unlike most); and the TGF-beta result is now suspect on pre-analytic grounds (see immune-tgfbeta-artefact).

Bears on: Innate immune hyperactivation Persistent sickness behaviour / vagal signalling Mast cell activation · Test: research only

Meta-analysis of 42 studies finds small but significant elevations of TNF, IL-2, IL-4, TGF-beta and CRP, with 12 other proteins showing no difference. Several studies

Pooling all the cytokine studies shows a little extra inflammation on average, but the effects are small and inconsistent, so no blood test comes out of it.

Strawbridge 2019 (Neurosci Biobehav Rev) meta-analysed 42 studies of circulating inflammatory proteins in CFS versus unaffected controls: TNF ES 0.274 (p<0.001), IL-2 0.203 (p=0.006), IL-4 0.373 (p=0.004), TGF-beta 0.967 (p<0.001), CRP 0.622 (p=0.019); 12 proteins did not differ. The authors conclude inflammation is unlikely to be a primary feature in all patients and that subgroups may exist. Blundell 2015 reviewed 38 papers and found elevated TGF-beta in 5 of 8 studies and no other consistent cytokine, with no case-control differences after exercise. Corbitt 2019 reached an explicitly inconclusive verdict. Independent support for low-grade inflammation comes from UK Biobank: Beentjes/Ponting 2025 found inflammation, insulin-resistance and liver markers shifted in both sexes among 1,455 cases vs 131,303 controls, not explained by inactivity, with small effect sizes.
