Bears on: Innate immune hyperactivation Persistent sickness behaviour / vagal signalling · Test: CRP and ESR are routine but usually normal or only slightly raised; not diagnostic

The most-replicated single cytokine finding, elevated TGF-beta, is largely a blood-handling artefact driven by platelet activation during centrifugation. Refuted

The one cytokine that kept showing up high turned out to depend on how fast the blood was spun, because platelets release it.

Roerink 2018 (Neth J Med) measured plasma TGF-beta1 in two female CFS cohorts (50 patients/48 controls; 90/29) with controls recruited by patients as age-matched acquaintances. Within each cohort there was no patient-control difference, but between cohorts values differed greatly, traced to the centrifuge g-force: the lower force (1361 g) produced more platelet activation and higher P-selectin and TGF-beta. This is the clearest documented pre-analytic trap in ME/CFS immunology and it retrospectively undercuts Blundell's 5-of-8 TGF-beta tally and Montoya 2017's overall TGF-beta elevation. Roerink 2017 (J Transl Med), using a 92-marker proximity extension assay in 50 patients vs 48 neighbourhood controls, found TGF-beta no different and only IL-12p40 and CSF-1 raised.

Evidence

Roerink 2017, J Translational Medicine50 vs 48case-control, 92-marker PEA + ELISA, plus anakinra RCT samplesIL-12p40 and CSF-1 higher; TGF-beta not different; anakinra had no effect on circulating cytokines other than IL-1Ra

Blocking IL-1 with anakinra for four weeks did not improve fatigue in CFS, and did not change circulating cytokines beyond IL-1Ra itself. Refuted

A drug that blocks one of the main inflammation signals did not help, which argues against simple ongoing inflammation driving symptoms.

Roerink and colleagues ran a randomised placebo-controlled trial of daily anakinra 100 mg for four weeks in 50 severely fatigued female CFS patients (reported in Ann Intern Med 2017 and in the accompanying cytokine paper). After correction for multiple testing, anakinra had no effect on circulating cytokines other than IL-1Ra, and the trial did not produce clinical benefit. A companion endocrine analysis (Roerink 2018, Horm Behav) found a blunted cortisol awakening response in patients (4.2 vs 6.1 nmol/L, p=0.036) and a small anakinra effect on hair cortisol, indicating the drug was biologically active. The trial was short (4 weeks) and in a mostly moderate, female, Dutch cohort, so it cannot exclude benefit from longer or different immunomodulation.

Cerebrospinal fluid cytokine profiles differ from controls with raised eotaxin (CCL11) and disturbed IL-1 signalling, but CSF studies are small and partly contradicted by later proteomics. Early

Spinal fluid from patients looks immunologically different from healthy people's, hinting at inflammation inside the nervous system. The studies are small.

Hornig 2015 (Mol Psychiatry) analysed CSF from 32 ME/CFS cases, 40 MS patients and 19 normal subjects with a 51-plex assay: raised CCL11 (eotaxin, an eosinophil chemokine) in cases and an inverse relationship between IL-1 receptor antagonist and CSF-1, CSF-2 and IL-17F without changes in IL-1 alpha or beta, interpreted as disturbed IL-1 signalling and a shift toward a Th2/allergic pattern. Peterson/Brenu 2015 found CSF cytokine differences in 18 patients. Against: a Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of NIH CSF proteomics found IL-17 proteins null in both serum and CSF, and neuronal injury markers (NEFL, GFAP) flat. Lumbar puncture cohorts are inevitably small and self-selected, and MS is an imperfect comparator.

Newly reported elevations of serum IL-11 and MMP-9 in female ME/CFS patients are unreplicated single-cohort findings. Early

A 2026 study found two new inflammation-related proteins raised in patients. Nobody has checked it yet.

Chinnappan 2026 (Front Immunol) quantified IL-11 and matrix metalloproteinase-9 in serum from 40 female ME/CFS patients and controls (Nova Southeastern/Institute for Neuro-Immune Medicine), reporting both elevated, with an EBV framing. IL-11 is a fibrosis- and inflammation-associated cytokine and MMP-9 a matrix-remodelling enzyme, so the finding is thematically compatible with the extracellular-matrix disturbance in Che/Lipkin 2025 and the lower vascular mural/matrix proteins found across four proteomic cohorts. But single-cohort, single-lab, two-analyte studies in this field have a poor replication record, and MMP-9 in particular is sensitive to sample handling and neutrophil contamination. Listed here as the kind of new lead a living review should carry with an explicit 'unreplicated' label.

Bears on: Innate immune hyperactivation Endothelial dysfunction · Test: research only

Innate immunity

Whole-blood immune responses to microbial antigens are exaggerated in ME/CFS and worsen after exercise, alongside complement activation and metabolic abnormalities. Early

When patients' blood cells are shown bits of bacteria, they over-react, and the over-reaction is worse the day after exercise.

Che, Lipkin and colleagues 2025 (npj Metabolic Health and Disease; medRxiv July 2025) studied 56 ME/CFS cases and 52 healthy controls recruited in New York and California with 47 matched pairs, combining plasma metabolomics, proteomics and immune responses to microbial stimulation before and 24 h after exercise. They report exaggerated innate responses to microbial antigens, complement activation, impaired TCA/beta-oxidation/urea-cycle energy production, disrupted extracellular-matrix homeostasis with release of pro-inflammatory endogenous ligands, reduced cell-cell adhesion with gut dysbiosis, copper-dependent redox disturbance and tryptophan-kynurenine dysregulation; many abnormalities worsened after exercise in patients but not controls and correlated with symptom intensity. This is a single-group study with very many readouts and no pre-registered primary endpoint; the stimulation assay is not standardised across labs. It is nonetheless one of the few designs that captures a post-exertional immune change at all.

Bears on: Innate immune hyperactivation Complement activation and thromboinflammation Gut dysbiosis Cell danger response (Naviaux) · Test: research only

Single-cell transcriptomics showed classical-monocyte dysregulation at baseline and platelet-activation signatures after exercise, but a re-analysis of the same data found no reproducible composition or expression differences. Contested

One study found patients' monocytes looked abnormal, and platelets reacted oddly to exercise. Reworking the same data did not confirm it.

Vu 2024 (Cell Rep Med) applied scRNA-seq to PBMCs from patients and controls at baseline and after exercise, reporting classical-monocyte dysregulation suggestive of inappropriate differentiation and tissue migration, with the fraction of 'diseased' monocytes correlating with severity, and post-exercise patterns indicating improper platelet activation with minimal change elsewhere. A Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of the same public dataset (GSE214283; 30 vs 28, 503,739 cells) with CellTypist majority voting and person-level pseudobulk found no composition differences at baseline (lowest q=0.41) or in the exercise change, and 0 genes at q<0.05 at baseline across 15 cell types (only NDUFA10 in non-classical monocytes in the 24 h change, q=0.037); platelet-RNA+ monocyte scores were null. There is no independent ME/CFS PBMC scRNA dataset from another group, which is the central problem. Older monocyte claims (Prieto 1989, naloxone-reversible monocyte dysfunction) were never replicated.

Cell-free RNA

Plasma cell-free RNA carries an immune-weighted ME/CFS signature that classifies cases with held-out AUC 0.81, with raised plasmacytoid-dendritic, monocyte and T-cell-derived transcripts. Early

Fragments of RNA floating in blood plasma, mostly from immune cells, differ enough between patients and controls to build a reasonably accurate classifier.

Gardella 2025 (PNAS) sequenced plasma cfRNA in 93 ME/CFS cases and 75 healthy sedentary controls. A LASSO generalised linear model trained on condition-specific signatures reached test-set AUC 0.81 and accuracy 77%. Deconvolution showed differences in platelet-derived cfRNA and elevated plasmacytoid dendritic, monocyte and T-cell-derived cfRNA; network analysis implicated cytokine signalling and T-cell exhaustion, converging with Iu 2024. Caveats: single cohort with internal hold-out rather than external validation; sedentary controls help but do not remove deconditioning confounding; cfRNA is sensitive to pre-analytic handling. A separate LLM-benchmarking paper using the same cohort (Gaudio 2026, Nat Commun) confirms the ME/CFS cohort is the hardest of three to classify, which is a useful calibration on effect size.

Evidence

Autoantibodies

Elevated IgG against beta2-adrenergic and M3/M4 muscarinic receptors, reported in about 30% of patients by ELISA, is not reproduced by unbiased high-throughput antigen profiling. Refuted

A commercial antibody test suggested many patients have antibodies against nerve-signal receptors. When measured with better, unbiased methods, the difference disappears.

Loebel 2015 (Brain Behav Immun) tested a Berlin cohort (n=268) plus pre/post samples from 25 rituximab-trial patients against a panel of GPCRs by ELISA versus 108 healthy controls: beta2, M3 and M4 antibodies significantly elevated, 29.5% of patients above threshold, correlating with IgG1-3 subclass levels and with activated HLA-DR+ T cells, TPO and ANA positivity; in rituximab responders with prolonged B-cell depletion beta2 and M4 antibodies fell, in non-responders they did not. Bynke 2020 partially validated this in two Swedish cohorts (M3 and M4 in both, beta1/beta2 in one; n=24+24 vs 24) with no correlation to severity and nothing detectable in CSF. The decisive negative is Germain, Jaycox, Ring and Hanson 2025 (IJMS 26:2799): 7,542 antibody-antigen interactions across 172 participants using REAP (6,183 extracellular human proteins, 225 viral antigens) and a 1,134-plex Luminex panel found no significant difference in any autoantibody reactivity, including beta-adrenergic receptors (no q below 0.68), with ADRB2, ADRA1A and GRK2 specifically not elevated. In POTS the same conclusion was reached with standard methodology: Hall 2022 (Circulation) found no difference across 11 receptors in 116 POTS vs 81 controls, with 98.3% of patients and 100% of controls above the manufacturer's alpha1 seropositivity threshold, i.e. the commercial cut-offs are not meaningful.

Removing autoantibodies by immunoadsorption helps in open-label cohorts but fails against sham control, and antibody removal does not predict who improves. Refuted

Filtering antibodies out of the blood made patients feel better in studies without a comparison group, and did nothing once a fake treatment was used for comparison.

Open-label positives: Scheibenbogen 2018 (10 patients, 5 sessions, beta2-selected) and Stein 2024 (Lancet Reg Health Eur; 20 post-COVID ME/CFS with elevated beta2-AR antibodies; total IgG down 79%, beta2 antibodies down 77%, mean SF-36 PF +17.75, 14/20 responders at six months). The controlled trials are negative: IAMPOCO (Stortz 2026, Lancet Reg Health Eur) randomised 40 post-COVID patients in a patient-blinded sham-controlled crossover - no difference in symptom severity (Post-COVID Functional Scale OR 1.17, 95% CI 0.41-3.36, p=0.771; MFI-20 difference 2.4, p=0.437; Chalder 0.09, p=0.970; Bell -2.6, p=0.246; MoCA -0.01, p=0.993; handgrip 1.3, p=0.234), with more adverse events on immunoadsorption (24 vs 10), and GPCR antibodies depleted by immunoadsorption but not sham - i.e. the mechanism worked and the patients did not improve. IA-PACS-CFS (Charite, NCT05710770, 65 randomised 2:1) also failed its primary endpoint per conference report; the paper is not yet published. Wossidlo 2026 (Infection; 18 patients) found significant antibody reduction, return to baseline within 3-6 months, no improvement in objective performance, only slight self-reported pain/fatigue change and no correlation between antibody change and symptoms. Anft 2025 (Mol Ther; 12 patients) found antibody and cytokine reduction with improved neuropsychological testing and handgrip but no improvement in self-reported symptoms or ME/CFS questionnaires, and rebound within a month.

Bears on: Autoimmunity (functional autoantibodies) Low blood volume and preload failure · Test: Offered privately in some clinics; controlled evidence is negative

BC007 (rovunaptabin), an aptamer that neutralises GPCR autoantibodies, showed secondary-endpoint fatigue improvement in a 30-patient exploratory trial but failed in the larger company-run phase II. Contested

A drug designed to mop up the suspect antibodies looked promising in a tiny trial and failed in the bigger one. The company ran out of money.

reCOVer (Hohberger 2025, eClinicalMedicine; EudraCT 2022-001781-35) was a prospective exploratory placebo-controlled double-blind randomised phase IIa trial with crossover at Erlangen: 30 post-COVID patients with GPCR functional autoantibodies and fatigue as major symptom, 1350 mg rovunaptabin or placebo at day 0 and day 48. Primary endpoint was safety (9 vs 5 treatment-emergent adverse events, p=0.13). Secondary endpoints improved: FACIT-Fatigue effect size 2.10 (p=0.0378), Bell score 3.64 (p=0.0004), Fatigue Severity Scale -2.66 (p=0.0088), and 4 of 8 quality-of-life items, with confirmed neutralisation of the autoantibodies. However the separately run Berlin Cures phase II (BLOC, NCT05911009; about 114 participants across 19 European centres, results announced November 2024) reported the drug well tolerated but with no superiority over placebo; the company subsequently halted work for lack of funds and the full data are not published. A 30-patient crossover trial with safety as its primary endpoint and multiple positive secondary endpoints is weak evidence against a failed larger trial.

IgG from long COVID patients transfers pain, fatigue-like behaviour and small-fibre nerve damage to mice in three independent 2026 studies; no equivalent published ME/CFS transfer experiment exists. Several studies

Inject antibodies from long COVID patients into mice and the mice become more pain-sensitive and less active, which is strong evidence those antibodies do something. Nobody has published the same experiment with ME/CFS antibodies.

Chen, Appelman and colleagues 2026 (Cell Rep Med) transferred pooled total IgG from 34 WHO-defined long COVID patients (31 analysed; 15 post-infection asymptomatic controls) into C57BL/6 mice at 260 mg/kg (about one third of the mouse's circulating IgG), 8 mice per group, stratified into three subgroups by plasma GFAP, NFL and interferon-beta: pronounced and persistent mechanical hypersensitivity, reproduced by IgG drawn from the same still-symptomatic patients two years later, with subgroup-linked autoreactivities validated by independent assays. De Sa, Iwasaki and colleagues 2026 (Cell) found CNS- and PNS-reactive autoantibodies correlating with neurological symptoms, IgG reacting with human locus coeruleus, thalamus, adrenal and thyroid and cross-reacting with mouse sciatic nerve and meninges, and passive transfer inducing fatigue-like behaviour, loss of balance, thermal hyperalgesia, small-fibre nerve damage and increased pain-related neuronal activity. Mignolet 2026 (Acta Neuropathologica) transferred IgG from neurological long COVID patients into mice: transient mechanical allodynia and thermal hypersensitivity in week 1 with no anxiety, depression or memory effect; abolished by IgG-depleted serum or papain-digested IgG; IgG accumulated in lumbar dorsal root ganglia colocalising with proprioceptive and nociceptive neurons without local neuroinflammation. These are the template experiments from the fibromyalgia field (Goebel 2021, JCI). The honest caveats: pooled IgG at high dose, pain readouts dominate, the fatigue-like readouts are indirect, and none of this is ME/CFS.

Purified IgG from ME/CFS patients fragments mitochondria and shifts energetics in human endothelial cells, an effect absent with multiple-sclerosis and healthy IgG and lost on Fab/Fc cleavage. Early

Patient antibodies damage the energy machinery of blood-vessel cells in a dish; antibodies from healthy people and from MS patients do not.

Liu, Hollmann, Prusty and colleagues (medRxiv Aug 2025; Brain Behav Immun Health Feb 2026, 101187) isolated immunoglobulin complexes by protein G from 106 individuals: 39 ME/CFS, 15 post-COVID ME/CFS, 20 MS disease controls and 41 healthy controls, applied them to HUVEC endothelial cells, fibroblasts and PBMCs, and assayed mitochondrial morphology by confocal microscopy and energetics by Seahorse. Endothelial mitochondrial fragmentation occurred with female ME/CFS IgG (p=0.0018 vs controls) with increased spare respiratory capacity and raised IL-1beta (p=0.046), and no effect from MS or healthy IgG; the effect was lost on cleaving IgG into Fab and Fc, with the Fab fragment reproducing the energetic change and Fc alone inducing a hypometabolic phenotype; mass spectrometry found excess extracellular-matrix proteins and SPEG in the immune complexes. Authors' own limits: large inter-plate Seahorse variability forcing split experiments, IgM not captured, unexplained sex difference, autoantigen array arm only 12 vs 3, and nominal p-values across many readouts. Single lab, no independent replication. The same group previously reported ME/CFS serum fragmenting mitochondria in cell lines (Schreiner 2020, ImmunoHorizons, n=10). Context matters: the headline serum-factor claim in muscle cells failed a well-powered replication (Ryback 2026, 67 vs 53, maximal respiration +2.50 pmol/min, 95% CI -1.62 to 6.62, p=0.23).

Humoral deficiency

A sizeable minority of ME/CFS patients have IgG subclass or mannose-binding-lectin deficiency, with IgG3 and IgG4 the commonest phenotypes, and registry data show strong enrichment of coded antibody deficiency. Several studies

Some patients are mildly short of particular antibody types, which fits a history of frequent infections. Others have the opposite, with raised antibody levels.

Guenther 2015 (Hum Immunol) retrospectively analysed 300 CFS patients: 25% had decreased levels of at least one antibody class or subclass, IgG3 and IgG4 deficiency commonest, while another 25% had elevated immunoglobulins with excess IgM and IgG2; MBL deficiency in 15% versus 6% in a historical control group; similar frequencies in a second cohort of 168. Lutz 2021 (Biomolecules) found in 262 Austrian patients that 64.9% had a reduction or deficiency in at least one immune parameter and 26.3% showed activation or inflammation, with 17.6% having unclassified antibody deficiency (IgG3/IgG4 most common) and MBL reduced in 32%, deficient in 7%. Finnish national registry data (FinnGen/FinRegistry via Risteys, as used in the Solving ME/CFS re-analysis) show postviral fatigue syndrome enriched for coded IgG subclass antibody deficiency by 20-90x observed/expected, alongside EDS/hypermobility (about 100x) - but healthcare-use bias inflates such registry enrichments, and the published literature on immunoglobulins in ME/CFS is explicitly contradictory (12 studies for, 7 against in that review tally). Both clinic series lack contemporaneous matched controls.

Mast cells

Clinically relevant mast cell activation is reported in up to a quarter of ME/CFS patients, associates with orthostatic intolerance and POTS, and those patients report more benefit from mast-cell-directed treatment. Early

A quarter of patients have symptoms of over-reactive mast cells (flushing, rashes, food and smell sensitivity), and those patients more often have the fast-heart-rate-on-standing problem.

Rohrhofer 2025 (Diagnostics) analysed an Austrian patient-centred survey (687 completed) plus a retrospective clinical cohort (383 patients): mast cell activation prevalence rose over the disease course, up to 25.3% meeting criteria for clinically relevant MCA, and patients with MCAS plus orthostatic intolerance reported symptom alleviation after mast-cell-targeted treatment significantly more often than those without MCAS, while beta-blocker response did not differ (p=0.637); MCA involvement was significantly associated with orthostatic intolerance, especially POTS. Laboratory-level work is thin and small: Nguyen 2017 and Balinas 2018 (both Marshall-Gradisnik group, n=11-18) characterised mast cell progenitor phenotypes and TLR3 responses in PBMCs. There is no replicated serum tryptase or urinary mediator finding in ME/CFS, criteria for MCAS are themselves contested, and self-reported treatment response is not a controlled outcome. One small retrospective case series of continuous high-dose oral cromolyn in ME/CFS with MCAS (5 patients) reported benefit.

Sickness behaviour

In the interferon-alpha fatigue model, higher baseline IL-6 and IL-10 and a larger early cytokine and fatigue surge predict fatigue that persists after the immune trigger is gone. Early

Giving people interferon as hepatitis treatment causes fatigue; in a third it does not go away afterwards. Those people had a more reactive immune system before treatment started.

Russell 2019 (Psychoneuroendocrinology) followed 55 patients on interferon-alpha for chronic hepatitis C at baseline, during 6-12 months of treatment, and six months after, comparing with 54 CFS patients and 57 healthy volunteers. Eighteen (33%) had persistent fatigue (higher six months post-treatment than baseline). Those who went on to persistent fatigue had a greater fatigue increase in the first four weeks (7.1 +/- 1.5 vs 4.0 +/- 0.8, p=0.046), a trend to higher baseline IL-6, significantly higher baseline IL-10, and larger treatment-induced rises in both (more than doubled by week 4 relative to the others: p=0.011 for IL-6, p=0.001 for IL-10). This is the only human design that measures the immune system before the trigger. Limits: iatrogenic cytokine exposure is not a natural infection, HCV patients differ in many ways, n=18 in the key group, and the model's cytokine differences did not persist to follow-up. It sits alongside the acute sickness-behaviour literature (Capuron 2002: neurovegetative symptoms including fatigue appear within two weeks of interferon-alpha and are less paroxetine-responsive than mood symptoms).

Acute-infection symptom severity, and the pro-inflammatory cytokine response and genotypes behind it, predict who develops post-infective fatigue, while microbiological and psychological factors do not. Replicated

How severe your initial infection is, not which germ you had or your personality, predicts whether you stay ill. Cytokines track how ill you feel at the time.

The Dubbo prospective cohort (Hickie 2006, BMJ) followed 253 patients from acute EBV, Coxiella burnetii or Ross River virus infection: 29 (12%) had a disabling fatigue-pain-cognitive-mood illness at six months and 28 (11%) met CFS criteria, with a stereotyped phenotype at similar incidence after each infection, predicted largely by acute illness severity and not by demographic, psychological or microbiological factors. Vollmer-Conna 2004 (Psychol Med) showed in 21 acute Q fever and 48 acute RRV/EBV patients that spontaneously released IL-1beta and IL-6 from PBMC cultures correlated consistently with fever, malaise, pain, fatigue, mood and concentration, i.e. cytokines index the acute sickness response in humans. Vollmer-Conna 2008 (Clin Infect Dis) found IFN-gamma +874T/A and IL-10 -592C/A polymorphisms acted synergistically on illness severity, cytokine levels and duration across all three infections. This is the most solidly replicated immune-related causal structure in the field, but it explains the onset and early course rather than why illness persists for years, and the same group's later work found no persisting cytokine abnormality.

Long COVID

Long COVID immune profiling finds exhausted T cells, myeloid shifts, raised antibodies to non-SARS-CoV-2 viruses especially EBV, and low cortisol, giving a reference phenotype for post-infectious illness. Several studies

Long COVID studies, which are larger and better funded, find a similar picture to ME/CFS: worn-out T cells, signs of old viruses waking up, and low cortisol.

Klein 2023 (Nature) enrolled 275 individuals with or without long COVID for multidimensional immune phenotyping with unbiased machine learning: differences in circulating myeloid and lymphocyte populations, exaggerated humoral responses to SARS-CoV-2, higher antibody responses to non-SARS-CoV-2 pathogens particularly EBV, and lower cortisol in long COVID, with cortisol among the strongest discriminating features. Yin 2024 (Nat Immunol) found systemic inflammation, sex-specific perturbation of cytolytic subsets, more CD4+ T cells poised to migrate to inflamed tissue, exhausted SARS-CoV-2-specific CD8+ T cells and mis-coordination between T and B cell responses. These converge with the ME/CFS exhaustion and herpesvirus-reactivation strands; complement dysregulation in active long COVID (Cervia-Hasler 2024, Science) is, unusually for this space, independently replicated. The caution is that long COVID cohorts are heterogeneous, most participants do not meet ME/CFS criteria, and the low-cortisol finding has not replicated consistently in ME/CFS.

Genetics vs immunity

Common-variant genetics shows no enrichment of ME/CFS risk in any blood immune cell type, implying most immune findings are downstream consequences rather than inherited causes. Replicated

The largest genetic study points at brain cells, not immune cells. So the immune abnormalities are probably effects of the illness rather than its root cause.

DecodeME (15,579 PEM-required cases vs 259,909 controls, SNP heritability about 9.5% on the liability scale) shows enrichment in brain tissue and neurons with no enrichment in blood immune cell types; the Solving ME/CFS re-analysis reproduced all 8 loci exactly and found MAGMA enrichment in 11 brain regions and pituitary and none of 29 immune cell types (Th17 p=0.52), with S-LDSC enrichment only in CNS tissues and chromatin and no signal in ImmGen or blood-cell ATAC-seq. HLA-DQA1*05:01 is protective (p=1.4e-10) but the earlier ME/CFS HLA candidates (C*07:04, DQB1*03:03 from Lande 2020) are not among DecodeME's hits, and the TRA locus (Ueland 2022) did not replicate. Infection-onset and other-onset cases are genetically indistinguishable (rg 0.98). The qualifier: a GWAS of common variants in 15,000 people can miss rare-variant immune contributions, and the one NK-relevant gene near a lead locus (RAB27A, needed for cytotoxic granule release) is not the authors' preferred candidate but is as plausible as their pick.

Key reviews

  • Baraniuk, Eaton-Fitch & Marshall-Gradisnik 2024, Frontiers in Immunology: The definitive pooled estimate for the NK cytotoxicity literature (28 papers, g 0.96) - read alongside Querec 2023 for why it has not become a test.
  • Strawbridge 2019, Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews: The only quantitative meta-analysis of circulating inflammatory proteins (42 studies); gives the honest effect sizes.
  • Corbitt 2019, BMC Neurology: Systematic review concluding cytokines are not reliable biomarkers - the counterweight to single-cohort cytokine papers.
  • Mountford 2024, Pain Reports (international workshop position statement): Sets out how passive-transfer evidence should be read in symptom-based disorders, which is the key methodological frame for the 2026 IgG mouse studies.
  • Fehrer 2026, Autoimmunity Reviews (3rd Charite Fatigue Center conference): Current expert survey of the autoimmunity/post-COVID strand including unpublished trial results.
  • Wirth & Scheibenbogen 2020, Autoimmunity Reviews: The most-cited mechanistic version of the beta2-adrenergic autoantibody hypothesis; useful to read now that its testable predictions have mostly failed.
  • Solving ME/CFS re-analysis, deep2/singlecell_methyl and deep2/proteome SUMMARY.md: Systematic re-analysis of public immune-cell, methylation, repertoire and protein data; documents which published immune claims fail, and two specific artefacts (granulocyte contamination, cell-leak) that mislead naive users of these datasets.

Infection and viruses

The most solid finding in this area is about onset: about 1 in 10 people meet ME/CFS criteria six months after several unrelated infections (EBV, Q fever, Ross River virus, Giardia, SARS-CoV-2), and how severe the first illness was predicts this better than psychological factors do. Post-COVID cohorts confirm that infection raises the rate of new ME/CFS several-fold. Whether any virus is still active in people who already have ME/CFS is far less clear. Blood antibody and PCR studies of herpesviruses give mixed results. Tissue findings for enterovirus, HHV-6 and SARS-CoV-2 are small or unreplicated, though some of them are striking. SARS-CoV-2 antigen and RNA do persist in a minority of people for months, but three randomised trials of nirmatrelvir in established long COVID (about 1,200 people) were negative, and antiviral trials in ME/CFS are tiny and unreplicated. The XMRV episode, a retrovirus finding that turned out to be lab contamination, is a reminder that one striking virus finding needs blinded multi-lab replication.

Post-infectious onset

About 11-12% of people with confirmed EBV, Q fever or Ross River virus infection meet CFS criteria at 6 months, at a similar rate for all three pathogens, and the severity of the acute illness predicts it. Replicated

Three very different germs (a herpesvirus, a bacterium and a mosquito-borne virus) left about 1 in 10 people with the same long-lasting fatigue illness. The sicker someone was at the start, the more likely they were to stay ill.

The Dubbo prospective cohort (n=253, rural Australia) followed people from laboratory-confirmed acute infection: 29/253 (12%) had a post-infective fatigue syndrome at 6 months and 28 (11%) met CFS criteria. The phenotype was 'stereotyped' across pathogens, and acute severity predicted it, whereas demographic, psychological and microbiological factors did not. Because the result does not depend on which pathogen caused the infection, it points to the host response rather than to the particular microbe. The cohort was small, with few cases per pathogen, and was followed to 12 months.

Working model: step 1, Infection and immune priming (evidence for)

Bears on: Innate immune hyperactivation Persistent sickness behaviour / vagal signalling Cell danger response (Naviaux) · Test: No predictive test; documentation of the acute infection (serology/PCR at onset) is useful for subtyping.

After infectious mononucleosis in adolescents, 13%, 7% and 4% met paediatric CFS criteria at 6, 12 and 24 months; all 13 cases still ill at 24 months were female. Replicated

After glandular fever, many teenagers are still unwell at six months, but most recover over two years. Those still ill at two years were all girls.

Katz 2009 (n=301 adolescents aged 12-18, Chicago) screened for non-recovery and made diagnoses by blind review. Greater fatigue severity at 12 months predicted persistence, and acute-phase steroids did not raise risk. Jason and colleagues' follow-up of a larger college-student mono cohort (about 238 cases) found that baseline GI symptoms and low IL-13/IL-5 predicted non-recovery, per a secondary summary in the Solving ME/CFS re-analysis. Together with Dubbo, these data show the spontaneous recovery rates any treatment trial in recent-onset illness has to beat.

Working model: step 1, Infection and immune priming (evidence for)

Bears on: Herpesvirus reactivation (EBV, HHV-6) Immune (T-cell) exhaustion · Test: EBV serology (VCA IgM/IgG, EBNA IgG) confirms the IM trigger; no predictive test.

A waterborne Giardia outbreak in Bergen (2004) left chronic fatigue in 26% of exposed people vs 11% of matched controls 10 years later (adjusted OR 3.0), and more than half of those referred with lasting fatigue met CFS criteria. Several studies

A gut parasite outbreak in Norway, which was not a virus, also left a lasting excess of chronic fatigue and IBS a decade later.

Litleskare 2018 followed 1,252 laboratory-confirmed cases and 2,504 age- and sex-matched controls: at 10 years, chronic fatigue was 26% vs 11% (aOR 3.01, 95% CI 2.22-4.08) and IBS 43% vs 14% (aOR 4.74). Response rates at 10 years were around 46% of cases, so selection bias is possible. 'Chronic fatigue' here is a questionnaire measure, not a CFS diagnosis. Naess 2012 clinically evaluated 96 referred patients with persistent post-Giardia fatigue and found 58 (60%) met CDC CFS criteria. A gut-confined protozoan producing the same syndrome is strong evidence against any single-virus explanation.

Q fever fatigue syndrome (QFS) follows roughly 20% of acute Q fever and persists more than 10 years after infection in many patients, almost all of whom report post-exertional malaise; doxycycline did not help. Several studies

After the large Dutch Q fever outbreak (2007-2010), many people developed a lasting ME-like illness. Antibiotics aimed at the bacterium did not improve it.

Spronk 2023 surveyed 368 QFS patients 10 or more years after infection: median EQ-5D index 0.63, and 98.9% reported PEM complaints. Younger and middle-aged patients did worse. The Qure RCT (n=154) found that doxycycline was no better than placebo, and the initial CBT benefit had faded by 1-year follow-up (Raijmakers 2019). The failure of an antimicrobial against the original pathogen is consistent with a post-infectious host process rather than ongoing Coxiella infection. The ~20% figure comes from the Reukers 2019 introduction, a secondary source.

In RECOVER-Adult, new ME/CFS (IOM criteria) developed at 2.66 per 100 person-years after SARS-CoV-2 infection vs 0.93 in uninfected participants (HR 4.93), and 4.5% of infected participants met criteria. Replicated

COVID-19 roughly multiplies the chance of developing new ME/CFS by four to five. About 1 in 20 infected adults in a large US study met the diagnostic criteria.

Vernon 2025 (RECOVER-Adult, n=11,785 infected vs 1,439 uninfected) found 531/11,785 (4.5%) vs 9/1,439 (0.6%), and 88.7% of post-COVID ME/CFS cases also met RECOVER long COVID criteria. PEM (24%) was the most common ME/CFS symptom. The criteria were applied from self-report. A meta-analysis of 13 studies (1,973 long COVID patients) found 51% met ME/CFS criteria, but heterogeneity was high and the populations were selected clinic cohorts (Dehlia 2024). Registry signals of the same direction exist for H1N1 influenza (HR 2.04, Norway, Magnus 2015) and for COVID (HR ~1.6, Chen 2024 via the Solving ME/CFS re-analysis). Healthcare-seeking bias inflates some registry estimates (af Geijerstam 2026, via re-analysis), and the INSPIRE cohort found no excess after a COVID-positive vs COVID-negative test (Unger 2024, via re-analysis).

Bears on: Viral persistence Innate immune hyperactivation Autoimmunity (functional autoantibodies) · Test: No test; diagnosis is clinical (IOM 2015 criteria).

In Finnish registry data, ME/CFS (G93.3) is enriched 3-6-fold for prior viral infections (HSV, EBV, influenza, COVID, viral CNS infection) but not for bacterial pneumonia or erysipelas. Contested

In national health records, people with ME/CFS more often had earlier viral illnesses, but not more bacterial ones, which suggests viruses play a particular role.

Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of FinnGen R12 and FinRegistry (Risteys) found observed/expected ratios of 2-6 for viral infection codes vs ≤1 for bacterial codes, and protozoal intestinal infection was also enriched (18x). Limitations: FinnGen and FinRegistry overlap, so they are not independent. Coding and healthcare-seeking bias can inflate associations, and the timing of infection relative to onset is not always resolved. Infection-onset ME/CFS shares genetic risk with other onsets (DecodeME). The Giardia and Q fever outbreaks show that non-viral triggers also occur, so the viral excess is not absolute.

Open question: Is a herpesvirus still active, or did it leave an immune imprint?

Bears on: Viral persistence Herpesvirus reactivation (EBV, HHV-6) Innate immune hyperactivation · Test: n/a

EBV

In large well-characterised cohorts, standard EBV and other herpesvirus seroprevalence and overall IgG reactivity do not differ between ME/CFS patients and controls. Several studies

Ordinary EBV antibody tests look the same in people with ME/CFS as in healthy people, so a 'high EBV titre' on a routine panel does not diagnose anything.

UK ME/CFS Biobank (Cliff 2019; 251 ME/CFS including 54 severe, 107 healthy, 46 MS): no seroprevalence differences for six herpesviruses, whereas EBV seroprevalence was higher in MS. Blomberg 2019 (Swedish Canada-criteria cohorts vs blood donors, multiplex assay) found no significant overall differences, only minor relative differences for some antigens. Loebel 2017 peptide array (92 CFS vs 50 HC, 3,054 EBV peptides) found profiles 'quite similar' to controls. The exception was raised IgG to an EBNA-6 repeat, which has homology to human proteins. A meta-analytic tally in the Solving ME/CFS re-analysis lists 10 positive vs 2 negative EBV-antibody studies, so smaller older studies were more positive than the larger recent ones, a pattern typical of publication bias.

Charité studies report a deficient EBV-specific memory B- and T-cell response in CFS (absent or low EBNA-1/VCA antibody-secreting memory B cells in up to 76% of patients, fewer polyfunctional EBNA-1-specific T cells), while CMV responses were normal. Early

Instead of fighting EBV too hard, some patients' immune memory for EBV seems weak, which could let the virus reactivate more easily.

Loebel 2014 (PLoS One): EBNA-IgG low or absent in 10% of patients, and memory B-cell ELISpot showed diminished EBNA-1/VCA antibody-secreting cells in up to 76%. Ex vivo EBV-induced TNF-α/IFN-γ was lower, and triple-cytokine EBNA-1-specific CD4/CD8 cells were reduced, with no CMV difference. EBER-DNA but not BZLF-1 RNA was more frequent in blood cells, suggesting increased latent, not lytic, load. Sepúlveda 2022 re-analysed the 2017 array and found classification only when restricted to infection-onset patients (two candidate antigens, needing confirmation). The Solving ME/CFS single-cell re-analysis found a non-significant trend toward more EBV-specific TCRβ in severe patients' CD8 (0.88% vs 0.45%, p=0.06), which points the other way, to expansion rather than deficiency. Newer long COVID tetramer work (Ma 2026, Cell Rep Med) finds SARS-CoV-2-, CMV- and EBV-specific CD8 T cells skewed to terminally differentiated, exhausted, cytolytic states in long COVID.

Bears on: Herpesvirus reactivation (EBV, HHV-6) Immune (T-cell) exhaustion · Test: research only

Detectable cell-free EBV DNA in plasma has been reported more often in ME/CFS (24% vs 4% in one Bulgarian study), but EBV DNA in blood cells is equally common in patients and controls. Early

Almost everyone carries EBV in their blood cells. Some small studies find free-floating viral DNA, a sign of activity, more often in patients, but this has not been firmly confirmed.

Shikova 2020 (58 vs 50): PBMC EBV DNA 81% vs 84% (no difference), plasma EBV DNA 24.1% vs 4% (p=0.0027). Loebel 2014 found more EBER-DNA but not BZLF-1 RNA in blood cells. In long COVID, EBV viremia at acute infection predicted later PASC (Su 2022, n=309), but EBV viremia at a median of 4 months did not associate with long COVID in Peluso 2023 (n=280), while serologic markers (EA-D IgG) did. Persistently detectable EBV DNA months after IM warrants exclusion of chronic active EBV, which is rare but treatable.

Bears on: Herpesvirus reactivation (EBV, HHV-6) Viral persistence · Test: EBV DNA PCR (whole blood/plasma) is clinically available; mainly to exclude chronic active EBV.

Genetic instruments for higher EBV DNA load in blood (Kamitaki 2026) are associated with ME/CFS risk in the Million Veteran Program (OR 1.59, p=0.012) but not significantly in DecodeME (OR 1.13, p=0.25). Early

People whose genes make them carry more EBV appear somewhat more likely to get ME/CFS in one large dataset but not clearly in another. This is a weak hint that EBV control matters.

A Solving ME/CFS Mendelian randomisation re-analysis used EBV load instruments from Kamitaki 2026 (n≈655k). It gave a combined OR of about 1.23 (p≈0.02), and HLA instruments at r²<0.01 held (p=0.012, 0.043). HLA patterns that raise antibodies to the lytic EBV proteins ZEBRA and EA-D also align with higher risk, but negative-control serologies (VZV, HHV-6B) align similarly, so the HLA signal is not EBV-specific. Genetic correlation of ME/CFS with infectious mononucleosis was 0.11 ± 0.14, and with EBV load 0.05 ± 0.04, both non-significant. Reverse MR was underpowered. Not yet replicated by an independent group.

Bears on: Herpesvirus reactivation (EBV, HHV-6) Genetic susceptibility acting through neurons Autoimmunity (functional autoantibodies) · Test: research only

Antibodies against herpesvirus dUTPases (EBV, HHV-6, VZV), proposed as a marker of lytic or abortive-lytic reactivation, are higher in ME/CFS in studies from one lab, including a 2026 longitudinal study (873 serum samples, 40 patients vs 16 controls) where levels tracked fatigue severity. Early

One research group measures antibodies to a viral enzyme made when herpesviruses partly wake up. They repeatedly find more of these antibodies in ME/CFS, but other labs have not yet checked.

Halpin 2017: 30.9-52.7% of ME/CFS patients had antibodies to multiple herpesviral and/or human dUTPases vs 17.2% of controls, and anti-EBV dUTPase was higher in ME/CFS. Palomo 2026 (J Med Virol): longitudinal sampling, with EBV/HHV-6/VZV dUTPase IgG significantly higher (p<0.001). 72.5% of patients co-expressed antibodies to multiple herpesvirus and HERV-K dUTPases vs 31% of controls, and EBV and HHV-6 dUTPase IgG correlated with fatigue. The controls were few (n=16). In healthy cohorts positivity ranges from 40-84% and rises with age (Alharshawi 2022), so baseline rates are high. The assays are not commercial, and all data come from the Ariza lab.

Serologic evidence of recent EBV reactivation (EA-D IgG) is associated with long COVID fatigue (OR 2.12) in a 280-person cohort, consistent with an earlier small report. Several studies

People with long COVID more often have antibody signs that EBV recently reactivated, which may be one route by which COVID leads to lasting illness.

Peluso 2023 (JCI, n=280): LC fatigue and neurocognitive symptoms were associated with EA-D IgG positivity or high EBNA IgG, independent of covariates, but not with EBV viremia. Prior CMV infection was associated with lower LC risk. Gold 2021 (n=68) reported 66.7% of LC vs 10% of controls positive for EA-D IgG or VCA IgM, a small study with a convenience control group. Cervia-Hasler 2024 found classical complement activation linked to higher herpesvirus antibody titres in active LC. Serology cannot distinguish a cause of LC from a consequence of a general immune disturbance.

Bears on: Herpesvirus reactivation (EBV, HHV-6) Complement activation and thromboinflammation · Test: EBV EA-D IgG is clinically available; interpretation is non-specific.

Herpes-complement

In active long COVID, classical complement pathway activation tracked raised antibody titres against several herpesviruses, alongside markers of haemolysis, platelet activation and monocyte-platelet aggregates. Early

In long COVID, the blood's complement defence system stays switched on, and this goes along with higher antibodies to herpesviruses. One explanation is that immune complexes against reactivated viruses keep complement firing.

Cervia-Hasler 2024 (Science) ran proteomics on >6,500 proteins in 268 longitudinal samples from Zurich/Basel cohorts followed to 12 months. Active LC showed terminal complement dysregulation and ongoing alternative and classical pathway activation, and the classical arm was associated with increased anti-herpesvirus (e.g., EBV, CMV) titres. Machine learning put complement and thromboinflammation proteins at the top. The cohort was mostly post-hospital-era COVID. No ME/CFS (non-COVID) replication yet. Complement activation fits several mechanisms, and herpes reactivation is only one of them.

Evidence

StudynDesignResult

  • Would antivirals reduce complement activation in LC?

HHV-6

HHV-6 microRNA (miR-aU14) was detected by in situ hybridisation in brain and spinal cord tissue from 3 ME/CFS post-mortem donors but not in 24 controls (Kasimir 2022). Early

A small autopsy study found signs of active HHV-6 in the brain and spinal cord of three people with ME/CFS and none in controls. This needs repeating in many more brains.

Kasimir 2022 (Front Mol Biosci) used FISH against an HHV-6 miRNA in frontal lobe, basal ganglia and spinal cord from 3 ME/CFS donors, 3 disease controls and 21 Cambridge Brain Bank controls. The authors also report evidence of EBV activity in tissue. Limitations: n=3 cases, no blinding is described in the abstract, miRNA FISH specificity in post-mortem tissue, and no quantitative PCR or sequencing confirmation. The authors argue that blood negativity in many studies reflects localised tissue reactivation. In vitro, HHV-6 reactivation from integrated genomes fragments mitochondria and induces an antiviral state, and patient serum transferred a similar effect (Schreiner 2020, Immunohorizons).

Inherited chromosomally integrated HHV-6 (iciHHV-6, ~1% of people) has been reported at roughly twice the population rate in a neurological/fatigue clinic cohort, but this has not been confirmed in a large ME/CFS sample. Early

About 1 in 100 people are born with HHV-6 built into one of their chromosomes. One small study suggested this is more common in ME/CFS, and the large UK DecodeME study is checking.

A 2013 University of South Florida study reported iciHHV-6 in >2% of adults with CFS and neurological symptoms vs ~0.8% population estimates. It was a small, selected clinic cohort, and the information here comes from secondary reports only. UK prevalence is about 1.4%, rising to ~3% in parts of Scotland and Ireland, so ancestry confounding matters. DecodeME has an approved sub-study to measure iciHHV-6 in ~4,500 participants, comparing infection-onset vs other onsets. No published result had been found as of this review. iciHHV-6 can produce false 'high HHV-6 DNA' results on commercial PCR panels, a common source of misinterpretation.

Enterovirus

Enteroviral VP1 protein was found in stomach biopsies from 82% of 165 CFS patients vs 20% of controls, with EV RNA in 37% vs 5%, but this has not been independently replicated with blinded methods. Contested

One clinician-researcher found enterovirus protein in the stomach lining of most patients he biopsied. Other labs have not confirmed it, and the antibody stain used may cross-react.

Chia 2008 (J Clin Pathol): 135/165 consecutive CFS patients' antrum biopsies stained positive for VP1 in parietal cells vs 7/34 controls (p≤0.001), and EV RNA was found in 9/24 vs 1/21 paraffin samples. Paired samples taken years apart stayed positive. The patients were the author's own referral population. The controls were biopsies taken for other gastric conditions, and the 5D8/1 VP1 antibody has known cross-reactivity concerns. Earlier muscle work found EV RNA in 41/158 postviral fatigue vs 2/152 controls (Bowles 1993), but later muscle studies were inconsistent. O'Neal & Hanson 2021 concluded the methods used were inadequate either to confirm or to rule out persistent EV infection, and a Cornell EV-targeted RNA-seq thesis (2022) detected no EVs in patients or controls.

SARS-CoV-2 persistence

SARS-CoV-2 spike, S1 or nucleocapsid antigen is detectable in plasma more often after COVID than in pre-pandemic samples (excess +11% at 3-6 months, +5.4% at 10-14 months), with more antigenemia after more severe acute illness. Several studies

In about 1 in 10 people, bits of the virus can still be found in the blood months after COVID, which suggests a hidden reservoir. Whether this causes long COVID is less certain.

Peluso 2024 (Lancet Infect Dis; 171 post-COVID vs 250 pre-pandemic controls, Simoa) found 2% assay positivity in pre-pandemic controls. Antigenemia was associated with hospitalisation and worse acute illness. The association with LC symptoms was modest and not consistent across all symptom groups (detail from secondary reports). Swank 2022/23 (n=63) reported spike in a majority of PASC patients up to 12 months, a small sample later tempered by larger work. In PAX LC, circulating S1/spike levels did not change after 15 days of nirmatrelvir (Bhattacharjee 2026 preprint).

SARS-CoV-2 RNA and protein persist in gut and other tissues for months to two years in a minority of people, and in a Beijing tissue study, viral RNA in tissue was associated with long COVID symptoms (OR 5.17). Several studies

Viral genetic material can hide in the gut and other organs long after the nose test is negative. Several groups have now seen this, and people with long COVID seem to have it more often.

Zollner 2022 (n=46 IBD patients, ~7 months): gut mucosal RNA in 32/46 and nucleocapsid in 24/46, associated with post-acute symptoms. Natarajan 2022 (n=113): fecal RNA in 12.7% at 4 months and 3.8% at 7 months, linked to GI symptoms. Zuo 2024 (Lancet ID; 317 samples from 225 patients): RNA in 30%/27%/11% of solid tissues at 1/2/4 months, with tissue RNA associated with LC symptoms (OR 5.17). Peluso 2024 (Sci Transl Med; n=24 PET) found T-cell activation (F-AraG) in gut wall and spinal cord linked to LC, and RNA in rectosigmoid tissue up to 676 days in some participants. These are mostly convenience tissue samples, and some people without LC also carry RNA.

Antiviral trials

Three randomised placebo-controlled trials of 15-25 days of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir in established long COVID (STOP-PASC n=155, PAX LC n=100, RECOVER-VITAL n=959; about 1,214 people in total) found no benefit on primary or secondary outcomes. Refuted

Paxlovid, the COVID antiviral, has been tested several times in people who already have long COVID, and it did not help.

STOP-PASC (Geng 2024, JAMA IM): 15 days, 2:1 randomisation, no difference in pooled severity of 6 symptoms at 10 weeks; mostly vaccinated participants, mean 17.5 months after infection. PAX LC (Sawano 2025, Lancet ID): adjusted PROMIS-29 physical difference -0.55 (p=0.54). RECOVER-VITAL (Baden 2026, Lancet ID; 69 sites): 15- or 25-day regimens, no benefit in cognitive, autonomic or exercise phenotypes. All were safe apart from dysgeusia. Caveats: participants were not selected for antigenemia or reservoir evidence, illness was long-standing, and the drug's tissue penetration is uncertain. Ensitrelvir was also null per a secondary summary.

Treating acute COVID-19 with nirmatrelvir may reduce later long COVID: a small terminated Norwegian RCT found 26% vs 43% at 3 months (RR 0.60), echoing observational VA data, but larger prospective evidence is lacking. Early

Taking the antiviral early, while COVID is still active, might lower the chance of developing long COVID, but the only trial so far was small and stopped early.

PANORAMIC Norway (Oppegaard 2026, Lancet ID): enrolled 144 of a planned 2,000 before stopping for poor recruitment, and found long COVID in 17/66 vs 33/77 (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.37-0.98, p=0.039). An unblinding effect via dysgeusia (86% vs 18%) is possible because the outcomes were self-reported. VA cohort (Xie 2023, JAMA IM; 35,717 treated vs 246,076) reported lower risk, while Fung 2023 (older Medicare patients) found no reduction. Metformin during acute COVID (COVID-OUT) also reduced later LC, per the Solving ME/CFS treatments summary. Together this suggests the early acute phase may be a window for intervention, which fits the Dubbo finding that acute severity predicts later illness.

In a 30-patient RCT of 6 months of valganciclovir in CFS patients selected for high HHV-6 and EBV IgG, the primary MFI-20 outcome was not significant, though some secondary fatigue and cognitive trajectories favoured the drug. Early

A strong antiviral helped some tiredness and thinking measures in a small trial, but missed its main goal. It has never been repeated, and it can lower white blood cell counts.

Montoya 2013 (J Med Virol): 2:1 randomisation. The MFI-20 difference at 9 months was non-significant. Trajectories for MFI-20 mental fatigue (p=0.039), FSS (p=0.006) and cognition (p=0.025) were significant, and responder status was 7.4x more likely (p=0.029). Monocytes fell and neutrophils rose. These came from multiple secondary endpoints with no multiplicity correction. Preceding uncontrolled data: Kogelnik 2006 (n=12, 9 responders) and Watt 2012 chart review (n=61, 52% responders, baseline titres did not predict response). Lerner's valacyclovir 'EBV subset' series had small controlled phases and are largely uncontrolled. Antibody titre selection is a weak marker of active infection.

Endogenous retroviruses

Human endogenous retrovirus (HERV) expression in blood cells differs between ME/CFS, fibromyalgia and controls in small studies (HERV-K raised in moderate ME/CFS; HERV microarray profiles clustered n=43 participants perfectly by diagnosis). Early

Old viral DNA built into our genome can switch back on. Small studies hint that its activity pattern differs in ME/CFS, but nothing is confirmed.

Rodrigues 2019: qPCR found HERV-K overexpressed only in moderately affected patients, with no HERV-W difference. Giménez-Orenga 2025 (eLife; HERV-V3 microarrays, >350k HERV elements, PBMC, n=43 women): hierarchical clustering separated ME/CFS, FM, co-diagnosed and controls 'perfectly'. That sample is very small with very many features, so overfitting is likely without an independent validation set. HERV-K dUTPase antibodies co-occur with herpesvirus dUTPase antibodies in the Ariza lab data (Palomo 2026). Herpesviruses such as EBV can transactivate HERVs, which links this to the herpes hypothesis.

Temelimab, an antibody against HERV-W envelope protein, did not reduce fatigue versus placebo in a 203-person RCT of HERV-W-positive post-COVID patients. Refuted

A drug designed to block an endogenous retrovirus protein was tested in long COVID patients who had that protein, and it worked no better than placebo.

Nehme 2026 (Brain Behav Immun; GeNeuro-funded, NCT05497089): 24 weeks of monthly IV 54 mg/kg in participants selected for HERV-W ENV positivity. The PROMIS fatigue change was -3.2 vs -3.8 points, with no secondary benefit. Note that temelimab targets HERV-W, not HERV-K, so it does not test the HERV-K findings in ME/CFS. No temelimab trial in non-COVID ME/CFS exists.

Retroviruses (XMRV)

The 2009 report of the mouse retrovirus XMRV in 67% of CFS patients was a laboratory contamination artefact: blinded multi-lab and original-investigator studies found no XMRV/pMLV, and the Science paper was retracted. Refuted

In 2009 a mouse-derived virus was reported in most CFS patients. Careful blinded testing, including by the original scientists, showed it was contamination, and the paper was withdrawn.

Lombardi 2009 (Science) was partially retracted in 2011 and fully retracted later that year. Simmons 2011 (Blood XMRV Scientific Research Working Group): coded replicate samples sent to 9 labs, and reactivity was similar in CFS and controls. Alter 2012 (mBio; Lipkin-led, 147 CFS vs 146 controls, including the original investigators' labs) found no XMRV or pMLV. Lessons for this field: sensitive PCR contamination (mouse DNA in reagents and cell lines), unblinded testing, and premature clinical use (antiretrovirals were taken by some patients). The episode also set back trust and funding for virus research in ME/CFS.

Parvovirus B19

Parvovirus B19 exposure was as common in CFS as in blood donors, but antibodies to the viral NS1 protein (a marker of persistent or recent active infection) were found in 41.5% vs 7%, and viral DNA in 11 patients vs no controls. Early

Most people have had parvovirus, but signs of a lingering infection were much more common in patients in one large study.

Kerr 2010 (200 vs 200). Kerr's earlier reports described CFS onset after acute B19. No independent large replication.

Key reviews

  • O'Neal & Hanson 2021, Front Med: Critical review of enterovirus methods in ME/CFS: why past studies neither proved nor excluded persistent infection.
  • Proal et al. 2023, Nat Immunol: Review of evidence for a SARS-CoV-2 tissue reservoir in long COVID and research priorities for antiviral trials.
  • Hickie et al. 2006, BMJ: The foundational prospective cohort showing a stereotyped post-infective syndrome across pathogens.
  • Alter et al. 2012, mBio: The definitive blinded study closing the XMRV episode, and a model for testing a pathogen claim.
  • Blomberg et al. 2019, Front Immunol: Careful multiplex herpesvirus serology in Canada-criteria ME/CFS with a discussion of why serology is limited.

Metabolism and blood omics

Blood metabolomics and proteomics consistently find that ME/CFS patients differ from controls on average, but the differences are small (mostly 0.2-0.5 SD), partly cohort-specific, and confounded by medication, caffeine, diet and sample handling. The better-supported signals are modest: lower plasmalogens and some phosphatidylcholines, slightly lower carnitines, lower gut-derived IPA, lower aromatic lactates (a new cross-cohort re-analysis finding), higher methionine sulfoxide, and lower muscle-derived proteins in blood that are not explained by activity. Bigger claims, such as a uniform hypometabolic 'cell danger' state, an IDO metabolic trap, divergent metabolic or proteomic responses to exercise, reproducible methylation signatures, and diagnostic classifiers with near-perfect accuracy, have not held up in independent data or remain untested outside the original lab. No omics test is ready for diagnosis. The largest gaps are severe patients, sampling during the 48-72 h PEM window, disease controls, and pairing omics with fresh-cell function.

Metabolomics: overall

Blood metabolome differences between ME/CFS and controls are real at group level but small (mostly 0.2-0.5 SD) and partly cohort-specific; early near-perfect classification did not carry over to new cohorts. Replicated

Patients' blood chemistry differs from healthy people's on average, but only slightly, and the specific list of chemicals changes from study to study.

Single-cohort studies reported AUCs of 0.82-0.96 (Naviaux 2016, Nagy-Szakal 2018, Che 2022), but these were estimated within the training data. A harmonised re-analysis of 10 public cohorts found 74 compounds at q<0.05 with pooled effects mostly 0.2-0.5 SD; two Cornell cohorts agreed only weakly (rho 0.16) and cross-cohort transfer AUCs were 0.56-0.83. Medication exposure (paracetamol, gabapentin, psychoactives, acid suppressants detected in blood) and caffeine are major confounders that most original papers did not adjust for.

Metabolomics: cell danger response

Naviaux 2016's picture of a homogeneous 'hypometabolic' dauer-like state (80% of discriminating metabolites decreased) has not been confirmed as a uniform pattern in later independent cohorts. Contested

One influential 2016 study said patients' cells were in a protective 'low-power' mode, with most chemicals reduced. Later studies found more mixed and smaller changes.

Naviaux's 45/39 cohort with targeted LC-MS/MS found lower sphingolipids, phospholipids, purines and other pathways and proposed the cell danger response (CDR). An Open Medicine Foundation validation cohort was reported informally (2018) to reproduce 23 of 30 pathway abnormalities, but no peer-reviewed replication paper was found. Hoel 2021 found heterogeneous metabotypes rather than one state; Che 2022 and Xiong 2023 partly echo the lipid reductions. In the cross-cohort re-analysis, the Naviaux data still carry some replicated signals (e.g. low aromatic lactates on a non-Metabolon platform), but there is no global hypometabolic shift across cohorts.

Metabolomics: lipids and sphingolipids

Lower plasmalogens, some phosphatidylcholines and sphingomyelins are reported across several cohorts and platforms, with modest effect sizes. Several studies

Some fats that form cell membranes, especially a type called plasmalogens, are a little lower in patients' blood in several studies.

Che 2022 (106/91) reported lower plasmalogens/ether phospholipids, PCs and sphingomyelins (p<0.001) and proposed peroxisomal dysfunction. Naviaux 2016 found lower sphingolipids; Xiong 2023 lower sphingomyelins; Nagy-Szakal 2018 higher ceramides only in the IBS subgroup. In the cross-cohort re-analysis PC(14:0/16:0) was -0.42 SD (4 cohorts, 3 non-Metabolon) and plasmalogen P-16:0/18:2 -0.38 SD; dihydroceramide d18:0/16:0 was +0.28. Diet (dairy, fish) and BMI are not well controlled.

Metabolomics: aromatic lactates

Four aromatic 2-hydroxy acids (phenyllactate, 4-hydroxyphenyllactate, indolelactate, imidazole lactate) are lower in ME/CFS in 5 of 5 cohorts (combined -0.53 SD, I²=0), robust to drug, caffeine, diet and kidney-function adjustment. Several studies

A family of small chemicals made from amino acids is consistently lower in patients across five separate studies. It is a group-level difference, not a test.

Solving ME/CFS re-analysis: p=4e-11, holds on Naviaux's targeted LC-MS/MS platform (-0.64), -0.64 in people with no prescription drug detected, -0.73 in men. The precursor keto acids are not lower, so either the reduction step or a dietary source (fermented foods) is implicated. In BioMapAI paired stool, gut species do not predict these compounds (CV R²≈0), unlike IPA. They do not track severity (|r|<0.2). Not yet reported by original study authors; needs targeted, fasting confirmation and D- vs L-isomer separation (bacterial D vs host L).

Metabolomics: tryptophan / gut metabolites

Indole-3-propionate (IPA), a gut-bacterial tryptophan product, is lower in ME/CFS plasma in 4 of 4 cohorts (-0.33 SD) and tracks butyrate-producing gut species. Several studies

A chemical made only by certain gut bacteria is a bit lower in patients, which fits the gut-bacteria differences found in several studies.

Pooled -0.33 SD (95% CI -0.49 to -0.16), p=0.0001; individual AUC only 0.57-0.60. In BioMapAI paired stool, IPA correlates with F. prausnitzii and Bifidobacterium and inversely with R. gnavus; adjusting for IPA-linked species reduces the difference from -0.40 to -0.09 (optimistic same-data selection). Xiong 2023 and BioMapAI report reduced microbial butyrate and altered tryptophan metabolism. Interpreted as a gut-ecology marker rather than a host defect.

Metabolomics: kynurenine pathway / IDO trap

The IDO metabolic-trap model predicts tryptophan-kynurenine pathway disruption, but blood data are inconsistent: one cohort found higher kynurenine, others found no difference or slightly lower kynurenine. Contested

A mathematical theory proposed that a tryptophan-processing enzyme gets stuck in ME/CFS. Blood measurements of that pathway point in different directions in different studies.

Kashi, Davis and Phair 2019 modelled IDO1 substrate inhibition plus common non-functional IDO2 variants producing a bistable 'trap'; it is a hypothesis paper with no patient data. Kavyani 2024 reported higher kynurenine correlating with severity and lower downstream 3-HK, 3-HAA, QUIN, picolinate. Groven 2021 (49 CFS/57 FM/54 HC women) found differences mainly in FM, not CFS vs controls. The cross-cohort re-analysis found kynurenine -0.27 SD (lower), kyn/trp ratio -0.19 (q=0.06), lower kynurenine with >4 years illness, and no change in IDO1/KYNU proteins. Plasma kynurenine says little about intracellular IDO kinetics, which is what the model is about.

Metabolomics: acylcarnitines and fatty acids

Free carnitine and long-chain acylcarnitines are slightly lower in ME/CFS across cohorts, contrary to the earlier idea of excess circulating fatty acids. Several studies

Carriers that move fats into the cell's power stations are a little lower in patients' blood.

Reported as altered/low in Naviaux 2016, Nagy-Szakal 2018, Germain 2017 and Germain 2022 (carnitines low). Cross-cohort re-analysis: carnitine -0.21 SD, long-chain acylcarnitines -0.22 SD, long-chain fatty acids slightly lower in all 4 cohorts examined; acetylcarnitine/carnitine ratio null. Germain 2020 reported lower acyl cholines. Effect sizes are small and diet/fasting status is rarely recorded.

Metabolomics: energy metabolism

Several studies infer impaired carbohydrate oxidation (pyruvate dehydrogenase restraint, TCA/urea cycle shifts), but simple blood ratios (lactate/pyruvate, citrulline/arginine) do not differ across pooled cohorts. Contested

Some studies suggest patients' cells burn sugar less efficiently. Blood measures that should show this are mostly normal when many studies are pooled.

Fluge 2016 (200/102) found low TCA-fuelling amino acids in women and higher PDK1/2/4 mRNA in PBMCs; Hoel 2021 described energy strain with altered fuel use in subsets; Yamano 2016 found TCA/urea-cycle ratios (validation AUC 0.75). Armstrong 2015 (NMR, 34/25 women) reported lower blood lactate and glutamate and higher glucose. In the pooled re-analysis, lactate/pyruvate (-0.10), citrulline/arginine, ornithine/arginine and hypoxanthine/xanthine were null; creatine/creatinine +0.19. These are inferences from plasma about tissue metabolism; direct tissue flux measurements are scarce.

Metabolomics: ketones

Ketone bodies are associated with ME/CFS in UK Biobank NMR data, but 3-hydroxybutyrate shows no consistent difference in pooled case-control cohorts. Contested

One very large data set links ketones (fuel made from fat) to ME/CFS; smaller studies pooled together do not.

Huang 2024 (1,194 ME/CFS in UK Biobank, NMR) reported lipoprotein and ketone-body associations; their ML model (19 baseline characteristics + 9 NMR biomarkers) reached AUC 0.83, with much of the signal from non-omic features. Fasting time and diet differ by group and strongly affect ketones. Pooled re-analysis: 3-hydroxybutyrate null; ketones used as a covariate did not explain other signals.

Metabolomics: exercise response

Germain 2022 reported growing metabolic divergence after a 2-day CPET; within-person re-analysis finds the exercise response itself barely differs (blunted lactate and glucose rise aside). Contested

A study took blood before and after two exercise tests and saw bigger differences after. Re-analysed person by person, the changes caused by exercise look mostly the same in patients and controls.

Germain 2022 (60/45, 1,157 metabolites, 4 time points) found female significant counts rising from 6 to 54 across time points. Re-analysis: day-1 and day-2 case-control differences correlate 0.85 and are only ~6% larger on day 2; within-person change scores are at chance (permutation p=0.12-0.61). Surviving signals: smaller lactate rise (likely lower workload), no post-exercise glucose rise in patients, oxidised cys-gly rising only in patients. Five of 8 people with missing post-exercise samples were severely affected men.

Metabolomics: collagen turnover

Collagen breakdown products (hydroxyproline, galactosyl-hydroxylysine and related) are higher in ME/CFS plasma (+0.52 SD, 4/4 Metabolon cohorts; hydroxyproline also up on 3 other platforms). Early

Fragments released when collagen (the body's connective-tissue protein) is broken down are a bit higher in patients.

Solving ME/CFS re-analysis only: p=2e-8 for the module; hydroxyproline +0.31 SD across 8 cohorts. Galactosyl-hydroxylysine weakens after drug adjustment. Collagen/gelatin supplements and diet are not excluded. Fits loosely with lower ECM/fibroblast and vascular mural proteins in the proteome re-analysis, but the direction (more breakdown, less matrix protein) needs direct markers (CTX-I, PIIINP).

Redox / oxidative stress

Markers of oxidative stress (methionine sulfoxide, oxidised glutathione products, lower brain glutathione) are repeatedly reported, but they are non-specific and also seen in depression. Several studies

Signs that cells are under chemical 'rust' stress show up in several studies, but the same signs appear in other illnesses too.

Methionine sulfoxide/methionine +0.35 SD in 7/7 cohorts across 3 platforms (I²=0), though methionine oxidises during storage; 5-oxoproline/glutamate -0.25 SD (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis). Germain 2018 proposed broad redox imbalance; Germain 2022 data show oxidised cys-gly rising after exercise in patients only. Shungu 2012 (MRS, 15 CFS/15 MDD/13 HC) found lower cortical glutathione and higher ventricular lactate in both CFS and depression. Antioxidant trials have not shown clear benefit.

NAD+

NAD+ depletion is a proposed mechanism but has not been directly established in ME/CFS cohorts; NAD precursor trials raise NAD+ without clear clinical benefit. Early

NAD+ is a molecule cells need for energy. The idea that patients lack it is mostly theory; supplements raise it but have not clearly helped.

Reviews (Dehhaghi 2022) link the kynurenine pathway to NAD+ synthesis. Castro-Marrero 2015 (n=73) and 2021 (n=207) RCTs of CoQ10 200 mg + NADH 20 mg reported modest improvements in some fatigue/cognitive scores. A long-COVID RCT of nicotinamide riboside 2 g/day (n=58) raised blood NAD+ 2.6-3.1x but showed no between-group difference in cognition or fatigue (p=0.59), with high dropout. Vitamin B3 pathway changes appeared in Abujrais 2024 untargeted data.

Proteomics and blood traits: UK Biobank

In UK Biobank, ME/CFS cases show many small blood-trait differences (inflammation, insulin resistance, liver markers) that replicate partly in All of Us and are not explained by low physical activity. Several studies

In a huge UK database, people with an ME/CFS diagnosis have many slightly different blood results, and this is not just because they move less.

Beentjes, Ponting and colleagues used semi-parametric (Super Learner, one-step) estimators with activity, walking pace and other mediators. 9 of 14 tested traits replicated in All of Us; people reporting PEM showed stronger differences. Caveats: diagnosis is from records/self-report, so case definition is loose; UK Biobank skews healthier and older; differences are small and single traits do not separate groups. Olink proteomics summary statistics show LEP, ADH4, BCHE, complement factors up and CA14, SOD3 down (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis).

Proteomics: tissue-of-origin

A set of muscle-derived intracellular proteins is lower, as a group, in resting ME/CFS blood in three SomaScan cohorts, and this is not explained by activity measures; individual proteins such as myoglobin, CA3 and troponins do not replicate on their own. Several studies

Proteins that normally leak from muscle into blood are a little lower in patients, perhaps meaning less muscle or slower muscle turnover, not ongoing muscle damage.

Hoel 2026 reported reduced intracellular skeletal-muscle proteins. Solving ME/CFS re-analysis: muscle theme d -0.50 (95% CI -0.76 to -0.24), q=0.002, I² 0.07 across Hoel (-0.85), Germain (-0.43), Walitt (-0.34); UKB competitive shift negative; not mediated by walking pace, not related to steps, Bell score or time reclined. Lean mass was not measured, so reduced muscle mass remains a plausible explanation. Per-protein re-pool (Solving ME/CFS kb matrix v2, Nov 2026): no single muscle protein replicates at FDR. CKM g -0.44 (3 of 3 cohorts, p=0.02, q=0.63; not measured in UK Biobank) and MYL3 g -0.32 (3 of 3) are the most consistent; myoglobin (-0.66 / -0.04 / +0.49 / -0.24 across Germain, UKB, Hoel, Walitt), CA3 (low only in Hoel) and troponins (pooled within ±0.1) disagree. The set-level shift is therefore real but modest and weighted by Hoel 2026.

Proteomics: SomaScan artefacts

Most of the ~845 FDR-significant serum proteins in Hoel 2026 appear driven by a sample-handling (cell-leak) signal that is absent from other cohorts; about 13 survive adjustment. Contested

A large protein study found hundreds of differences, but a re-analysis suggests most came from how samples were handled rather than the illness.

Solving ME/CFS re-analysis built a nuclear/cell-leak score: case-control d -1.16 in Hoel, ~0 in Germain, Walitt serum and Walitt CSF. After adjustment Hoel keeps 13 FDR hits (COMP, C6, ANTXR2, LAMA2, FAP and others). Hoel's raw statistics correlate with Germain only through intracellular proteins, and not after adjustment. Hoel authors validated a selection by antibody methods. Across ~6,000 proteins meta-analysed in 4 cohorts, only 32 reach q<0.05 and replicated effects are d 0.25-0.5 (ITGAV, NOTCH3, THBS1, LUM, ADH4, GSTA1, BAFF up).

Proteomics: replicated small shifts

Hepatocyte enzymes (ADH4, GSTA1, AGXT, BCHE) are modestly higher, and vascular mural/matrix proteins (ITGAV, NOTCH3, LUM, THBS1, TGF-beta family) modestly lower, in more than one cohort. Early

A few groups of blood proteins, from the liver and from the walls of small vessels, are slightly shifted in several data sets.

Liver set d +0.40 (q=0.013) but defined after seeing data and tracks BMI; up in Germain and UKB, partly Hoel, not in long COVID. Mural/ECM: ITGAV -0.34 (4 cohorts), NOTCH3 -0.32, TGF-beta set -0.44 (q=0.013); a long COVID UK Olink set also shows lower ECM/endothelial proteins. Endothelial 'activation' markers go down, not up, and platelet/microclot proteins are not raised. Expected candidates (renin, ACE, endothelin, BNP, EPO, hepcidin, NEFL, GFAP, IL-6, CRP) are null.

Proteomics: exertion

Germain 2025 reported patient-specific proteomic changes during recovery after a 2-day CPET, but a within-person re-analysis of the same data finds no protein whose exercise response differs at FDR. Contested

One large study reported that patients' blood proteins react differently to exercise. When re-analysed person by person, no single protein clearly did.

Germain 2025: 79 ME/CFS vs 53 sedentary controls, 6,361 proteins, 2 CPETs 24 h apart; pathway-level claims of suppressed T/B-cell and IL-17 signalling and raised glycolysis. Re-analysis: 0 FDR hits for differential change; no tissue score changes with exertion. Smaller EV studies after CPET (Giloteaux 2024, 18/17 women; Glass 2025, 10/12 men) report altered EV cargo responses (TCA down, complement up at 15 min; ER-stress proteins correlating with PEM), but n is small.

Extracellular vesicles

Plasma extracellular vesicle (EV) counts may be higher in ME/CFS, but no EV protein or microRNA difference has survived multiple-testing correction in a replicated cohort. Early

Tiny particles cells release into blood may be more numerous in patients, but their contents have not shown a reliable difference yet.

Rydland 2026 (49/50, SEC + MS proteomics): higher EV concentration; 11 of 424 proteins differ nominally (erythroid, hepatocyte, plasma-cell origin), none after FDR. Re-analysis of Rydland and Giloteaux EV data: no FDR hits. Eguchi 2026 EV-miRNA study had 6 ME/CFS. EV isolation methods vary widely and platelet activation during handling changes EV counts.

CSF proteomics

CSF proteomics in ME/CFS is limited to small cohorts and has not produced a replicated protein difference; the largest recent study (31 patients) had no controls. Early

Studies of the fluid around the brain and spine are few and small, and have not found a consistent difference.

Bragee 2026 (31 patients, 902 proteins): within-patient associations with POTS (neutrophil degranulation, platelet activation) and severity (complement, coagulation, IGFBP); re-analysis found 0 FDR hits POTS vs no-POTS. Walitt 2024 CSF SomaScan (~17 vs 21) showed no FDR hits in re-analysis, and no rise in neuronal injury markers. Earlier CSF proteome reports (Schutzer 2011, Baraniuk 2005) were small.

Transcriptomics and single-cell

Blood transcriptome and single-cell RNA studies report monocyte and platelet abnormalities, but no gene or cell subtype difference replicates across independent cohorts. Contested

Studies reading which genes are switched on in blood cells found possible differences, but they have not repeated in other groups of patients.

Vu 2024 (scRNA, ~30/28, before and 24 h after CPET) reported classical monocyte dysregulation correlating with severity and platelet activation signatures post-exercise. Re-analysis of the same data at person-level pseudobulk: 0 genes at q<0.05 at baseline in 15 cell types; composition null. Across 4 bulk RNA cohorts, 0 genome-wide FDR genes; a plasma-cell/immunoglobulin score is lower in 2/4 (meta d -0.42, p=0.06). Higher mitochondrial RNA fraction in lymphocytes (CD8 Tem d +0.85) is a lead that did not replicate in bulk PBMC. Walitt 2024 reported sex-specific PBMC expression differences in 17/21 people.

Epigenetics / DNA methylation

Reported genome-wide blood DNA methylation differences have not replicated across cohorts, at least one large set is explained by cell-composition differences, and epigenetic clocks are not accelerated. Contested

Chemical tags on DNA were reported to differ in patients, but a closer look shows the differences mostly reflect which blood cells were in the sample.

de Vega 2014/2017/2018, Trivedi 2018 (13/12 discovery, 17,296 CpGs; pyrosequencing in 33/31) and Helliwell 2020 (RRBS, 10/10) each reported many differentially methylated sites with little overlap. Re-analysis of 4 cohorts (177/107): in GSE93266, control 'PBMC' DNA contained much more granulocyte DNA (median 48% vs 14%); 44,794 FDR CpGs fall to 0 after composition adjustment; meta-analysis 0 CpGs at q<0.05. Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge, DunedinPACE null in T cells and saliva. Commercial epigenetic-age tests are not supported for ME/CFS.

Diagnostics: nanoneedle impedance

A nanoelectronic impedance assay separated 20 ME/CFS from 20 controls perfectly after hyperosmotic stress, but there is no published independent replication. Early

A chip measuring how blood cells react to salt stress separated a small group of patients from controls completely. Nobody outside the lab has confirmed it.

Esfandyarpour 2019 (PNAS) used PBMCs incubated in plasma; patients' impedance rose after NaCl stress, controls' did not; plasma swap suggested a plasma factor. The only independent attempt found was a 4 vs 4 bioimpedance preprint (Fernandez 2023) with a different device, which reported higher impedance at one frequency and did not test the original protocol. No disease-control group (e.g. MS, depression) was reported in the original at scale; device-to-device variability is unaddressed in published work.

Diagnostics: Raman spectroscopy

Raman spectroscopy of PBMCs or plasma separates ME/CFS from controls in single-centre studies (plasma AUC 0.83-0.85), without external validation. Early

A laser technique that reads the chemical 'fingerprint' of blood looked promising in two labs, but has not been tested in new patients elsewhere.

Xu 2019 (single-cell Raman, PBMCs) found higher phenylalanine-associated bands in patients, similar to mtDNA-depleted rho0 cells; small n. Heidarifard 2026 (115 ME vs 45 sedentary controls, plasma at rest and 90 min after a standardised stress) reported AUC 0.85 and 0.83, specificity 73% and 69%. Models are trained and tested within one cohort; spectral features are hard to map to specific molecules.

Plasma cell-free RNA classified ME/CFS vs sedentary controls with test-set AUC 0.81 and suggested platelet, pDC and monocyte-derived differences; not yet externally validated. Early

RNA fragments floating in blood plasma could tell patients from controls about 4 times in 5 in one study.
