Diagnostics: machine-learning classifiers

Multi-omic machine-learning classifiers (BioMapAI and others) perform well in cross-validation but drop to AUC ~0.6-0.77 on external cohorts, so none is usable for diagnosis. Contested

Computer models trained on many blood and stool measurements do well on the data they learned from but much worse on new patients.

BioMapAI (Xiong 2025, 249 participants, 4-year longitudinal sampling) reached 10-fold CV AUC 0.915 with all omics; on external cohorts AUC was 0.72 and 0.59 (Guo stool), 0.61-0.77 (Raijmakers), 0.68 (Germain metabolome) and 0.61 (Che), with only 19-79% feature overlap. Repeated visits per person raise the question of whether CV folds were split by person; disease controls were not included. A small metabolite panel derived in the Solving ME/CFS re-analysis transferred with AUC 0.60-0.83. Huang 2024 UK Biobank AUC 0.83 relied heavily on 19 baseline (non-omic) characteristics. No multi-omic layer converges on a shared pathway beyond chance (re-analysis).

Most comprehensive blood studies

Even the deepest blood omics studies sample mainly at rest, in mild-to-moderate patients, in plasma or serum only, and rarely test fresh-cell function or the 48-72 h PEM window. Replicated

The biggest blood studies so far mostly leave out the sickest patients, the days when symptoms flare after effort, and live-cell tests.

Walitt 2024 (NIH, 17/21) is the deepest per person but tiny and excluded many severe patients by design. BioMapAI has 4 years of visits but resting samples only. Germain 2022/2025 and Giloteaux/Glass cover 0, 15 min and 24 h after CPET but not 48-72 h, and the most impaired cannot do CPET (5 of 8 missing post-exercise samples were severe men). UK Biobank is large but one baseline time point with loose case definition. Hoel 2021/2026 are resting serum. Fresh-cell assays (PBMC respiration, NK function, red-cell deformability) are rarely paired with omics; compartments like muscle, CSF and gut tissue are rarely sampled together.

Hormones

The most consistent hormone finding in ME/CFS is a mildly under-active stress-hormone (HPA) axis: on average cortisol is slightly low in saliva, urine and hair, and feedback suppression is exaggerated. A 2026 meta-analysis of 46 case-control studies confirms this pattern. The shifts are small, most patients fall inside normal reference ranges, and they may be a consequence of illness, sleep disruption or inactivity rather than a cause. Low-dose hydrocortisone gave at best a small, short-lived benefit with side effects, and fludrocortisone failed in two large trials. Newer leads concern the hormones that hold water and salt in the body: low vasopressin and a 'renin-aldosterone paradox' that would fit the low blood volume seen in many patients. These come from small or uncontrolled studies, and the vasopressin finding is not matched by copeptin, which is the more reliable test. The female preponderance (about 1.5 to 3 times more women) is solid, but genetics shows no sex-specific risk variants, and the role of sex hormones, menopause and gynaecological conditions is still only descriptive.

HPA axis

On average, people with ME/CFS have mildly lower free cortisol (salivary awakening and morning cortisol, 24-h urinary cortisol and hair cortisol) than healthy controls. Replicated

Cortisol is the body's main stress and energy-mobilising hormone. On average it runs a little low in ME/CFS, but the gap is modest and most individual results are still normal.

Woo et al. 2026 pooled 46 case-control datasets (1,388 patients, 1,349 controls, 71.9% female) and found lower salivary awakening and morning cortisol, 24-h urinary free cortisol and hair cortisol. Hair cortisol, which reflects about 3 months of exposure, was also lower in a small adolescent study (Vroegindeweij 2024). In the Solving ME/CFS literature tally, 19 groups report lower cortisol and 5 higher. In untargeted plasma metabolomics the signal is weak and inconsistent: Germain 2020 −0.64 SD, Germain 2022 −0.13, BioMapAI −0.05, with men −0.35 (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis). The meta-analysis does not separate cause from effect: sleep disruption, inactivity, illness duration and antidepressant use can all lower cortisol.

Bears on: HPA axis blunting Persistent sickness behaviour / vagal signalling · Test: Yes: 9am serum cortisol, salivary awakening cortisol, short Synacthen test (mainly to exclude true adrenal insufficiency)

Challenge tests show a blunted cortisol response to ACTH and exaggerated cortisol suppression after a glucocorticoid dose, consistent with enhanced negative feedback. Several studies

When the stress-hormone system is pushed or braked in a test, it responds less to the push and more to the brake than in healthy people.

Woo 2026 included 12 pharmacological challenge studies: impaired cortisol release after ACTH stimulation and greater suppression after dexamethasone or hydrocortisone. The pattern resembles the 'hypocortisolism with enhanced feedback' described in PTSD, fibromyalgia and atypical depression, so it is not specific to ME/CFS. Insulin stress tests in the Cleare 1999 trial showed the adrenal glands were not suppressed by low-dose hydrocortisone. POTS patients showed normal adrenal responses to ACTH (Laurin 2023, n=8 vs 5).

Lower cortisol in long COVID, reported in a 2023 Nature cohort, has not held up in later clinic and cohort studies that controlled for sampling time. Contested

One high-profile study found low cortisol in long COVID. Later studies that timed the blood draws carefully mostly found normal levels.

Klein 2023 (n=275) reported lower cortisol in long COVID among other immune features. Dalhuisen 2024 (UCSF, n=200, banked 8am–12pm samples) found no overall difference (median 8.9 vs 8.8 µg/dL). Its sub-hour analyses were inconsistent: lower at 8–9am but higher at 9–10am in the ME/CFS-like group. Quach 2025 (Stanford clinic, n=86, 5–10am) found only 1 low value; 36% were above range. Camici 2026 (Rome, n=96) found normal blood cortisol but flattened salivary rhythms. Post-COVID controls without symptoms showed the same salivary pattern, so the change may follow infection rather than long COVID itself.

HPA axis treatment

Low-dose hydrocortisone produced at most small, short-term fatigue benefits in two RCTs, at the cost of adrenal suppression and bone loss at higher doses. Contested

Replacing some cortisol was tried in the 1990s. The effect was small, side effects were real, and it is not recommended.

McKenzie 1998 (JAMA, n=70, 25–35 mg/day for 12 weeks): global wellness responders 66.7% vs 54.3% (p=0.31). A secondary 5-point improvement was 53% vs 29% (p=0.04), but cosyntropin tests showed adrenal suppression. A sub-study (n=23) found lumbar spine bone density fell 2.0% on hydrocortisone. Cleare 1999 (Lancet, n=32 crossover, 5–10 mg for 1 month) found fatigue fell 4.5 points more than on placebo; 28% vs 9% reached normal-range fatigue. The trial was short, strictly selected (no psychiatric comorbidity) and never replicated. Blockmans 2003 (n=100 crossover, hydrocortisone 5 mg plus fludrocortisone 50 µg for 3 months) was null.

Salt-retaining hormones (treatment)

Fludrocortisone, a synthetic salt-retaining steroid, did not improve CFS with neurally mediated hypotension in a 100-person RCT, and failed again in combination with hydrocortisone. Refuted

A drug that makes the kidneys hold salt and water was expected to help low blood pressure on standing. In proper trials it did not help overall.

Rowe 2001 (JAMA, n=100, tilt-positive neurally mediated hypotension, 0.1 mg/day for 9 weeks): ≥15-point wellness improvement in 14% vs 10% (p=0.76). Blockmans 2003 (n=100) found no effect of hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone. Small open series in POTS still report individual responders, and the trials did not select for measured hypovolaemia or low aldosterone.

Evidence

StudynDesignResult
Rowe 2001, JAMA100RCTNo benefit (14% vs 10% responders)

Adrenal and pituitary disease

Diagnosed adrenal insufficiency and hypopituitarism are 7 to 13 times more common than expected among Finnish patients coded with postviral fatigue syndrome. Early

A small minority of people labelled ME/CFS may have a real, treatable gland failure. That makes basic hormone screening worthwhile.

In Finnish registry data (FinRegistry about 1,622 G93.3 cases, FinnGen 348), the crude observed/expected ratio is 9.5–13 for adrenal insufficiency and 6.7–7.6 for hypopituitarism. Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone prescriptions are enriched 11–62x (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of Risteys). These figures are not adjusted for age or sex and are inflated by healthcare use. They may reflect misdiagnosis, a true subgroup, or steroid treatment causing adrenal suppression. Case reports describe isolated ACTH and GH deficiency first labelled as CFS, which improved with hydrocortisone (Tokumasu 2021).

Solving ME/CFS re-analysis (FinnGen/FinRegistry Risteys) dataabout 1,622 and 348 casesregistry co-occurrence (O/E)Adrenal insufficiency O/E 9.5–13; hypopituitarism 6.7–7.6
Tokumasu 2021, BMJ Case Reports1case reportIdiopathic ACTH + GH deficiency mimicking CFS

  • What fraction of a well-phenotyped ME/CFS cohort fails a Synacthen test?
  • Is this misdiagnosis, a subgroup, or a treatment effect?

Bears on: HPA axis blunting Pituitary / vasopressin deficiency · Test: Yes: 9am cortisol, ACTH, short Synacthen test; pituitary panel if indicated

Water balance (ADH/vasopressin)

After overnight fluid deprivation, plasma vasopressin was undetectable in 82% of 111 Swedish ME/CFS patients despite high plasma osmolality in 57%, suggesting partial central diabetes insipidus-like physiology. Early

Vasopressin (ADH) is the hormone that tells the kidneys to keep water. Some patients appear to make too little of it even when their blood is concentrated, which could worsen low blood volume.

Huhmar 2025 was a consecutive, uncontrolled clinic series (n=124). Urine osmolality was below 750 mOsm/kg in 66%. In the 13 patients tested with copeptin, which is a more stable marker of vasopressin secretion, all values were within the reference range, though at the low end. Brain MRI showed no hypothalamic or pituitary lesions. Miwa 2016 (18 vs 15) found ADH 2.2 vs 3.3 pg/mL (p=0.02) alongside lower aldosterone and small hearts. In open label use, desmopressin improved orthostatic symptoms in 5 of 10 patients. Vasopressin immunoassays are unreliable, and the normal copeptin results argue for caution.

Miwa 2016, J Cardiology18 vs 15case-controlLower ADH (p=0.02) and aldosterone (p=0.004)

Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone

Patients with POTS and with ME/CFS show normal or low renin and low aldosterone despite reduced blood volume (the 'renin-aldosterone paradox'). Several studies

When blood volume is low, the kidneys should release renin and the adrenals aldosterone to retain salt. In POTS and ME/CFS this response seems muted.

Raj 2005 (POTS 15 vs 14, iodine-131 albumin) found a plasma volume deficit of 334 vs 10 mL with unchanged renin activity and aldosterone of 190 vs 380 pmol/L (p=0.017). Miwa 2016 (ME 18 vs 15) found aldosterone 104 vs 157 pg/mL (p=0.004) and renin activity 1.6 vs 2.5 (p=0.06). The adrenal glands respond normally to ACTH in POTS (Laurin 2023), so the defect is upstream of the adrenal. In SomaScan and Olink proteomics, renin, ACE and BNP show no group difference (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis), but those assays measure protein abundance, not posture-stimulated activity.

Thyroid

In one Dutch case-control study, CFS patients had normal TSH but lower total T3, T4 and free T3, with a higher reverse-T3 fraction ('low T3 syndrome' pattern in 16% vs 7%). Early

The thyroid itself looks normal by standard tests, but the active thyroid hormone (T3) runs slightly lower, as seen in many long-term illnesses.

Ruiz-Núñez 2018 (98 vs 99, age/sex matched): TT3 −12.5%, TT4 −11.9%, deiodinase activity −14.4%, rT3 fraction +13.3%. FT3 below range in 16/98 vs 7/99 (OR 2.56, 95% CI 1.00–6.54). The median difference in free T3 was tiny (0.1%), and thyroid values correlated with hsCRP. This pattern ('non-thyroidal illness') appears in many chronic and inflammatory states and is usually adaptive. It has not been independently replicated in ME/CFS. There is no trial of T3 treatment in ME/CFS.

Growth hormone

Reports of low IGF-1 and reduced growth hormone responses in CFS conflict, and the largest controlled study found an intact GH/IGF system. Contested

Growth hormone helps with repair and energy. Early small studies hinted it was low, but a larger careful study found it normal.

Allain 1997 found lower IGF-I (214 vs 263 µg/L) and IGF-II and a reduced GH response to hypoglycaemia. Berwaerts 1998 (20 vs 20) found IGF-I SDS −0.39 vs +0.33 (p=0.02) and a trend to lower nocturnal GH (p=0.06), but normal stimulated GH peaks. Cleare 2000 (37 vs 37, medication-free) found no difference in IGF-I/IGFBPs, urinary GH or GHRH and insulin-stress responses. In a GH treatment RCT (Moorkens 1998, n=20) IGF-1 rose but quality of life did not improve.

Sex differences

ME/CFS and long COVID are more common in women (ME/CFS prevalence about 1.4% vs 0.9%; DecodeME 82% female), but genetic risk variants are not sex-specific. Replicated

More women than men get ME/CFS and long COVID. Inherited risk looks the same in both sexes, so the difference probably lies in hormones, immunity or exposure, not in different genes.

Lim 2020 meta-analysis: pooled prevalence 1.36% in women vs 0.86% in men. Clinic cohorts are typically 75–85% female. In RECOVER-Adult (n=12,276), female sex raised long COVID risk (RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.06–1.62), but not at age 18–39 (RR 1.04). At age 40–54 the RR was similar for menopausal (1.42) and non-menopausal (1.45) women. DecodeME: 12,833 female and 2,746 male cases, no sex-biased loci, and two female-discovered signals replicate in males. The mostly male Million Veteran Program replicates the polygenic signal (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis).

Evidence

Sex hormones and menopause

Women with CFS report more endometriosis, heavy bleeding, pelvic pain, hysterectomy and earlier menopause than controls in US population-based case-control studies. Early

Gynaecological problems and early menopause are more common in women with ME/CFS. We do not know which comes first or why.

Boneva 2015 (Georgia, 84 cases vs 73 controls) reported earlier menopause (37.6 vs 48.6 years; adjusted OR 1.22 per year), endometriosis 29.8% vs 12.3% (aOR 3.67), hysterectomy 54.8% vs 19.2% (aOR 3.23) and non-menstrual pelvic pain (aOR 12.0). The Wichita sample (36 vs 48) showed similar but mostly non-significant patterns. Surgical menopause after hysterectomy or oophorectomy confounds the 'early menopause' result, and recall bias is possible. 2026 survey work (Habermann-Horstmeier) describes different symptom structures by sex and a menopausal-status proxy, but it is cross-sectional and self-reported.

Sex hormones

Lower plasma androgenic steroids in ME/CFS (Cornell metabolomics) is mostly an age and sex artefact and does not replicate in BioMapAI. Contested

An earlier claim that patients have low 'male-type' steroid hormones mostly disappears once age and sex are accounted for.

Across the two Cornell cohorts the androgenic steroid class was −0.42 SD, but in Germain 2022 the effect shrinks after age/sex/BMI adjustment. BioMapAI (n=236) shows −0.01 (p=0.90) and Che testosterone −0.18 (p=0.22) (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis). Cleare 2004 measured DHEA/DHEA-S and their response to CRH as a separate question.

In app-based tracking, symptoms varied across the menstrual cycle (lowest in the early luteal phase), crashes were more frequent during menstruation, and users of combined hormonal contraception reported fewer crashes (OR 0.55). Early

Symptoms and crashes followed the menstrual cycle in tracking data, and people on the combined pill had fewer crashes.

Goodship 2025 preprint (ME/CFS and long COVID, Visible app data; contraception analysis n=70). Self-report, self-selected users, observational. Fits the sex-hormone findings but cannot show cause.

Test: Symptom diary

Melatonin and circadian rhythm

Melatonin may help the subgroup with delayed melatonin onset, and melatonin plus zinc modestly reduced physical fatigue in one small RCT. Early

Melatonin is the night-time hormone. A small trial and an open study suggest it can help some patients, especially those whose body clock runs late.

van Heukelom 2006 (open-label, n=29 with DLMO after 21:30; 5 mg 5 h before DLMO for 3 months) improved fatigue, concentration and activity, more when DLMO was after 22:00. Fatigue normalised in 8/27. Castro-Marrero 2021 (RCT, n=50, melatonin 1 mg plus zinc 10 mg for 16 weeks) reduced physical fatigue at the last visit and improved SF-36 physical summary. Multiple outcomes were tested and the trial was not replicated.

Bears on: HPA axis blunting · Test: Research/private: salivary dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO); actigraphy

Genetics of hormone systems

ME/CFS genetic risk is enriched in brain tissues and the pituitary, but genetically predicted morning cortisol does not change risk. Early

Genes linked to ME/CFS are especially active in the brain and the pituitary, the master hormone gland. Genetically high or low cortisol does not seem to cause ME/CFS.

In a DecodeME + Million Veteran Program meta-analysis (Maccallini 2026 preprint, 19,470 cases), tissue enrichment implicated multiple brain regions and the pituitary, with no peripheral tissue. MR using a single morning-cortisol instrument gave OR 1.04 (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis), which is underpowered. The pituitary result could reflect neural gene expression shared with brain rather than endocrine function.

  • Woo 2026, Molecular Psychiatry: Most comprehensive meta-analysis of HPA findings (46 studies, all sample types and challenge tests).
  • Zhang & Wang 2024, Front Endocrinol: Review of HPA changes and HPA-targeted treatments in CFS.
  • Wirth 2026, Preprints.org: Hypothesis review of why vasopressin and RAAS fail to correct hypovolaemia (not peer reviewed).
  • Miwa 2026, Front Med: Clinical update on small heart, orthostatic intolerance and down-regulated volume hormones.

Gut and microbiome

Gut bacteria differ between people with ME/CFS and healthy controls more consistently than almost any blood measure. Fewer butyrate-producing species (Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, Coprococcus, Anaerostipes, Eubacterium rectale) and more Ruminococcus gnavus-type species appear in at least four independent cohorts across three labs, including a pre-specified test in the NIH cohort. The same pattern appears in long COVID. Blood levels of a gut-made metabolite, indole-3-propionate (IPA), are lower in four of four plasma cohorts, and re-analysis traces this to the R. gnavus-type overgrowth. What is not established is whether any of this causes symptoms. Dysbiosis is milder in long-standing illness, does not track severity reliably, and genetically predicted gut metabolite levels do not change ME/CFS risk. Markers of a 'leaky gut' (LPS, sCD14) come from a handful of studies, and the only randomised faecal transplant trial (n=11) was negative. Larger trials are under way.

Dysbiosis

Stool from ME/CFS patients has fewer butyrate-producing bacteria (notably Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, Eubacterium rectale, Roseburia, Coprococcus) and reduced microbial capacity to make butyrate. Replicated

Some 'good' gut bacteria that feed the gut lining by making butyrate are consistently scarcer in ME/CFS.

Guo 2023 (106 vs 91, shotgun metagenomics, qPCR and stool SCFA) found lower F. prausnitzii and E. rectale and lower butyrate synthesis capacity. Its classifier was robust across US sites and to a validation cohort. Xiong 2023 (75 short-term, 79 long-term vs 79) found reduced butyrate biosynthesis genes and lower plasma butyrate, mostly in short-term patients. Giloteaux 2016 (16S, 48 vs 39) found lower diversity and fewer Firmicutes. Nagy-Szakal 2017 (50 vs 50) found lower Faecalibacterium in the IBS subgroup. In the NIH Walitt cohort (15 vs 17), a pre-specified 14-species signature built on other cohorts separated patients with AUC 0.87; all butyrate producers combined were −0.87 SD (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis). The NIH authors' own per-species tests did not pass FDR (min q 0.088).

Ruminococcus gnavus, Flavonifractor plautii, Ruthenibacterium lactatiformans and Enterocloster species are increased in ME/CFS, consistently across BioMapAI, Guo 2023 and NIH cohorts and in long COVID. Several studies

Alongside the loss of 'good' species, a group of bacteria often linked to gut inflammation is overgrown.

In BioMapAI/JAX data (143 vs 88 people), R. lactatiformans (β +0.69), R. gnavus (+0.68) and F. plautii (+0.60) were raised (all q<1e-3). Guo 2023 agreed in direction for 14/17 shared species (binomial p=0.013; Solving ME/CFS re-analysis), but Guo listed only nominally significant species. In the NIH cohort, R. gnavus was +0.80 SD (p=0.014), E. bolteae +0.91 and C. symbiosum +0.77. Long COVID shows the same direction: Liu 2022 (106 patients followed 6 months) found higher R. gnavus and lower F. prausnitzii in post-acute COVID syndrome.

Gut dysbiosis is strongest in the first years of illness and largely resolves in patients ill for more than 10 years, while their metabolic and clinical abnormalities persist. Early

Gut differences are clearest early in the illness and fade later, even though patients stay ill. This argues against gut bacteria alone keeping the illness going.

Xiong 2023: short-term (<4 years, n=75) patients showed significant microbial dysbiosis, while long-term (>10 years, n=79) patients had largely resolved dysbiosis but more severe metabolic and clinical aberrations. This comes from one cross-sectional comparison of two cohorts, not follow-up of the same people. The NIH cohort, which is mostly under 5 years ill, still shows the signature (AUC 0.87).

Microbial metabolites

Plasma indole-3-propionate (IPA), a gut-bacteria product of tryptophan, is lower in ME/CFS in 4 of 4 plasma cohorts (pooled −0.33 SD), and the deficit is fully explained by stool composition, mainly the R. gnavus-type overgrowth. Several studies

A protective molecule that only gut bacteria make is slightly low in patients' blood. The overgrown bacteria seem to crowd out the microbes that make it.

Pooled across Germain 2020, Germain 2022, Che 2022 and BioMapAI: −0.33 SD (95% CI −0.49 to −0.16), p=0.0001. As a test it is weak (AUC 0.57–0.60). In 231 people with paired stool and plasma, a stool model predicted plasma IPA (CV Spearman 0.44), and adjusting for it removed the patient-control gap (−0.36 → −0.06). R. gnavus, F. plautii and R. lactatiformans were each inversely related to IPA. The IPA-producing C. sporogenes guild was not reduced. Fruit intake tracks IPA. No severity association survived FDR (all Solving ME/CFS re-analysis).

The replicated deficit of aromatic lactates (indolelactate, phenyllactate, 4-hydroxyphenyllactate) in ME/CFS blood is not predicted by stool bacteria or bacterial genes, so it is probably host-side or due to absorption, not dysbiosis. Early

Another set of low blood molecules looks like gut products, but the gut bacteria data do not explain them, so probiotics aimed at them are unlikely to help.

Aromatic-lactate score −0.55 SD (p 6.5e-6) in BioMapAI, and −0.53 SD across 5 cohorts. Stool species and gene models predict it at zero (CV Spearman 0.01). 0/4,429 KEGG genes and 0/1,696 taxa associate with it, and Bifidobacterium plus Lactobacillus abundance is uncorrelated (rho −0.01). Adjusting for diet, medications, IBS and kidney function makes the deficit larger, not smaller. In Esteban 2026, stool aromatic metabolites were higher in patients, which hints at reduced absorption (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis).

Dysbiosis and symptoms

Links between specific gut bacteria and symptom severity are inconsistent: F. prausnitzii tracked fatigue in one cohort, but nothing survived correction for multiple testing in a 143-patient re-analysis. Contested

It is not yet clear that people with more abnormal gut bacteria are sicker.

Guo 2023 found F. prausnitzii abundance inversely associated with fatigue severity. Nagy-Szakal 2017 reported correlations between distinct taxa and pain, fatigue and motivation within subgroups. In BioMapAI (143 patients), no taxon or metabolite module associated with severity, orthostatic intolerance or duration at FDR. The best nominal result was lower IPA with worse GI symptoms (p=0.005, q=0.41) (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis).

IBS and GI symptoms

IBS is about seven times more common in ME/CFS (pooled OR 7.20; prevalence about 37%), and IBS status drives much of the measured microbiome difference. Replicated

Many people with ME/CFS also have irritable bowel syndrome. Studies need to separate the two, because IBS changes gut bacteria by itself.

Rajabi 2026 meta-analysis: 22 studies, 18 pooled. OR 7.20 (2.77–18.76), I² 72%; pooled IBS prevalence 37% (23–54%), varying by ME/CFS criteria. Brown 2026 (116 vs 80): 53% vs 8% prior IBS diagnosis, with GI symptom burden tracking fatigue, cognitive, pain and flu-like symptoms. In Nagy-Szakal 2017, IBS co-morbidity was the strongest factor separating microbiome networks, and the top marker taxa differed between IBS and non-IBS subgroups. Genetically, ME/CFS correlates with IBS (rg 0.57) and its heritability is enriched in enteric neurons (Lee 2026 medRxiv; from Solving ME/CFS genetics summary).

Gut permeability and translocation

Blood markers of bacterial translocation (LPS, LPS-binding protein, sCD14, IgA/IgM to enterobacterial LPS) are raised in several small ME/CFS studies, but standardised replication is lacking. Contested

Some studies suggest bits of gut bacteria leak into the blood ('leaky gut') and trigger inflammation. The evidence is small, uses different tests, and comes mostly from a few labs.

Giloteaux 2016 (48 vs 39) found LPS, LBP and sCD14 elevated and correlated with each other. I-FABP (gut-cell damage) was also measured. Maes 2007 reported higher serum IgA and IgM against LPS of gram-negative enterobacteria, correlated with severity and IBS symptoms. De Meirleir 2018 (140 vs 140, retrospective) found sCD14 among the most discriminating serum markers. In the Solving ME/CFS tally, 5 groups report raised LPS/sCD14 and 2 do not. Brown 2026 found higher IgM to LPS only in the subgroup with more flu-like symptoms. Endotoxin assays are contamination-prone, sCD14 is a general monocyte activation marker, and no study has used a direct permeability test (lactulose/mannitol). Maes' 'leaky gut diet' studies were uncontrolled.

Virome and mucosal immunity (Quadram Institute)

Quadram Institute studies of severe ME/CFS with household-matched controls report altered gut phage communities and reduced serum IgG reactivity to gut microbes, in very small samples. Early

A Norwich team is studying the viruses that infect gut bacteria, and the immune response to gut microbes, comparing patients with people in the same household. Their samples are tiny so far.

Hsieh 2023 combined virus-like-particle and whole-metagenome sequencing in a small severe-ME/CFS cohort. It defined a core of tailed Caudoviricetes phages and predicted ME/CFS-specific virus-host links involving Anaerotruncus. Seton 2023 (5 pairs with same-household controls) found reduced serum IgG capacity and reactivity to stool microbes. In a twin pair discordant for ME/CFS, Giloteaux 2016 reported lower diversity and expanded Caudovirales phages in the ill twin. The virome of the Norwegian Comeback FMT trial (Quadram/UEA thesis 2024) and a RESTORE-ME trial virome analysis are in progress, and no results are published.

Treatment: faecal transplant

The only published randomised faecal microbiota transplant trial in CFS (n=11) found no benefit, and a larger Norwegian RCT (n=80) has not yet reported. Early

Transferring stool from a healthy donor has been tried once in a proper small trial and did not help. A bigger trial is under way.

Salonen 2023 (Finland, donor FMT n=5 vs autologous n=6 by colonoscopy) found no change in VAS, MFIS, 15D or EQ-5D at 1 or 6 months, and no adverse events. It was underpowered. Kenyon 2019 reported improvement in a retrospective non-randomised series. The Comeback Study (NCT03691987, Harstad; 80 participants randomised 1:1:2 to two donors or autologous placebo, primary outcome FSS at 3 months) published its protocol in 2024. As of October 2026 no results have been reported.

Treatment: probiotics and diet

Probiotic trials in CFS are small; one 39-person RCT of Lactobacillus casei Shirota reduced anxiety but did not target fatigue. Early

No probiotic has been shown to improve ME/CFS itself.

Rao 2009 (n=39, 24 billion CFU daily for 2 months) raised stool Lactobacillus and Bifidobacteria and reduced Beck anxiety scores (p=0.01). Fatigue was not the primary outcome. Venturini 2019 was an uncontrolled pilot. Re-analysis argues against Bifidobacterium/Lactobacillus products for the indolelactate deficit, because their abundance does not track it. Fibre and polyphenols have a better mechanistic case for IPA, but there are no trials (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis).

Genetics of the gut-brain axis

ME/CFS genetic risk overlaps with IBS and is enriched in enteric neurons, but genetically predicted gut-derived metabolites (IPA, indolelactate, kynurenine, bile acids) do not change ME/CFS risk. Early

The genes involved overlap with those for irritable bowel syndrome and gut nerves. But inheriting higher or lower levels of gut metabolites does not change ME/CFS risk, so those metabolites are probably effects, not causes.

Solving ME/CFS MR (DecodeME discovery, MVP replication): IPA OR 1.19 (0.93–1.53), indolelactate 0.99, kynurenine 1.01, glycocholate 1.02, all null. Lee 2026 (medRxiv, from Solving ME/CFS genetics summary): rg with IBS 0.57 and heritability enrichment in enteric neurons (FDR 0.004). Wielscher 2026 (preprint): 'barrier-microbiome' traits show among the strongest genetic overlap, with IBS contributing most pleiotropy. OLFM4, a DecodeME locus, is highly expressed in ileal stem cells and neutrophils.

Long COVID

In long COVID, the gut microbiome at hospital admission predicted persistent symptoms, and at 6 months patients had more R. gnavus and fewer butyrate producers, mirroring ME/CFS. Several studies

Long COVID shows a gut pattern similar to ME/CFS, and in one study the gut profile early in COVID predicted who stayed ill.

Liu 2022 (Hong Kong, 106 patients, 258 serial stool samples; 68 controls) reported that admission microbiota composition was associated with PACS. Patients who recovered had normalised microbiomes, while PACS showed higher R. gnavus and B. vulgatus and lower F. prausnitzii. Butyrate producers (B. pseudocatenulatum, F. prausnitzii) showed the largest inverse correlation with PACS. Antibiotic use and hospital care in severe COVID are confounders.

Multi-omics classifiers

Microbiome-based machine-learning classifiers distinguish ME/CFS from controls in held-out and external cohorts (BioMapAI, Guo 2023), but they are research tools with modest real-world specificity. Several studies

Computer models can tell patient and control stool apart better than chance, but this is not a diagnostic test yet.

BioMapAI (Xiong 2025, Nat Med; 249 participants over 4 years) integrated metagenomics, plasma metabolomics, immune profiling and labs to predict severity. It classified held-out and external cohorts and linked SCFA, BCAA, tryptophan and benzoate metabolism to MAIT/γδT inflammation. Guo 2023's classifier generalised across US sites. Classifiers have not been tested against disease controls (IBS, depression, MS, fibromyalgia), so specificity is unknown. Within-cohort cross-validation in the plasma metabolome transferred poorly (AUC 0.56; Solving ME/CFS re-analysis).

Key reviews

  • König 2022, Front Immunol: Broad review of microbiome hypotheses (dysbiosis, permeability, SCFA, D-lactate, tryptophan) and interventions.
  • Nikolova 2025, Int J Mol Sci: Recent overview of gut microbiome mechanisms in ME/CFS.
  • Rajabi 2026, Front Med: First meta-analysis quantifying IBS overlap.
  • Perera 2025, Int J Mol Sci (Quadram): Argues that mucosal viruses are an under-studied piece.

Genetics

ME/CFS runs in families, and twin, genealogy and three-generation cohort studies put familial or heritable risk at roughly 20 to 50%. In 2025 DecodeME (15,579 cases) found the first eight robust genome-wide loci, with SNP heritability of about 8 to 10%. Each variant shifts risk only slightly (odds ratios 1.07 to 1.10), so no gene test can diagnose or predict ME/CFS. The overall genetic signal replicates in independent biobanks (MVP, FinnGen, UK Biobank), but the individual loci mostly do not yet, partly because those biobanks use loose case definitions. Across several analyses the signal points to neurons in the brain (and possibly the pituitary), not blood immune cells. It overlaps strongly with chronic pain, fibromyalgia, IBS and migraine, and partly with depression, though the specific ME/CFS loci do not share causal variants with depression. Earlier small candidate-gene and HLA findings mostly failed to replicate. Several 2025–2026 follow-ups (Mendelian randomisation, rare variants, a UK Biobank/All of Us GWAS) are preprints that still need confirmation.

Heritability and family studies

ME/CFS aggregates in families: relatives of cases have about 2-3x the risk, MZ twins are more concordant than DZ twins, and familiality in a 153,803-person Dutch cohort was 42%. Replicated

Having a close relative with ME/CFS raises your own risk, which means genes (and perhaps shared environment) play a part.

In the Utah Population Database (Albright 2011), relative risk was 2.70 (1.56–4.66) for first-degree relatives, 2.34 for second-degree and 1.93 for third-degree, with excess distant relatedness (p=0.010). Buchwald 2001 (146 female twin pairs) found 55% MZ vs 19% DZ concordance for idiopathic chronic fatigue and estimated heritability up to 51%. Its confidence intervals are wide, and it measured chronic fatigue, not strict ME/CFS. Bos 2025 (Lifelines, 153,803 people, 90,397 with a first-degree relative) found recurrence risk ratio 1.45–2.23 within disorders and familiality 42% (33–50) for ME/CFS. Familial correlations were 0.97 with fibromyalgia and 0.83 with depression. Familiality includes shared household environment.

Genome-wide association (GWAS)

DecodeME (15,579 PEM-defined cases vs 259,909 controls) identified 8 genome-wide significant loci, each with a small effect (OR about 1.07-1.10), and SNP heritability of about 8-10%. Several studies

The largest DNA study of ME/CFS found eight regions of the genome linked to the illness. Each nudges risk only a tiny amount.

Lead genes as assigned: RABGAP1L, BTN2A2/TRIM38, FBXL4, SUDS3, OLFM4, CCPG1, CA10, ARFGEF2/CSE1L/ZNFX1 (the chr20 signal p=1e-11). Four loci (RABGAP1L, FBXL4, OLFM4, CA10) were nominally associated (p<0.05) with PEM-plus-fatigue cases in UK Biobank and Lifelines, but none passed multiple-testing correction in external sets. There was no sex-biased locus, and ARFGEF2 and CA10 replicated in males. The CA10 signal colocalises with multisite chronic pain. As of October 2026 this is still a medRxiv preprint, with no peer-reviewed version. Gene assignments are weak at some loci: the 6q16 lead is about 890 kb from FBXL4, and the chr1 lead sits inside DARS2 (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis). An absolute-risk calculation shows one risk copy moves baseline risk from about 0.9% to about 0.97–0.99%.

A 2026 UK Biobank GWAS with stricter, multi-source case definitions (1,268 cases) reports 7 loci that replicate in disjoint UK Biobank or All of Us cohorts (near BICD1, GRIN2A, CSMD1, RORA, CLYBL), though none replicate in all three. Early

A new study using carefully confirmed cases in two biobanks found seven genetic regions that repeated in a second group. It is a preprint and the groups are small.

Slaughter 2026 (medRxiv) used TarGene with electronic health records plus survey data to confirm case and control status. 176 variants passed FDR<5% in discovery, and replication cohorts had 319 (UKB) and 371 (All of Us) cases. Fine-mapping at one locus colocalised with reduced CLYBL expression in putamen, but the CLYBL stop-gain variant was not associated. No gene-by-sex or gene-by-deprivation interactions survived correction. FDR-based discovery in a small sample and no overlap with DecodeME's 8 loci call for caution. GRIN2A (an NMDA receptor subunit) fits the glutamatergic signal.

Replication in biobanks

The genome-wide DecodeME signal replicates in independent cohorts: genetic correlation 0.65-0.73 with the Million Veteran Program CFS GWAS and 0.80-0.90 with UK Biobank CFS, plus concordant directions for sub-threshold SNPs in FinnGen. Replicated

Even though single hits do not yet repeat everywhere, the overall genetic fingerprint of ME/CFS shows up again in other large populations, including mostly male US veterans.

Solving ME/CFS re-analysis derived MVP-only statistics (3,891 independent cases) from the public DecodeME+MVP meta. rg 0.73 ± 0.16. DecodeME SNPs at p<1e-5 were concordant 42/63 in MVP (p=0.006) and 41/61 in FinnGen postviral fatigue (p=0.005). Pan-UKB self-report CFS gave rg 0.90, but it shares controls. An independent GitHub re-analysis (trafalmadorian97) reported rg 0.65 with MVP and 0.80 with Neale UKB. The MVP cohort is mostly male, so polygenic risk applies across sexes.

Tissue and cell-type enrichment

Genome-wide ME/CFS heritability is enriched in brain tissues and neurons (including glutamatergic synapse genes and subcortical/cerebellar neuron types), with no enrichment in blood immune cells. Several studies

The genes involved are mainly active in nerve cells in the brain, not in blood immune cells. This suggests the brain is central to inherited risk.

DecodeME: MAGMA gene-property enrichment in all 13 GTEx brain tissues and no others. Independent S-LDSC re-analysis (trafalmadorian97 GitHub): CNS tissues and chromatin only. ImmGen and blood-cell ATAC-seq were null, and medium spiny neuron clusters were implicated. Maccallini 2026 (DecodeME+MVP): brain regions and pituitary, glutamatergic synapse gene sets, with 7/12 gene sets replicating in rare-variant genes from HEAL2. Lee 2026 (medRxiv): inhibitory neurons (p=1.2e-7) and enteric neurons. Immune abnormalities may still be downstream of illness. A locus-level permutation with only 8 loci could not place any tissue (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis).

Shared genetics with other conditions

ME/CFS genetics overlaps most with chronic pain, fibromyalgia, IBS and migraine, and substantially with depression, but none of the 8 DecodeME loci share a causal variant with depression. Several studies

Genes that raise ME/CFS risk also raise risk of chronic pain and gut-brain conditions. This is shared biology, not evidence that ME/CFS is depression.

The CA10 locus colocalises with multisite chronic pain (PPH4 92.8%). Re-analyses report the highest rg with fibromyalgia, then multisite pain, as well as syncope, migraine and asthma. Lee 2026 medRxiv: rg with major depression 0.60 and with IBS 0.57. MR in Solving ME/CFS re-analysis: depression OR 1.82 (MVP 1.36) and multisite pain OR 3.3, but reverse MR is also positive (ME/CFS → depression OR 1.15) and heterogeneity is high, which indicates shared liability rather than one-way causation. A UK Biobank MR (Song 2025) found no causal effect of depression on ME/CFS.

Infection response genes

Three DecodeME loci lie near infection-response genes (OLFM4, RABGAP1L, BTN2A2/TRIM38), and the OLFM4 effect is larger in infection-onset cases, but infection- and non-infection-onset cases are genetically highly correlated. Early

Some risk genes help the body respond to infections, which fits the common post-viral onset. But people whose illness began without an obvious infection carry similar overall genetic risk.

Infection-onset GWAS (9,738 cases): 3 loci (6p22.2, 20q13.13, OLFM4). The OLFM4 beta was 0.095±0.017 with infection onset vs 0.034±0.022 without. The no-infection GWAS (5,841) found nothing, which is a power issue. Independent re-analysis finds high rg between onset subgroups. OLFM4 is a neutrophil and ileal stem-cell protein. ZNFX1 (a dsRNA sensor) and CSE1L (needed for STAT1 import) sit at the chr20 locus. Genetically higher EBV DNA load gave OR 1.13 (ns) in DecodeME and 1.59 (p=0.012) in MVP (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis). MHC-based negative controls (VZV, HHV-6B) also aligned, so the result is not EBV-specific. The long COVID FOXP4 variant is not associated with ME/CFS (p=0.59).

Two autoimmunity risk alleles, PTPN22 rs2476601 (OR 1.63) and CTLA4 rs3087243 (OR 1.53), were associated with ME/CFS only in patients whose illness began with an infection. Early

Gene variants known to raise the risk of autoimmune disease were more common in patients who fell ill after an infection.

Steiner 2020 (Berlin; 305 vs 201). Candidate-gene design, modest size. DecodeME did not report these loci at genome-wide significance, which a candidate effect of this size would not necessarily reach.

HLA

Reported HLA associations are inconsistent: Lande 2020's HLA-C*07:04 and DQB1*03:03 risk alleles are not among DecodeME's hits, and DecodeME's protective HLA-DQA1*05:01 signal is barely visible at SNP level. Contested

HLA genes shape immune responses and are linked to autoimmune diseases. Claims of specific HLA types in ME/CFS have not held up consistently.

Lande 2020 (426 Norwegian CCC cases vs 4,511 controls) reported HLA-C*07:04 (OR 2.1) and DQB1*03:03 (OR 1.5); carriers of either were 19.2% vs 12.2%. DecodeME reported DQA1*05:01 as protective (p=1.4e-10; 21.7% vs 23.2%), with no DRB1*03:01 or DQB1*02:01 signal. In Solving ME/CFS re-analysis, the best DQ2.5 tag SNP was OR 0.96 (p=0.025). That gap suggests the imputed-allele p-value is inflated, possibly because HLA was imputed separately for cases and controls, a problem the authors flagged. MHC z-scores correlate only 0.21 between DecodeME and MVP. A purely in-silico 2025 study modelled Lande alleles binding herpes peptides, with no patient data.

NK-cell receptor genes

Specific inhibitory KIR alleles (e.g. KIR3DL1*020, KIR3DL2*009) were more or less common in 418 Norwegian patients than 473 controls, though KIR gene content did not differ. Early

Variants in genes for natural killer cell 'brake' receptors may differ slightly in ME/CFS. This has not been checked in another cohort.

Ramadan 2025 used high-resolution KIR sequencing with HLA ligand annotation. Patient-enriched alleles were KIR3DL3*002 (OR 1.43), KIR3DL1*020 (OR 2.20) and KIR3DL2*009 (OR 1.56); reduced alleles were KIR3DL3*013 (OR 0.60) and KIR3DL2*010 (OR 0.46, p=0.0005). There was no association with gene content or copy number. Nominal p-values without a replication cohort; KIR is poorly captured by GWAS arrays, so DecodeME cannot test it.

Earlier GWAS and candidate genes

Before DecodeME, small GWAS and candidate-gene studies (GRIK2, NPAS2, TPPP, TRA locus and many others) produced no association that replicated in UK Biobank or later cohorts. Refuted

Older genetic studies were too small. Their 'hits' did not hold up when tested in larger groups.

Smith 2011 (40 vs 40, 116k SNPs plus expression) flagged GRIK2 and NPAS2. Hajdarevic 2022 (Norwegian 427 discovery, Danish 460, UKB 2,105) found no genome-wide significant loci; the best signal was TPPP (p=8.5e-7) and the top SNP did not replicate. Dibble 2020 concluded that most candidate gene associations are not replicated by the UK Biobank CFS cohort. Ueland 2022's T-cell receptor alpha signal did not replicate (from Solving ME/CFS genetics summary).

Mendelian randomisation

Proteome-wide cis-MR finds genetically higher plasma EPHB1 (a pain-sensitisation receptor) and CLEC3B (tetranectin) associated with ME/CFS risk in DecodeME, replicating in the independent MVP cohort. Early

Using genes as a natural experiment, two blood proteins look like they may influence ME/CFS risk. One of them is involved in how the nervous system amplifies pain.

Solving ME/CFS re-analysis of about 1,950 UKB-PPP and 1,690 deCODE plasma proteins (Wald ratio). EPHB1: OR 1.18/SD (p=2e-4), MVP 1.29 (p=0.0016), combined FDR 0.002; its pQTL is in LD with the regional DecodeME peak (r² 0.84). CLEC3B: OR 1.21, MVP 1.44 (p=0.0008), but not in LD with the regional peak. PRDX6 (1q25) was protective (0.75; MVP 0.70, p=0.037), and dermatopontin was nominal on both platforms. Only 4/93 nominal hits replicated, versus about 2.3 expected by chance, so these are leads. There was no formal colocalisation because full pQTL statistics need a login, and there are no usable drugs.

MR of DecodeME suggests higher mitochondrial DNA copy number is protective and higher GlycA and mean platelet volume raise risk, while genetically predicted metabolite leads (IPA, kynurenine, ketones, carnitine, bile acids) and vitamin D, BMI and blood pressure are null or unreplicated. Early

Genetic natural experiments hint that inflammation and blood platelets may contribute to risk. Many blood molecules that are low in patients look like effects of being ill, not causes.

Wielscher 2026 (Research Square, not peer reviewed) reported mtDNA copy number as protective and GlycA and MPV as risk-raising. It also found the strongest genetic overlap in barrier-microbiome, neurovascular and energetics traits. Solving ME/CFS MR found indolelactate OR 0.99, kynurenine 1.01 and 3-hydroxybutyrate 0.99, all null. Palmitoylcarnitine 0.88 did not replicate. Vitamin D OR 0.88 (p=0.03) was not replicated and had a pleiotropic Egger intercept. Many published two-sample MR papers on CFS use small UK Biobank self-report GWAS; one was retracted in 2025.

Rare variants and sequencing

Whole-genome sequencing of 464 cases and 611 controls with a deep-learning rare-variant model (HEAL2) proposes 115 loss-of-function-intolerant risk genes, partly overlapping the common-variant synaptic signal. Early

Looking at rare DNA changes, one study suggests a set of genes, many active in nerves and immune cells. The method is new and the sample is small.

Zhang 2025 (medRxiv) reports that a genetic score from personal rare variants tracked PEM, unrefreshing sleep, brain fog and muscle pain. Patient multi-omics showed reduced expression of the risk genes, including in cytotoxic CD4 T cells. Maccallini 2026 found 7 of 12 common-variant gene sets replicate among HEAL2 genes. Deep-learning gene prioritisation in about 1,000 genomes has high overfitting risk, and there has been no independent sequencing replication. No single rare variant has been shown to cause ME/CFS. A verified, specific rare-variant 'Mendelian ME/CFS' report does not exist to my knowledge.

Combinatorial analyses

Proprietary combinatorial SNP analyses (PrecisionLife) report thousands of multi-SNP signatures in UK Biobank and DecodeME, with top vs bottom decile of signature count giving OR 1.64. Contested

A company's method finds combinations of DNA variants linked to ME/CFS, but the method is closed and hard for others to check.

Das 2022 (2,382 UKB cases) mapped 84 SNP combinations to 14 genes, including CLOCK, SLC15A4, INSR and KCNB1. Sardell 2026 (J Transl Med, DecodeME vs UKB controls) reported 22,411 signatures from 7,555 SNPs in 2,311 genes, reproducible across three disjoint DecodeME case sets (p=4e-21 for count), 259 core genes, and 76/180 long-COVID genes overlapping. 'Reproducible' here means within related cohorts sharing UK Biobank controls; the method is proprietary and the gene list is very broad.

TRPM3 ion channel

TRPM3 ion channel dysfunction in NK cells and TRPM3 SNPs are reported repeatedly by one research group, but the SNP studies are tiny and no TRPM3 association appears in GWAS. Contested

A calcium channel called TRPM3 is reported to work poorly in immune cells of ME/CFS patients. Nearly all of this comes from one team, and large DNA studies do not point to the TRPM3 gene.

Marshall-Gradisnik 2016 genotyped B cells from 11 patients vs 11 controls and reported SNPs/genotypes in TRPM3 and acetylcholine receptor genes. Functional work: Sasso 2026 used patch-clamp at two sites run by the same consortium (36 vs 42) and found reduced TRPM3-like currents in NK cells. Independent-lab replication and blinding details are lacking, and TRPM3 is not among DecodeME, MVP or Slaughter 2026 loci. Functional changes could be acquired rather than inherited.

Connective tissue

Joint hypermobility and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome are over-represented in ME/CFS (Beighton ≥4 in 60% of children with CFS vs 24% of controls; 50% in a Swedish severe cohort; EDS about 100x expected in Finnish registries). Several studies

People with very flexible joints, or hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, seem more likely to have ME/CFS or long COVID with PEM. No gene test exists for the hypermobile type.

Barron 2002 (58 incident paediatric CFS vs 58 controls): median Beighton 4 vs 1, OR 3.5 (1.6–7.5). Bragée 2020 (229 severe CCC patients, no controls): 50% hypermobile, with high rates of possible intracranial hypertension and craniocervical findings on MRI. Finnish FinnGen/FinRegistry postviral fatigue shows EDS O/E 106–153, which is crude and inflated by healthcare use (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis). Lubell 2026 (online survey, 1,816 people after COVID) found extreme hypermobility OR 3.15 for long COVID with high post-exertional symptom exacerbation, rising to OR 9.46 with a pre-COVID orthostatic/neurocognitive profile. Hypermobile EDS has no known causal gene, and connective-tissue genes are not among GWAS hits. Collagen breakdown markers are raised in 4/4 Metabolon cohorts (Solving ME/CFS re-analysis).

Mitochondrial DNA

Mitochondrial DNA haplogroups and common mtDNA SNPs are not associated with ME/CFS status, though some variants were associated with particular symptoms. Early

Inherited types of mitochondrial DNA do not differ between patients and controls.

Billing-Ross 2016 (Cornell cohorts) found no haplogroup or SNP association with disease status but reported variant links to symptom severity. Hanson 2016 is the authors' reply clarifying this. MR suggesting higher mtDNA copy number is protective (Wielscher 2026) concerns copy number, not haplogroup. The chr1 DecodeME lead lies in DARS2, a mitochondrial tRNA synthetase, which is a weak hint.

Key reviews

  • Dibble 2020, Hum Mol Genet: Critical review of pre-DecodeME genetics showing candidate genes do not replicate.
  • DecodeME 2025, medRxiv preprint: Primary report of the 8 loci, HLA, sex and onset analyses; summary statistics public on OSF.
  • Maccallini 2026, Research Square preprint: DecodeME+MVP meta-analysis with tissue, cell-type and rare-variant cross-replication.

Treatment trials and natural history

No treatment has replicated, placebo-controlled evidence of benefit in ME/CFS or post-COVID ME/CFS. Since 2019 the large, well-controlled trials have been negative: rituximab, Paxlovid (three trials), immunoadsorption against sham (two trials), ivabradine for long-COVID POTS, temelimab, and low-dose naltrexone for fatigue. The positive signals (daratumumab, cyclophosphamide, low-dose rapamycin, low-dose aripiprazole, single-dose pyridostigmine, 40-session HBOT) come from small, open-label or single-centre studies, and they need to be read against placebo response rates of 35-40% or more. Graded exercise is no longer recommended in England (NICE 2021), and patient surveys and a German rehab study report frequent worsening, while pacing and volume/compression measures are the most highly rated but untested by trials. Natural history data show low full recovery in adults (median ~5%), prevalence of ~0.2-1%, a female excess of 3-4:1, no clear rise in all-cause mortality, and a marked rise in suicide.

Immune: B-cell depletion

B-cell depletion with rituximab did not improve fatigue or function versus placebo in a 151-person phase III trial (RituxME). Refuted

A drug that removes antibody-making B cells looked promising in small Norwegian studies, but a large placebo-controlled trial found it worked no better than a dummy infusion.

RituxME (Fluge 2019): 77 rituximab vs 74 placebo over 24 months; overall response 26.0% vs 35.1% (difference 9.2 points favouring placebo, 95% CI -5.5 to 23.3, p=0.22); no difference on any secondary endpoint; serious adverse events 26% vs 19%. Six-year follow-up (Rekeland 2024): SF-36 physical function 32.9 to 45.5 on rituximab vs 32.3 to 43.1 on placebo. The earlier positive phase II results (Fluge 2011, 2015) were small and partly open-label; the phase III result is the standard example of how large the placebo/natural-course improvement can be in ME/CFS trials.

Immune: broad immunosuppression

In an open-label phase II study, 55% of 40 patients responded to six IV cyclophosphamide infusions, and many responders stayed improved at 6 years, but there was no control arm. Early

A chemotherapy drug that suppresses the immune system was followed by improvement in about half of a small Norwegian group, but without a comparison group the effect cannot be separated from natural improvement or placebo.

CycloME (Rekeland 2020): 600-700 mg/m2 every 4 weeks x6; 22/40 (55%) responders; SF-36 PF 35.4 to 54.4 at 18 months and 56.7 at 6 years; 44.1% had SF-36 PF >=70 at 6 years versus 20.4% of RituxME placebo patients (different trial, not randomised). Nausea in ~90%; 11 serious adverse events in 8 patients. Response was higher in carriers of HLA-DQB1*03:03 and/or HLA-C*07:04 (83% vs 43%), an unreplicated post hoc finding. The authors themselves advise against use outside trials because of toxicity (infertility, bladder and cancer risk).

Immune: plasma-cell depletion

In an open-label pilot, 6 of 10 women with moderate-to-severe ME/CFS improved markedly after the anti-CD38 antibody daratumumab, and low baseline NK-cell count predicted non-response. Early

A drug that removes long-lived antibody-producing plasma cells was followed by large, lasting improvements in six of ten patients. This is the most striking recent signal, but it is ten people with no placebo group.

Fluge 2025: 4-7 subcutaneous injections after a 12-week run-in. Mean SF-36 PF 25.9 to 55.0 at 8-9 months (p=0.002); in the 6 responders 32.2 to 78.3; 5 sustained improvement (SF-36 PF ~88) with step counts above 10,000/day for weeks. Mean steps 3,359 to 5,862. IgG fell 54% in responders vs 40% in non-responders. Low baseline NK-cell counts associated with no response. No serious adverse events. A randomised trial is planned in Norway; Charité is pursuing a related approach with inebilizumab. Given RituxME's ~35% placebo response, n=10 open-label cannot establish efficacy.

Immune: antibody removal

Removing antibodies by immunoadsorption was no better than a sham procedure in two controlled trials (IAMPOCO, n=40; IA-PACS-CFS, n=65), although open-label series had reported 50-70% responders. Refuted

Filtering antibodies out of the blood seemed to help in uncontrolled studies. When patients were compared with others who had a fake procedure, both groups improved similarly.

Stein 2025 (open-label, post-COVID ME/CFS with raised beta2-adrenergic receptor antibodies, n=20): 70% 'responders', SF-36 PF +17.75 at 4 weeks; antibody fall did not distinguish responders. IAMPOCO (Mainz, tryptophan adsorbers, patient-blinded sham crossover, n=40): no difference on the Post-COVID Functional Scale (OR 1.17, p=0.771) or fatigue, cognition, grip strength; 24 vs 10 adverse events. IA-PACS-CFS (Charité, 44 IA vs 21 sham, 5 sessions): 'no statistically or clinically significant differences' on Chalder fatigue at day 60 (preliminary, conference). Critics note IA-PACS-CFS did not select for autoantibody-positive patients; IAMPOCO removed GPCR antibodies and still showed no benefit. A 2025 antigen-profiling study found no elevated GPCR autoantibodies in ME/CFS at all.

Immune: GPCR-antibody neutralisation

The aptamer BC007 (rovunaptabin) failed to beat placebo in the company's 114-person long-COVID trial; a 30-person investigator-led trial reported secondary-endpoint gains. Contested

A drug designed to neutralise antibodies against blood-vessel and heart receptors was tested twice in long COVID. The larger trial found no benefit; a smaller exploratory one reported improvements on fatigue scales.

reCOVer (Erlangen, Hohberger 2025): n=30 with GPCR autoantibodies, primary endpoint safety (9 vs 5 adverse events, NS); secondary endpoints improved (FACIT fatigue p=0.038, Bell score p=0.0004, FSS p=0.009) in an exploratory crossover analysis. BLOC (Berlin Cures, NCT05911009, ~114 participants, 19 sites): topline November 2024 showed no difference from placebo; data unpublished; the company stopped operating. The negative result is larger but unpublished; the positive one is small, exploratory and multiplicity-prone. Combined with the immunoadsorption sham trials and the negative antigen-profiling study, the GPCR-autoantibody route has weakened.

Immune: immunoglobulin

IVIG has no consistent controlled evidence: 1990s ME/CFS RCTs conflicted, and a 30-person trial in autoimmune POTS found no difference from albumin. Contested

Infusions of pooled antibodies from donors are sometimes used for severe patients. Old trials gave mixed answers and the most recent small trial in POTS found the same improvement with a volume-matched control infusion.

iSTAND (Vernino 2024): 16 IVIG vs 14 albumin, 0.4 g/kg x8 over 12 weeks; COMPASS-31 change -5.5 vs -10.6 (p=0.63); responders 46.7% vs 38.5% (NS). Albumin also expands volume, so the comparator may have masked or matched a volume effect. 1990s ME/CFS RCTs: Lloyd 1990 (n=49) positive, Peterson 1990 (n=30) negative, Vollmer-Conna 1997 (n=99) negative. In the Eckey/Xiao 2025 patient survey IVIG was rated among the most helpful in the severe multisystemic cluster (self-report, selected users). The RECOVER-AUTONOMIC IVIG arm in long-COVID POTS has not yet reported (as of Oct 2026).

Immune: TLR3 agonist

Rintatolimod (Ampligen) gave a modest placebo-adjusted gain in treadmill time in a 234-person phase III trial, but the result was borderline and the FDA declined approval. Contested

An immune-stimulating drug given by drip twice a week helped exercise time a little in one large company trial; regulators did not find this convincing.

AMP-516 (Strayer 2012): 40 weeks IV 400 mg twice weekly; intention-to-treat placebo-adjusted exercise tolerance +21.3% (p=0.047), +28% after compliance correction; reduced use of symptomatic drugs (p=0.048). Lead authors employed by the manufacturer. FDA issued a complete response letter in 2009 and has not approved it. A 2020 post hoc analysis suggested better response in illness of 2-8 years' duration. Not replicated by an independent group.

Immune/viral: HERV-W

The anti-HERV-W envelope antibody temelimab did not improve fatigue versus placebo in 203 HERV-W-positive long-COVID patients. Refuted

A drug aimed at a dormant virus-like gene product that can be switched on after infection did not help long-COVID fatigue in a proper trial.

GNC-501 (GeNeuro, 2024): IV temelimab vs placebo, primary endpoint 3-point fall in PROMIS Fatigue SF-7a at week 24; no clinically meaningful difference and most secondary endpoints negative; well tolerated. Company suggested shorter disease duration or changes in HERV-W status may matter (post hoc). Company press release; full peer-reviewed paper not seen.

Immune/metabolic: mTOR inhibition

Low-dose rapamycin (6 mg weekly) was followed by self-reported improvement in about three-quarters of completers in an uncontrolled decentralised study; randomised trials are pending. Early

A low weekly dose of an immune-modulating drug thought to restart cellular clean-up (autophagy) was followed by improvement in many patients, but no one in the study got a placebo.

Ruan 2025: 86 enrolled, 70 reached day 30; 52 (74.3%) reported improvement in fatigue, PEM and orthostatic intolerance, with MFI and SF-36 gains; autophagy markers (pSer258-ATG13 down, BECLIN-1 up) moved and correlated with outcomes. No serious adverse events. Follow-on metabolomics (Gile 2026) in responders only. Uncontrolled response rates of this size are similar to placebo responses in RCTs (35-40%+) plus attrition bias. The Mount Sinai placebo-controlled trial in long COVID (NCT06960928, ~80-90) ends Nov 2026.

Antiviral: SARS-CoV-2

Three randomised trials of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (Paxlovid) for 15-25 days in established long COVID (total ~1,200 people) found no benefit on any phenotype. Refuted

If leftover coronavirus were driving long COVID, an antiviral might help. Three good trials found it did not, at least at the doses and durations tested.

RECOVER-VITAL (Baden 2026): 959 randomised to 15 or 25 days vs placebo-ritonavir, cognitive, autonomic and exercise phenotypes; no primary benefit (e.g. autonomic -6.4%, 95% CI -18.5 to 5.7). STOP-PASC (Stanford, n=155, 15 days) and PAX LC (Yale, n=100, 15 days, PROMIS-29) also null. STOP-PASC immune profiling found no EBV reactivation or microclot differences versus controls. The trials do not exclude a role for persistence in tissue reservoirs that this drug fails to reach, or effects in very early or highly selected patients.

Antiviral: herpesviruses

Valganciclovir in 30 patients selected for high HHV-6 and EBV antibody levels improved some secondary fatigue and cognition scores in a small RCT; it has not been replicated. Early

Antivirals against herpesviruses have been tried in patients with high antibody levels, with modest results in one small trial. High antibodies show past infection, not necessarily active virus.

Montoya 2013: 2:1 randomised, 6 months; reported benefit on MFI mental fatigue (p=0.039), Fatigue Severity Scale (p=0.006) and cognition (p=0.025); primary endpoint detail not confirmed this session. Preceded by an open-label series (Kogelnik 2006, 9/12 near-resolution). Neutropenia risk requires monitoring. Lerner's valacyclovir/valganciclovir EBV-subset series are uncontrolled. Selection by IgG titre is a weak marker of active replication.

Neuro-immune: low-dose naltrexone

The first sizeable placebo-controlled trial of low-dose naltrexone in post-COVID ME/CFS (66 vs 71, 16 weeks, up to 4.5 mg) found no fatigue benefit, with over 40% improving on placebo. Refuted

Low-dose naltrexone is widely used off-label and many patients report benefit. In a proper trial, the drug did not reduce fatigue more than placebo. Pain and subgroup results are still being analysed.

The trial is Canadian (Nacul, University of British Columbia; NCT05430152), presented at the Berlin International ME/CFS Conference, May 2026; preliminary and unpublished. Earlier evidence was retrospective (Polo 2019, n=218, 74% self-reported benefit) or uncontrolled long-COVID series. The LIFT trial (pyridostigmine x LDN factorial, n=160, Harvard/OMF, NCT06366724) and a RECOVER paediatric trial are pending. Effects on pain, sleep or specific subgroups remain possible.

Neuro: low-dose aripiprazole

In a retrospective single-clinic review, 74% of 101 patients on very low-dose aripiprazole (mostly 0.25-2 mg) reported improvement; there is no randomised trial. Early

A tiny dose of an antipsychotic drug, thought to act on dopamine and brain immune cells, was linked to improvement in a clinic's records, but this kind of study cannot rule out placebo or selective reporting.

Crosby 2021 (Stanford): 101 patients; ~74% reported improvement in brain fog, fatigue, unrefreshing sleep or energy; side effects included insomnia, akathisia, vivid dreams. Circulation: cholinergic / preload

A single 60 mg pyridostigmine dose raised peak oxygen uptake relative to placebo on a repeat invasive exercise test in 45 ME/CFS patients with preload failure, largely because the placebo group got worse; longer trials are negative or pending. Early

Pyridostigmine boosts nerve signalling that tightens veins and returns blood to the heart. In a one-day lab study it stopped exercise capacity dropping on a second test. Whether it helps daily life is untested; the factorial LIFT trial should answer that.

Joseph/Systrom 2022: 23 vs 22; peak VO2 +13.3 vs -40.2 mL/min (difference ~54 mL/min), with cardiac output and right atrial pressure maintained instead of falling; oxygen extraction unchanged. Same-day laboratory endpoint. São Paulo 2025 (ATS abstract, long COVID with RV preload dysfunction, n=32, up to 360 mg/day for 6-10 weeks): negative overall (p=0.35), borderline +103 mL in a post hoc subgroup. Kanjwal 2011 POTS retrospective (n=203): 43% improved, 19% stopped for GI effects. LIFT (n=160, 13 weeks, FUNCAP-55 and CPET endpoints) has not reported.

Circulation: heart-rate control

Ivabradine lowered standing heart rate but did not improve symptoms in 181 people with long-COVID POTS (RECOVER-AUTONOMIC), despite an earlier positive 22-person crossover in hyperadrenergic POTS. Refuted

Slowing a racing heart is not the same as making people feel better. A large trial in long-COVID POTS showed exactly that.

Taub 2021: 22 hyperadrenergic POTS (noradrenaline >600 pg/mL), 1-month crossover; lower HR and better RAND-36 QoL. RECOVER-AUTONOMIC (2026, ACC late-breaker): 181 adults, 12 weeks; no meaningful change in orthostatic intolerance or long-COVID symptoms vs placebo, though supine-to-standing HR change fell significantly. The factorial coordinated non-pharmacological care arm (diet-mediated volume expansion, rehab, education) is reported separately. Full paper pending. Whether a hyperadrenergic subgroup benefits remains open.

Circulation: vasoconstrictors and volume

Fludrocortisone did not beat placebo in a 100-person RCT in CFS with neurally mediated hypotension; midodrine reduces orthostatic heart rate acutely in small POTS studies but has no ME/CFS outcome trial. Refuted

Two standard drugs for low blood pressure on standing have been tried. Fludrocortisone, which makes the body hold salt, did not help in a proper trial in CFS. Midodrine tightens blood vessels and helps some POTS patients in the short term, but it has not been properly tested in ME/CFS.

Rowe 2001: fludrocortisone 0.1 mg vs placebo for 9 weeks in CFS + NMH on tilt; >=15-point wellness improvement in 14% vs 10% (p=0.76). Peterson 1998 (n=25) also negative. Midodrine: small acute crossover studies in POTS/orthostatic intolerance show lower standing HR (memory, not re-checked); risks include supine hypertension (relevant for bedbound patients). No ME/CFS RCT with function as endpoint. Grade refers to fludrocortisone; midodrine evidence is early.

Oxaloacetate 2 g/day reduced Chalder fatigue more than control (−25% vs −10%) in an 82-person company-run RCT in ME/CFS; a 69-person long-COVID trial missed its primary endpoint. Early

A supplement that feeds a step in energy metabolism reduced fatigue in one trial run with the manufacturer. A similar trial in long COVID did not meet its main goal.

RESTORE ME (Cash 2024): 90 days, 2,000 mg vs rice-flour control; fatigue −25% vs −10% (between-group p=0.0039); secondary analysis (Vernon 2025) showed cognitive gains at day 60. Sponsor (Terra Biological) involvement. REGAIN (long COVID, n=69, 42 days): primary Chalder negative, secondary cognition gains. No independent replication.

Physical: hyperbaric oxygen

Forty daily sessions of hyperbaric oxygen at 2.0 ATA improved cognition and symptoms versus sham in a 73-person long-COVID trial, but ten sessions at 2.4 bar showed no benefit in an 80-person sham-controlled trial. Contested

Breathing pure oxygen under pressure helped in an Israeli trial with 40 sessions, but not in a Swedish trial with 10 sessions. Dose may matter, or the positive trial may not hold up. It needs daily travel, which many patients cannot do.

Zilberman-Itskovich 2022 (Tel Aviv): 37 vs 36, 40 sessions, 5/week, 100% O2 at 2.0 ATA for 90 min with air breaks, sham at 1.03 ATA air; global cognition improved (d≈0.5, p=0.038), plus energy, sleep, psychiatric symptoms and pain; benefits persisted at ~1-year follow-up in 31 patients (Hadanny 2024); a cardiac substudy showed improved GLS. HOT-LoCO (Kjellberg 2025, Sweden): 40 vs 40, 10 sessions over 6 weeks, 100% O2 at 2.4 bar 90 min vs air at 1.2-1.34 bar; RAND-36 PF difference 0.63 (95% CI −7.0 to 8.3, p=0.87); both groups improved. Charité (Kedor, 2026 conference): 20 vs 40 sessions; improvements only in the 40-session group (no sham arm reported). The 'sham' pressure differs between trials and blinding of pressure is imperfect. No ME/CFS (non-COVID) RCT.

Rehabilitation: GET and CBT

PACE (n=641) reported modest gains in self-rated fatigue and function with CBT and graded exercise, but these were not matched by objective measures, used Oxford criteria, and vanished between groups by 2.5 years. Contested

The largest trial of talking therapy and gradually increasing exercise said both helped moderately. Re-analysis using the trial's own original plan found the benefits much smaller and limited to questionnaires that unblinded patients filled in.

White 2011: CBT and GET vs specialist medical care: Chalder fatigue −3.4 and −3.2 points, SF-36 PF +7.1 and +9.4 at 52 weeks; adaptive pacing no better than SMC. Long-term follow-up (Sharpe 2015): no between-group differences at median 31 months. Wilshire 2018 re-analysis using protocol-specified outcomes (data via FOI): CBT/GET did not significantly beat control after correction; recovery rates low (single digits to ~10%) and not different; objective measures (6-minute walk modest, step test, employment, benefits) largely null. Criticisms: Oxford criteria (fatigue only; PEM not required), outcome switching, unblinded self-report, mid-trial newsletter. Cochrane exercise review (Larun, re-dated 2024) rates evidence low-moderate and notes limited applicability to ME/CFS defined with PEM; a full update is pending.

Rehabilitation: guidance and harms

NICE's 2021 guideline (NG206) told clinicians not to offer graded exercise therapy, and patient surveys plus a 2026 German rehabilitation study report frequent worsening after exercise-based or even pacing-focused rehab. Several studies

England's health guidance body reviewed the evidence and concluded that the old exercise trials were low quality and that GET should not be offered. Large patient surveys and a German study suggest rehab programmes often make people worse.

NICE NG206 (Oct 2021): rated the GET/CBT evidence 'low' or 'very low' quality; recommends against GET or any programme based on fixed incremental increases; CBT may be offered only as supportive therapy, not as cure. Eckey/Xiao 2025 survey (n≈3,925): GET had a net score of about −72% (most harmful item). CFS_CARE (Charité, 2026 conference): a specialised rehab programme including pacing left 42 of 97 participants worse on the Bell scale, few better. Survey data are self-selected; CFS_CARE is uncontrolled and preliminary. Nevertheless the direction is consistent across sources.

Self-management: pacing

Pacing (staying within one's energy limits) is the top-rated approach in patient surveys and NICE's recommended foundation, but it has never shown benefit in a controlled trial (adaptive pacing was no better than usual care in PACE). Early

Patients consistently rate pacing as the most helpful thing they do, and guidelines recommend it. It has not been properly tested in a trial designed with patients, so its benefit rests on consensus and self-report.

Eckey/Xiao 2025: pacing net score ~75% (highest of >150 treatments). PACE APT arm (n=160): no difference vs SMC. Critics argue APT in PACE was not the envelope-style pacing patients use. Pacing is plausible as harm avoidance (preventing PEM) rather than a treatment. Heart-rate-guided pacing studies are small and uncontrolled.

Patient-reported outcomes

A 3,925-person survey rated >150 treatments; illness severity predicted perceived response more strongly than diagnosis, and symptom clusters (severe multisystemic, POTS-dominant, cognitive/pain, mild) preferred different treatments. Early

Thousands of patients rated what helped. The cheap supportive measures came top (pacing, fluids, compression), graded exercise came bottom, and different kinds of patients reported benefit from different things.

Eckey, Li, Morrison, Davis, Xiao, PNAS 2025: ME/CFS and long COVID ratings correlated (R²=0.68). Top: pacing 75%, fluids/electrolytes ~69%, compression ~62%; GET −72%. Clusters: severe multisystemic (IVIG, lymphatic drainage), POTS-dominant (compression, autonomic modulators), cognitive (CNS stimulants), mild. Self-selected social-media sample, no placebo, recall bias; useful for prioritising trials, not for efficacy claims.

Trial methodology

Placebo and natural-course improvement in ME/CFS and long-COVID trials is large (35% responders in RituxME, >40% in the LDN trial, both arms improving in IVIG, HBOT and immunoadsorption trials), so uncontrolled response rates of 50-75% are uninterpretable. Replicated

In almost every controlled trial, many people on the dummy treatment also improve. This is why open-label studies that report most patients getting better cannot show a treatment works.

RituxME placebo SF-36 PF 32.3 to 45.5 at 18 months; LDN >40% placebo responders; iSTAND albumin COMPASS −10.6; HOT-LoCO both arms improved; IAMPOCO both arms improved; BLOC failure attributed partly to placebo response. Contributing factors: regression to the mean (patients enrol when worse), natural fluctuation, expectation, and post-COVID spontaneous recovery in early cohorts.

Natural history: recovery

Full recovery from established adult ME/CFS is uncommon: a systematic review of 14 criteria-based cohorts found a median full-recovery rate of 5% (range 0-31%) and median improvement of 39.5%. Several studies

Most adults with long-standing ME/CFS do not fully recover, although many improve somewhat over years. Children and people early in the illness do better.

Cairns & Hotopf 2005: 28 studies, 14 with operational CFS criteria; full recovery median 5%, improvement 39.5% (8-63%); return to work 8-30%. Better outcome with lower baseline fatigue. Adolescents have better prognosis (studies report a majority improving or recovering over 5-10 years; memory, not re-checked). RituxME placebo arm at 6 years: 7.4% reached SF-36 PF >=90. Old cohorts used heterogeneous criteria; newer prospective data in post-COVID ME/CFS (Legler 2023) show little improvement to 20 months.

Natural history: post-COVID ME/CFS

About 4.5% of SARS-CoV-2-infected adults in RECOVER met IOM ME/CFS criteria (vs 0.6% uninfected; HR 4.93), and those meeting Canadian criteria at Charité stayed severely ill to 20 months while other long-COVID patients improved. Several studies

COVID roughly quintupled the rate of new ME/CFS. People whose long COVID meets ME/CFS criteria tend not to recover over the first two years, unlike milder long COVID.

Vernon 2025 (RECOVER-Adult, n=11,785 infected, 1,439 uninfected): incidence 2.66 vs 0.93 per 100 person-years; 88.7% of post-COVID ME/CFS also met long-COVID criteria; criteria based on self-report. Legler 2023 (Charité, n=106, 3-8, 9-16, 17-20 months): PCS-ME/CFS persistently severe; lower initial grip strength predicted persistence. Kedor 2022 (n=42): about half met CCC at 6 months.

Natural history: prevalence and sex ratio

ME/CFS affects roughly 0.2-1% of adults depending on criteria (US 2021-22: 1.3% self-reported diagnosis; England: 0.16% with a hospital-recorded diagnosis), with women affected 3-4 times as often as men. Replicated

Somewhere between 1 in 100 and 1 in 500 adults have ME/CFS, depending on how it is counted. About three to four in every four patients are women.

Lim 2020 meta-analysis (46 studies): pooled prevalence 0.39%, meta-analytic 0.68% (0.48-0.97); women ~1.5-2x more often in pooled data. Vahratian 2023 (NHIS 2021-22): 1.3% of US adults (women ~1.7% vs men ~0.9%) — self-report of a clinician diagnosis plus current illness. UK: Nacul 2011 primary-care minimum 0.2%; Samms & Ponting 2025 (Hospital Episode Statistics): 100,055 diagnosed in England (0.16%), F:M 3.88:1, peaking ~6:1 in the 40s; white people ~5x more likely diagnosed, suggesting under-diagnosis. DecodeME's cohort is ~83% female. Commonly cited UK total: ~250,000-400,000 (estimate). Long COVID: ONS estimated ~2 million self-reported (~3%) in England/Scotland in 2024 (memory).

Natural history: severity

Roughly a quarter of people with ME/CFS are estimated to be housebound or bedbound, and severity, not diagnosis, was the strongest predictor of reported treatment response. Early

A large minority are too ill to leave home. Severely ill patients are under-represented in almost every trial, so trial results may not apply to them.

The 25% severe figure (often cited from IOM 2015 and UK charity surveys) rests on clinic and survey estimates, not population sampling (memory). Eckey/Xiao 2025: severity shaped treatment ratings more than ME/CFS vs long COVID. RituxME and CycloME excluded the most severe; Fluge's daratumumab study included moderate-to-severe. The original Fluge 2016 serum effect came from severe patients and the 2026 replication used mostly moderate patients.

Natural history: mortality

In 2,147 secondary-care CFS patients in London, all-cause and cancer mortality were not raised, but suicide mortality was about seven times expected (SMR 6.85). Several studies

ME/CFS is not, on average, shown to shorten life in registry data, but suicide risk is markedly higher, and rare deaths from severe illness (for example malnutrition) are documented.

Roberts 2016 (SLaM CRIS, 2007-2013): 17 deaths; all-cause SMR 1.14 (0.65-1.85); cancer SMR 1.39 (0.60-2.73); suicide SMR 6.85 (2.22-15.98). Jason 2006 memorial-list analysis reported younger age at death from heart failure, cancer and suicide, but the sample is self-selected and biased. Deaths from severe ME with nutritional failure (e.g. UK coroner cases) are reported but not systematically counted. Small numbers of deaths limit precision.

Neuro: antidepressants

Fluoxetine did not improve fatigue in CFS in two RCTs. Refuted

An antidepressant (fluoxetine) did not help fatigue in two trials.

Subdomain label is a placeholder; propose new subdomain 'Neuro: antidepressants'.

Neuro: wake-promoting drugs

Solriamfetol produced a fatigue benefit at week 8 but not at the primary 6-week point in a small RCT. Early

A wakefulness drug showed a small late benefit in one small trial.

Key reviews

  • NICE 2021, NG206 ME/CFS guideline: Most thorough independent appraisal of GET/CBT evidence; current UK standard of care.
  • Eckey 2025, PNAS: Patient-reported treatment outcomes in ME/CFS and long COVID: Largest dataset on what patients use and rate; maps treatments to symptom clusters.
  • Wilshire 2018, BMC Psychology: PACE re-analysis: Protocol-based re-analysis of the most influential behavioural trial.
  • Blitshteyn 2025, Front Cell Infect Microbiol: Immunotherapies for POTS and long COVID: Overview of immune treatments and the trials still needed.
  • Proal 2025, Lancet Infect Dis: Targeting the SARS-CoV-2 reservoir: Rationale for antiviral/monoclonal trials after the Paxlovid failures.
  • Cairns & Hotopf 2005, Occup Med: prognosis of CFS: Still the standard systematic review of natural history.

What can be measured

Abnormalities graded replicated, several studies or early, with the test that measures each. 55 can be ordered through clinical services; 87 need a research setting. None is diagnostic on its own: each separates groups on average, with overlap between patients and controls.
