Who has been studied

About a quarter of people with ME/CFS are housebound or bedbound, but research samples are drawn mostly from people well enough to travel to a clinic. Of 400 cohorts behind the atlas, 15 report how many participants were mild, moderate or severe. Across those, 245 severe or very severe participants were assessed by a clinician or recruited for severity, against 2,653 by self-report, most of them in DecodeME, which collected saliva only. Overlapping cohorts are counted once.

Gaps nobody has closed

  • Blood flow, vessels and blood: No blinded, multi-centre replication of the van Campen cerebral blood flow method.
  • Blood flow, vessels and blood: Preload failure prevalence in unselected ME/CFS (iCPET cohorts are pre-selected).
  • Blood flow, vessels and blood: No placebo-controlled trials of volume expansion (saline, desmopressin, fludrocortisone) targeting measured low blood volume in ME/CFS.
  • Blood flow, vessels and blood: Microclots: no standardised blinded multi-lab assay and no in vivo demonstration.
  • Blood flow, vessels and blood: Retinal, sublingual and muscle capillary studies are almost all post-COVID; pre-pandemic ME/CFS is rarely studied.
  • Blood flow, vessels and blood: Severe and very severe patients are almost absent from vascular studies.
  • Blood flow, vessels and blood: Pericyte markers have never been stained in ME/CFS tissue.
  • Blood flow, vessels and blood: Complement activation fragments have not been measured with modern pre-analytics before and after exertion in ME/CFS.
  • Blood flow, vessels and blood: Whether endothelial dysfunction exceeds what activity-matched inactive controls show.
  • Blood flow, vessels and blood: Mechanism of low red-cell mass (marrow output vs destruction vs EPO signalling) is unstudied.
  • Muscle, exertion and energy: No ME/CFS (as opposed to long COVID) study has biopsied muscle before and after induced PEM; the registered Amsterdam study NCT05225688 and Systrom's OMF-funded biopsy study have not yet reported.
  • Muscle, exertion and energy: No independent replication of 2-day CPET from a group outside the Workwell/Ithaca/van Campen network that also reports test-retest variability in sedentary controls; Mancini 2026 null needs explaining.
  • Muscle, exertion and energy: Severe and housebound patients are almost absent from exercise, biopsy and MRS studies; a provocation-free design (e.g. orthostatic or small-muscle stressor) is needed.
  • Muscle, exertion and energy: No study pairs muscle biopsy, 31P-MRS, sodium MRI and invasive CPET in the same people to locate the limiting step in the oxygen cascade.
  • Muscle, exertion and energy: Serum-transfer studies have not used sera drawn during PEM, fractionation (IgG, complement, EVs), or blinded multi-lab sample exchange.
  • Muscle, exertion and energy: No pre-registered multi-site PBMC or muscle respirometry study with adequate controls exists.
  • Muscle, exertion and energy: Lean mass has not been measured alongside the low muscle-protein blood signal.
  • Muscle, exertion and energy: Handgrip fatigability needs external validation against deconditioned, depressed and other-fatigue controls before use as a trial endpoint.
  • Muscle, exertion and energy: Whether the amyloid-containing deposits in long COVID muscle also occur in ME/CFS, and what they are made of, is untested.
  • Nervous system and brain: No adequately powered (n>50 per group), multi-site TSPO-PET study in ME/CFS using a modern tracer and arterial input.
  • Nervous system and brain: No blinded, controlled imaging study of craniocervical anatomy in ME/CFS vs hypermobile and healthy controls, and no controlled trial of CCI surgery or CSF drainage.
  • Nervous system and brain: No skin-biopsy SFN prevalence study in unselected community ME/CFS with matched controls and blinded reading.
  • Nervous system and brain: Brain measures before and after exertion (MRS lactate, fMRI, CSF) in the same people across the 24-72 h PEM window are almost absent; Cook 2017 has not been directly replicated.
  • Nervous system and brain: No CSF study with a large healthy-control group and a pre-registered analysis; most recent CSF cohorts lack controls.
  • Nervous system and brain: No trial of treatments that target orthostatic hypocapnia or cerebral hypoperfusion (capnography-guided breathing, midodrine, compression) measuring function over weeks.
  • Nervous system and brain: Severe and very severe patients are largely excluded from imaging, CSF and sensory studies.
  • Nervous system and brain: Few studies stratify by orthostatic phenotype (POTS vs hypocapnia vs normal HR/BP), which may explain much of the inconsistency in perfusion and imaging results.
  • Nervous system and brain: No effort-based decision study in ME/CFS that calibrates task difficulty to each person's ability.
  • Immune system: No immune measurement during PEM: there is no paired rest / post-exertional-crash study of NK function, T-cell phenotype or autoantibodies, despite PEM being the defining feature.
  • Immune system: No published passive-transfer experiment with ME/CFS IgG (as opposed to long COVID or fibromyalgia IgG), even though that is now a standard, affordable design.
  • Immune system: No independent laboratory has attempted the TRPM3 patch-clamp or the IgG-endothelial-mitochondria assay; both rest entirely on one group each.
  • Immune system: No independent ME/CFS single-cell blood dataset exists outside one research group, so single-cell claims cannot be externally replicated.
  • Immune system: No prospective inception cohort with pre-infection immune samples large enough to test whether a 'primed' immune profile predicts ME/CFS after natural infection (the interferon-alpha model is the only proxy).
  • Immune system: Severe and very severe patients are almost absent from immune studies that require travel; the few in-home studies are small, and the one well-powered serum replication included only 6 severe patients.
  • Immune system: No standardised, multi-site-validated functional immune assay exists at all - NK cytotoxicity failed that test, and nothing has replaced it.
  • Immune system: Why antibody-removal trials fail while antibody-transfer experiments work is unexplained and untested (tissue-bound IgG, long-lived plasma cells, irreversible downstream damage are all untested explanations).
  • Immune system: The daratumumab signal has no randomised test yet, and no second study of its proposed NK-count predictor.
  • Immune system: Mast cell activation in ME/CFS has no objective mediator study with controls and no controlled treatment trial, despite being common and treatable in principle.
  • Immune system: Pre-analytic standardisation is still not routine: after the TGF-beta centrifugation artefact and the SomaScan cell-leak artefact, immune studies in this field still rarely report or adjust for handling variables.
  • Immune system: Tissue immunology is almost untouched: muscle, gut, dorsal root ganglia and brainstem immune cells have barely been examined in ME/CFS, while the long COVID IgG studies point precisely at peripheral sensory ganglia.
  • Infection and viruses: No adequately powered, replicated antiviral RCT in ME/CFS (valganciclovir n=30 in 2013 is still the best evidence).
  • Infection and viruses: No LC antiviral trial has enrolled people selected by biomarker evidence of persistence (antigenemia or tissue RNA).
  • Infection and viruses: No prospective trial of early antiviral treatment during infectious mononucleosis to prevent post-IM ME/CFS.
  • Infection and viruses: Blinded, multi-lab, sequencing-based tissue studies (gut, muscle, brain) for enterovirus, herpesvirus and SARS-CoV-2 in non-COVID ME/CFS are missing.
  • Infection and viruses: Longitudinal viral sampling timed to PEM crashes (plasma EBV/HHV-6 DNA, dUTPase, EA-D) has barely been done.
  • Infection and viruses: DecodeME iciHHV-6 prevalence results are not yet published.
  • Infection and viruses: Independent replication of dUTPase antibody findings outside the originating lab.
  • Infection and viruses: Whether post-COVID, post-EBV, post-Giardia and post-Q-fever ME/CFS share the same downstream biology.
  • Metabolism and blood omics: No multi-omic study in severe or housebound patients with home sampling.
  • Metabolism and blood omics: No dense sampling across a PEM episode (48-72 h and beyond); exertion studies stop at 24 h.
  • Metabolism and blood omics: Very few studies include disease controls (fibromyalgia, depression, MS, deconditioning, long COVID) needed to test specificity.
  • Metabolism and blood omics: Drug exposure, caffeine, fasting status and sample processing time are rarely recorded or adjusted, despite large effects on metabolomics and proteomics.
  • Metabolism and blood omics: No pre-registered, multi-site external validation of any diagnostic classifier (nanoneedle, Raman, cfRNA, BioMapAI).
  • Metabolism and blood omics: Targeted confirmation of low aromatic lactates (with D/L isomers) and high collagen breakdown in fasting, drug-free samples.
  • Metabolism and blood omics: Lean mass not measured alongside the low muscle-protein signal.
  • Metabolism and blood omics: Fresh-cell functional assays (PBMC respiration, NK cytotoxicity, red-cell deformability) are not paired with omics in the same people.
  • Metabolism and blood omics: Only one lab's PBMC single-cell RNA data exist; no independent scRNA cohort.
  • Metabolism and blood omics: Intracellular NAD+/NADH and tryptophan flux have not been measured directly in patient tissue.
  • Hormones: No controlled copeptin study with a standard stimulus (water deprivation, hypertonic saline or arginine) in PEM-defined ME/CFS.
  • Hormones: No study pairs measured blood volume with supine/upright renin, aldosterone and copeptin in the same patients.
  • Hormones: No longitudinal study shows whether low cortisol precedes illness, as it could in post-infection cohorts.
  • Hormones: No modern RCT of any hormone therapy using PEM-based criteria or biomarker selection, for example hydrocortisone only in Synacthen low-responders, or desmopressin with copeptin stratification.
  • Hormones: There are no trials of HRT or menstrual-cycle-linked interventions, and no prospective data on onset around perimenopause.
  • Hormones: Low T3 has not been replicated and never tested as a treatment target.
  • Hormones: Prevalence of true adrenal insufficiency or hypopituitarism among clinic ME/CFS patients is unknown.
  • Gut and microbiome: No prospective study samples stool before or at the triggering infection and follows people into ME/CFS, outside the hospitalised COVID cohort of Liu 2022.
  • Gut and microbiome: No microbiome study of ME/CFS uses disease controls (IBS without ME/CFS, depression, MS, deconditioned controls) to test specificity.
  • Gut and microbiome: No direct intestinal permeability measurement (lactulose/mannitol or similar) in a powered ME/CFS cohort; no study of translocation markers before and after exertion.
  • Gut and microbiome: Results of the 80-person Comeback FMT RCT and the RESTORE-ME virome work are not yet published.
  • Gut and microbiome: No intervention trial selects patients by microbiome signature (e.g. butyrate-producer loss) or tests fibre/polyphenols to raise IPA.
  • Gut and microbiome: Small-intestinal microbiota (which stool does not sample) has not been studied, though it could explain the aromatic-lactate deficit.
  • Gut and microbiome: Within-person longitudinal sampling is needed to test whether microbiome shifts track PEM or relapses.
  • Genetics: DecodeME is still a preprint; peer review and independent locus-level replication in a PEM-phenotyped cohort are needed.
  • Genetics: No GWAS of PEM severity or of illness course; DecodeME questionnaires would allow one.
  • Genetics: No recall-by-genotype studies (e.g. OLFM4 or CA10 risk homozygotes) to link variants to measurable biology.
  • Genetics: Non-European ancestry is almost absent from ME/CFS genetics.
  • Genetics: HLA needs joint imputation or sequencing of cases and controls; KIR findings need replication.
  • Genetics: No independent, blinded replication of TRPM3 functional or SNP findings outside the originating consortium.
  • Genetics: Hypermobility prevalence in population-based ME/CFS with blinded assessment is unknown, and genetic studies of hypermobility-ME/CFS overlap have not been done.
  • Genetics: Rare-variant evidence rests on one deep-learning study of about 1,000 genomes; larger sequencing studies are needed.
  • Treatment trials and natural history: No completed randomised trial of daratumumab, low-dose rapamycin (ME/CFS), aripiprazole or IV saline.
  • Treatment trials and natural history: No trial designed for severe or very severe (bedbound) patients with home-based objective endpoints.
  • Treatment trials and natural history: Almost no trial pre-specifies a biological selection marker; subgroup claims (NK cells, HLA, preload failure, illness duration) are all post hoc.
  • Treatment trials and natural history: Objective outcomes (actigraphy, 2-day CPET, step counts) are rarely primary endpoints, leaving self-report vulnerable to placebo response.
  • Treatment trials and natural history: Several key trials remain unpublished (BLOC/BC007, IA-PACS-CFS, Nacul LDN, RECOVER-AUTONOMIC full results, LIFT).
  • Treatment trials and natural history: Long-term natural history of PEM-defined, adult-onset ME/CFS from onset (including post-COVID) beyond two years.
  • Treatment trials and natural history: Systematic counting of deaths and harms (including rehab-induced deterioration) in ME/CFS.

Glossary

16S rRNA sequencingA cheaper method that identifies bacteria by one marker gene, usually only to genus level.
2-day CPETTwo CPETs 24 hours apart, used to see whether performance drops on the second day.
23Na-MRIAn MRI scan tuned to sodium, used to measure salt content in tissue.
31P-MRSA magnetic resonance scan that measures phosphorus-containing energy molecules (PCr, ATP) and acidity inside working muscle.
AcylcarnitinesFats bound to carnitine for transport into mitochondria; their profile hints at how fat is burned.
AntigenemiaViral protein detectable in the blood.
ATA / barUnits of pressure. 1 ATA is sea-level air pressure; HBOT trials use 2.0-2.4.
AUCHow well a test separates two groups: 0.5 is a coin flip, 1.0 is perfect. Values from the same data used to build a model are usually too optimistic.
AutoantibodyAn antibody that targets the body's own tissue instead of a germ.
Basement membraneA thin protein layer around each capillary; thickening can slow oxygen passing to tissue.
Beighton scoreA 9-point bedside test of joint flexibility; 4 or more (adults often 5) suggests generalised hypermobility.
ButyrateA short-chain fatty acid made by some gut bacteria from fibre. It fuels the cells lining the colon and dampens inflammation.
Cell danger response (CDR)Naviaux's idea that cells under threat switch into a protective, low-energy mode, which in ME/CFS fails to switch off.
Cell-free RNA (cfRNA)RNA fragments floating free in blood plasma, released when cells die or turn over. They give a readout of what many tissues and cells are doing.
Chronotropic incompetenceThe heart rate fails to rise as much as expected during exercise.
ColocalisationA test of whether two genetic signals in the same region share the same causal variant.
ComplementAbout 30 blood proteins in the innate immune system that tag and punch holes in targets; terminal complex (sC5b-9) marks full activation.
CopeptinA stable fragment released with vasopressin. It is easier to measure accurately than vasopressin itself.
Cortisol awakening responseThe normal rise in cortisol in the 30–45 minutes after waking, measured in saliva.
CPETCardiopulmonary exercise test: cycling or treadmill to exhaustion while breathing gases and heart rate are measured.
Craniocervical instability (CCI)Proposed abnormal movement at the skull-neck junction that compresses the brainstem; mainly discussed in hypermobile patients.
Cross-validation vs external validationTesting a model on parts of the same data set vs on a completely separate group of people. Only the second shows real-world performance.
CSFCerebrospinal fluid, which bathes the brain and spinal cord; sampled by lumbar puncture.
CytokineA small signalling protein immune cells use to talk to each other; also what makes you feel ill during an infection.
Cytotoxicity assayA lab test that mixes immune cells with target cells and measures how many targets they kill. It needs fresh blood, which is why results vary between labs.
Dexamethasone suppression testA dose of a strong steroid to see how much the body's own cortisol is switched off (feedback sensitivity).
Diffusion MRI / DTIMRI that tracks water movement along nerve fibres to infer white-matter structure.
DLMODim-light melatonin onset, the evening time melatonin starts rising. It is a marker of body-clock timing.
DNA methylation / epigenetic clockChemical tags on DNA that change gene activity; clocks estimate biological age from them. Results depend heavily on the mix of cell types.
dUTPaseAn enzyme some herpesviruses make when partly reactivated. It can itself stir up inflammation, and antibodies to it are used as a sign of reactivation.
DysbiosisAn imbalance in the gut microbial community compared with healthy people.
EA-D, VCA, EBNAParts of Epstein-Barr virus that antibodies are measured against. EA-D antibodies suggest recent reactivation, VCA IgM suggests a new infection, and EBNA IgG shows an old past infection.
EEfRTEffort-Expenditure for Rewards Task: repeated choices between an easy and a hard button-pressing task for money; used by NIH to define 'effort preference'.
Effect size (SD, d)How far apart the group averages are, in units of normal person-to-person spread. 0.2 is small, 0.5 moderate, 0.8 large.
Enterovirus VP1A coat protein of enteroviruses (the family of polio, coxsackie and echoviruses) used to stain tissue for evidence of infection.
Extracellular vesicles (EVs)Small membrane packages released by cells into blood, carrying proteins and RNA.
Fibrinaloid microclotA clot-like particle of misfolded fibrin seen under a microscope with an amyloid dye; its significance is disputed.
Flow-mediated dilation (FMD)Ultrasound measure of how much an arm artery widens after a cuff is released; a test of the vessel lining.
FMTFaecal microbiota transplantation: transferring stool from a healthy donor to a patient.
Genetic correlation (rg)How much the genetic risk for two traits overlaps (from −1 to 1).
GPCR autoantibody (beta2, M3, M4)Antibodies said to target receptors that nerves use to control blood vessels, heart rate and glands. Commercial tests exist; better methods have not confirmed differences between patients and controls.
GWASGenome-wide association study: compares millions of DNA letters between cases and controls to find regions linked to a disease.
Handgrip fatigabilityThe fall in grip strength across repeated maximal squeezes, and how well it recovers after rest.
Heart-rate variability (HRV)Beat-to-beat variation in heart rhythm; higher high-frequency HRV reflects stronger vagal (calming) nerve activity.
HERVHuman endogenous retroviruses: remnants of ancient viral infections that make up about 8% of our DNA and can sometimes be switched back on.
HLAImmune genes that present fragments of microbes to T cells; often linked to autoimmune disease.
HPA axisThe hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal chain that controls cortisol release.
HypocapniaLow carbon dioxide in the blood, usually from over-breathing; it narrows brain arteries.
Hypocapnia / POSHLow carbon dioxide from over-breathing. POSH means CO2 drops when upright; low CO2 narrows brain blood vessels.
IBSIrritable bowel syndrome, a disorder of gut-brain interaction causing pain and altered bowel habit.
iciHHV-6Inherited chromosomally integrated HHV-6: about 1 in 100 people carry HHV-6's genome in every cell, inherited from a parent. It can make blood HHV-6 tests look falsely 'high'.
iCPETInvasive cardiopulmonary exercise test: a bike test with catheters in the heart's arteries to measure filling pressures and oxygen use.
IDO metabolic trapA model in which the tryptophan-processing enzyme IDO1 gets stuck in a low-activity state because of substrate inhibition and inactive IDO2 variants.
IGF-1A blood marker of growth hormone activity.
IgG subclass deficiencyBeing low in one of the four flavours of the main blood antibody, which can make some infections more frequent.
Immunoadsorption / apheresisFiltering antibodies out of the blood through a column, like a short-term dialysis for antibodies.
Indole-3-propionate (IPA)A protective tryptophan breakdown product made only by certain gut bacteria.
Invasive CPET (iCPET)An exercise test with catheters in the heart and an artery, measuring filling pressures and oxygen use directly.
Locus (loci)A region of the genome. A GWAS 'hit' is a locus, not necessarily a known gene.
Low T3 syndromeLow active thyroid hormone with normal TSH, often seen in chronic illness rather than thyroid disease.
LPS / sCD14 / LBPLPS is a component of bacterial walls. sCD14 and LBP are proteins the body makes in response to it, used as markers of bacteria leaking into blood.
Lytic vs latentHerpesviruses hide quietly in cells for life (latent). When they 'wake up' and make new virus or viral proteins, that is lytic activity, or reactivation.
MAIT cellAn unconventional T cell that patrols mucosal surfaces such as the gut and responds to bacterial metabolites.
Mannose-binding lectin (MBL)A blood protein of the innate immune system that tags microbes for destruction; low levels are a common inherited variation.
Mast cell activationOver-release of histamine and other mediators by tissue immune cells, causing flushing, itching, gut symptoms and sensitivity to foods, smells and drugs.
Mendelian randomisation (MR)Using genetic variants as a natural experiment to test whether a trait (like EBV load) plausibly causes a disease.
MetabolomicsMeasuring hundreds to thousands of small molecules (sugars, fats, amino acids, drug traces) in a sample at once.
MicrobiomeThe community of bacteria, viruses and fungi living in the gut.
MR spectroscopy (MRS)An MRI method that measures chemicals such as lactate, choline and glutathione in brain tissue, and can estimate tissue temperature.
NASA lean test10 minutes leaning with shoulders on a wall while pulse and blood pressure are taken each minute. Cheap, but not validated for formal diagnosis.
Natural killer (NK) cellA white blood cell that kills virus-infected and abnormal cells without needing to be trained first.
NfL / GFAPProteins released when neurons (NfL) or astrocytes (GFAP) are damaged; raised in MS, stroke and dementia.
OCT-AOptical coherence tomography angiography: a non-invasive scan of the tiny vessels in the retina.
Odds ratio per alleleHow much one copy of a variant changes the odds of disease. 1.08 means 8% higher odds, which is a very small effect.
Open-labelEveryone, patients and doctors, knows who got the drug. Prone to placebo and expectation effects.
Orthostatic intolerance (OI)Symptoms (dizziness, fog, fatigue, nausea) that come on when upright and ease when lying down.
Oxford criteriaA 1991 definition of CFS needing only six months of disabling fatigue; it does not require post-exertional malaise and captures broader fatigue states.
OXPHOSOxidative phosphorylation: the mitochondrial process that uses oxygen to make most of the cell's ATP.
Oxygen extractionHow much oxygen tissues remove from the blood that flows through them.
Passive transferInjecting antibodies from a patient into an animal to see whether the symptoms travel with the antibodies. It is the strongest available test of whether antibodies cause something.
PBMCPeripheral blood mononuclear cells: lymphocytes and monocytes isolated from a blood sample.
PDH (pyruvate dehydrogenase)The enzyme that lets the product of sugar breakdown enter mitochondria; if blocked, cells make more lactate.
Peak VO2The most oxygen the body can take up and use per minute at maximal effort; the standard measure of aerobic capacity.
PEM (post-exertional malaise)A worsening of symptoms after physical, mental or emotional effort, often delayed by hours to a day and lasting days or longer.
PericyteA cell wrapped around capillaries that controls their width and helps keep their walls intact.
Placebo responseImprovement in people given a dummy treatment, from expectation, natural fluctuation and enrolling when at a low point.
PlasmalogensMembrane fats made partly in peroxisomes; thought to protect against oxidation.
PolygenicRisk spread across thousands of variants, each with a tiny effect.
PORHPost-occlusive reactive hyperaemia: the skin blood-flow surge after a cuff is released, a test of small vessels.
Post-infective fatigue syndrome (PIFS)A lasting illness of fatigue, pain, poor concentration and unrefreshing sleep that begins after a documented infection.
POTSPostural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome: heart rate rises by 30+ bpm (40+ in teenagers) within 10 minutes of standing, without a big blood-pressure drop, plus symptoms.
Pre-analytic artefactA difference created by how blood was collected, spun or stored rather than by the illness. TGF-beta in ME/CFS turned out to be one.
PreloadHow much blood fills the heart before each beat. Low preload means each beat pumps less.
Proteomics (SomaScan, Olink)Measuring thousands of proteins at once; SomaScan uses DNA-like aptamers, Olink uses antibody pairs. Both can be distorted by how a sample is handled.
Red cell volumeThe total amount of red blood cells in the body, measured with tracer methods, not by a standard blood count.
Renin and aldosteroneKidney and adrenal hormones that make the body hold salt and water when blood volume is low.
SDH (succinate dehydrogenase)A mitochondrial enzyme whose staining is used as a marker of mitochondrial content in muscle sections.
Seahorse assayA plate-based instrument measuring how fast cells use oxygen and make acid, used to estimate mitochondrial function.
SF-36 physical functionA 0-100 questionnaire score of physical ability; healthy adults score around 90-100, many ME/CFS patients 20-50.
Sham-controlledThe comparison group gets a fake version of a procedure (for example blood passed through a filter that removes nothing) so no one knows who got the real thing.
Sham-controlled trialA trial where the comparison group gets a convincing fake procedure, which matters enormously here because 35% improved on placebo in the rituximab trial.
Shotgun metagenomicsSequencing all DNA in stool to identify species and their genes, more detailed than 16S sequencing.
Small-fibre neuropathy (SFN)Loss of the thinnest nerves in skin and organs, which carry pain/temperature and control sweating and blood vessels; diagnosed by counting fibres in a 3 mm skin biopsy (IENFD).
SMRStandardised mortality ratio: observed deaths divided by the number expected for people of the same age and sex.
SNP heritabilityThe share of variation in risk explained by common DNA variants measured on chips.
Switched-memory B cellA B cell that has already met an antigen and changed the class of antibody it makes. Fewer of them, with more untrained (naive) cells, can suggest an unusual pattern of immune stimulation.
Synacthen (ACTH stimulation) testAn injection of synthetic ACTH, with cortisol measured afterwards, to check whether the adrenal glands work.
T-cell exhaustionA worn-out state that killer T cells enter after long periods of fighting an infection or tumour; they stay present but respond poorly.
TRPM3A calcium channel in cell membranes. One group reports it works poorly in patients' NK cells.
TSPO-PETA PET scan using a tracer that binds a protein raised in activated microglia and astrocytes, used as a marker of brain inflammation.
Type I / type II fibresType I fibres are slow, endurance, mitochondria-rich; type II are faster and more reliant on glycolysis.
Vasopressin (ADH)The pituitary hormone that makes the kidneys keep water.
Ventilatory (anaerobic) thresholdThe point during exercise when breathing rises faster than oxygen use because muscles lean more on lactate-producing fuel use.
Virome / phagesThe viruses in the gut, most of which infect bacteria (bacteriophages).
WASF3A protein that, when raised, disrupts the assembly of mitochondrial energy-producing complexes.
XMRVA mouse-derived retrovirus once reported in CFS. The finding was later shown to be lab contamination and retracted.

About this atlas

Compiled by Michael Jelly, with AI agents assisting, from published papers, preprints and re-analyses of public datasets. Grades are a judgement about replication; tell us where one is wrong. Findings used by the working model link to the step they support or contradict. The underlying data is in atlas-data.json.
